One day Henry steals a few minutes in the bank vault to read a magazine. Then noise, ruin, and darkness crash in upon him. When he climbs out, the world he knew is gone. At last no wife, boss, or clock bars his reading, and the tale turns on what such freedom is truly worth.
32675-the-strife-of-the-roses-and-days-o:
W. H. Hamilton Rogers gathers seven papers on the Wars of the Roses and Tudor days in the West of England, published in 1890. Each paper follows a western figure through strife, loyalty, and fall, with poems and illustrations by Roscoe Gibbs.

Subjects include Robert, Lord Willoughby de Broke, William, Lord Bonville for the White Rose, Henry Stafford under the White Boar, and John, Lord Cheney, unhorsed at Bosworth. Later papers treat Stafford of Suthwyke, Sir Thomas Arundell, and Theodoro Paleologus of the imperial line. A closing paper reaches into early Stuart times.
32685-cold-ghost:
Chester S. Geier tells of trappers Hager and Cahill in the far north of Alaska, driving a dogsled through a bitter storm toward a doctor in Moose Gulch. Cahill lies sick on the sled, and their season's furs weigh the dogs down, yet Hager dares not leave the catch unguarded at the cabin.

In the storm Hager sees his chance: slow the sled to a walk, and his partner dies, leaving no mark and no suspicion. Cahill, before dying, promises revenge, and Hager shrugs it off, sure the dead can do no harm. Snow covers his tracks, but the cold itself seems to remember what he did.
32712-cube-root-of-conquest:
Rog Phillips opens with Jan, a strong primitive hunter chasing a deer across rough ground. The deer leaps over a glistening square slab, four feet across, and vanishes as if around a tree. Nearby stand the twisted girders of a ruined bridge and the wreck of a city of tall towers.

Jan's world is thus a world after a fall, and later scenes widen the tale to other universes. There Carl and Hute build a time machine that might dodge dangers such as an atom bomb in their own world. Phillips asks what conquest truly gains, and what its root may be.
32751-the-moralist:
Jack Taylor tells of Xenon, a planet advertised as perfect, in this story from Galaxy Science Fiction of June 1956, illustrated by Weiss. The battleship Terra surveyed Xenon years before, finding point nine Earth gravity and almost twenty percent oxygen, with fertile soil, wide forests, and rivers full of fish.

A cataloguing group from the supply ship Hunter recommends immediate colonization, but warns to be careful who is sent, lest land-grabbers spoil the place. The narrator's friend Lee Spencer brings back the station's report. Then the death of a bird crystallizes rebellion, and the personnel elect themselves a league against Prunella and after-sundown elbow-bending, over a keg of illegal brandy.
32752-to-lhassa-at-last:
Powell Millington tells of a British expedition into Tibet, published by Smith, Elder in 1905. The book opens on leave in the Indian hills, then follows the march through Gnatong, over the Jalap-La, and on to Phari, Kangma, and Gyantse, where fighting and foraging test the column.

Twenty-three chapters weigh supply and transport above all: a maund of rice travels by bullock cart, pack animal, and porter from Siliguri toward Lhassa, past landslips and rivers. The party crosses the Tsangpo, reaches the Lhassa bazaar, signs a treaty, and marches back to India. Millington writes as a soldier who lived the road.
32841-the-laird-o-coul-s-ghost:
This eighteenth-century chap-book tells of the Laird of Coul's ghost, printed in London by Elliot Stock in 1892 from a manuscript in the possession of the Reverend Dr. Gordon of St. Andrew's, Glasgow. The manuscript was discovered in Collector Hamilton of Dalzell's papers, who died in the summer of 1788 at ninety-one.

Hamilton was twenty-five when the story was fledged in 1722, and it first appeared in type in 1750, hawked by flying stationers. The first conference records February 3, 1722, at seven at night, when Mr. Ogilvie, minister at Innerwick, met the Laird Maxwell of Coul on the burial road after death. Their dialogues weigh truth among the dead, good angels, and wicked spirits who fare ill when their reports prove false.
32891-phantom-of-the-forest:
Lee Francis's story, from Amazing Stories in November 1948, turns the yearly deer hunt back on the hunters. Earl Robinson drives through thick snow toward a hunting camp with companions, guns, and gear packed around them, while the storm makes every mile feel longer. The party has come for sport, confident in its rifles and numbers.

Then the forest answers in a way none of them expects, and the hunt takes on a stranger, more fearful shape. Francis uses the winter woods, the ice, and the waiting dark to build a tale of revenge from the wild side of the chase. It is a short pulp story with a plain moral at its core: those who kill for fun may one day meet something that hunts back.
32971-the-eagle-s-nest:
S. E. Cartwright's Eagle's Nest is a boys' adventure built around a schoolroom, a laburnum tree, and a nest reached by rope-ladder. It was published by Blackie and Son in 1899 and illustrated by William Rainey. Its chapters follow a wasp in the schoolroom, the boy who mounted the ladder, a victim, Jack and Jill, an early chase. An alarms jump, and a trespasser, before turning to little gardens, a new ladder, a brown bag, and keeping shop.

The frontispiece shows Lewis whispering to lie still as someone comes their way, and that spirit of hiding, watching, and small daring runs through the book. Cartwright, author of Tommy the Adventurous, writes for boys who liked outdoor mischief with a code of honor behind it. The story moves from school to garden to empty house, and its pleasures are those of a summer holiday spent mostly out of grown-up sight.
3323-the-ward-of-king-canute-a-romance-o:
Ottilie A Liljencrantz sets this romance in the Danish conquest of England. The fall of the house of Frode opens it, with Randalin, Frode's daughter, at the center. Where war-dogs kennel, when royal blood is young blood, and before the king follow, leading to the training of Fridtjof the page and the game of swords. Taken captive and the young lord of Ivarsdale carry the tale on.

King Canute himself presides over the story's world: a Danish king ruling an English land, with wards, hostages, and loyalties to settle. Liljencrantz writes the eleventh century as adventure, with courts, camps, and swordplay. Liljencrantz's eleventh century runs on courts, camps, and swordplay, with a page growing toward lordship under a conqueror's eye.
33615-three-young-ranchmen-or-daring-adv:
Captain Ralph Bonehill sends three young ranchmen into a string of western dangers in this 1901 boys' adventure. Thirty chapters follow Allen and his companions from an unpleasant discovery through trails, sinkholes, mountain caves, a snake's nest, a cyclone, and encounters in the dark. A captain's setback, a visitor at the ranch, and a letter add intrigue to the outdoor action.

The boys move against Captain Grady, shoot a grizzly bear, fight a wolverine, survive a buffalo stampede, and recover someone long lost. Bonehill writes in the brisk, episodic style of turn-of-the-century boys' books, where courage and loyalty settle every crisis. Young readers who enjoy ranch life, wild animals, and narrow escapes will find plenty of incident here.
33683-magnhild-dust:
Björnstjerne Björnson pairs two works in this translated volume, Magnhild and Dust, translated from the Norse by Rasmus B. Anderson. Magnhild was planned in the summer of 1873 while Anderson traveled across Norway with Björnson. It was written the following winter in Rome, and published in 1877 in Copenhagen and in German translation at the same time. Its story is set in Lærdalen, with Skarlie's home at Lærdalsören near the Sognefjord.

Anderson calls Magnhild a new departure and a new epoch in Björnson's fiction. It champions a woman united with a man like Skarlie, even though Björnson himself counted it among his less finished works. Dust completes the volume. Together the stories show a major Norwegian writer turning from peasant idylls toward modern questions of marriage, conscience, and women's rights.
33871-old-friends-are-the-best:
Jack Sharkey wrote this short science tale, first printed in Amazing Stories in March 1960. Its strange hero is a plant-like being that draws dissolved silicates from soil and stores them in a thousand green pods. It has no sense of time, and its faint pulse beats once each hundred years, with fifty years to contract and fifty to ease.

Sharkey tells the tale from the plant's slow point of view, against the rush of human life. The story turns on patience, endurance, and friendship across vast gulfs of time. It is a gentle, odd little tale, told with a light touch.
33932-company-b-307th-infantry-its-histo:
Julius Klausner, Jr., compiled this history of Company B, 307th Infantry, published in 1920. The company served from September 1917 to May 1919, and its battle honors run from Upton through Flanders, Vosges, Lorraine, Vesle, and Argonne, to home. A history, an honor roll, and a company roster fill the volume.

The opening pages honor companions who trained and fought with the men but did not return, urging the living to justify their sacrifice. The book preserves one infantry company's Great War in names, places, and dates. It serves families, researchers, and regimental historians.
33950-brother-francis-or-less-than-the-l:
Brigadier Eileen Douglas wrote this life of Francis of Assisi, first in the Salvation Army's Red-Hot Library, published in London, Melbourne, New York, and Toronto. Brother Francis, or Less than the Least, tells how Francis turned from worldly life to a life of poverty, preaching, and service. Early companions such as Bernard di Quintavelle appear in the narrative.

Douglas writes for Salvation Army readers, in plain, earnest prose that stresses humility and love of neighbor. The book presents Francis as a model of the least becoming great through service. It remains a warm, accessible life of the saint.
34156-the-undying-past:
Hermann Sudermann wrote this novel, translated by Beatrice Marshall and published in London and New York in 1906 by John Lane, the Bodley Head. The book opens at midday in a provincial railway station square. An old white mare nods between the shafts of a yellow mailcart, and hotel omnibuses clatter down a dusty boulevard toward stucco towers.

A station-master in a red cap, a barmaid wiping a glass case of cheese, and postmen wheeling letter-bags fill the scene as a train departs. Sudermann writes of a past that will not stay buried, in a small town's daily life. The novel offers a German tale of memory and return.
34371-pliocene-and-pleistocene-records-o:
Pliocene and Pleistocene Records of Fossil Turtles from Western Kansas and Oklahoma, by Edwin Galbreath, appeared in August 1948 in the University of Kansas museum series. The paper runs from page 281 to 284. Galbreath works from fragments in the university's fossil collection, gathered in the main while other fossils were being dug or saved.

Such fragments, he notes, can often be named by genus, and each name adds a new record of where and when a living kind once ranged. One mud turtle lot, number 7729, holds bits of shell from Edson Quarry in Sherman County, of middle Pliocene age. Another, from Nye Sink in Meade County, is Pleistocene in age. Short notes, deep time.
34410-the-treasure-of-the-isle-of-mist:
The Treasure of the Isle of Mist is a fairy tale by Tarn, published by Putnam at New York and London in 1920. The author calls the book a fairy tale for his daughter. The contents list eight chapters, from the gift of the search to the finding of the treasure. The scene is a sea loch in the Isle of Mist, in Scotland.

A scholar called the Student lives in a gray house with his daughter Fiona. Fiona is fifteen, long legged, and warm hearted, with a laugh for threats of mainland school. Meals at the house come by chance, sometimes dinner and sometimes sunset and salt herrings. An old hawker crossing the field opens the adventure. His white hair and bright eyes hide more than a pack of buttons. Chapters promise a haunted cave, a vanished urchin, and Fiona in the fairy world.
3457-the-man-of-the-forest:
Zane Grey sets this western in the White Mountains, where a lone hunter moves under great fir and spruce trees at sunset. Old Baldy, the highest peak, stands bare and gold in the last light, and the forest seems to swallow the man as he glides through it. He is friendly with an Indian hunter, but he hates the sound of white men's horses in those fastnesses.

The trouble comes from a gang of bad men hidden in the woods, and the novel follows pursuit, ambush, and rescue among the peaks. Grey writes the landscape in rich color and keeps the action moving. Readers who like classic westerns will find his familiar mix: a strong silent hero, a wild country, and a fight between lawless greed and solitary honor.
34764-quisisana-or-rest-at-last:
Spielhagen wrote a German novel of a sick man in search of rest. Goldschmidt made the sole English form the author passed. The book came out in New York in 1885. Its name, Quisisana, is the name of a cure place. Konski, a valet, wakes his chief with care at the start.

The chief lay on his left side once more, to his harm. He drank too much wine at the meal, the valet hints. Travel chests are oped and their goods set in drawers. Ill health and wealth in an ill match drive the tale. Rest at last is the hope its sub-title holds out. Grave prose suits a grave search for ease.
34824-roger-davis-loyalist:
Frank Baird wrote a tale of a loyalist boy in the war for America. Four plates aid the book from a Toronto house. Roger Davis is the boy whose king side marks the tale. Duncan Hale, a school chief, brings the first war news home. Roger's mother meets him half way from the gate in that scene.

The break out, life among foes, and a jail cell fill the front. Trial and break, then the great ask of king or folk, come next. The die is cast, and a ship for Nova Scotia ends that arc. Home work in the true north and a pact fill the rest. A chief's peril and a prize close the tale. Young past fans get Canada's birth.
35003-the-house-in-the-mist:
The House in the Mist, by Anna Katharine Green, came out in 1905. Bobbs-Merrill published the tales at Indianapolis. Green had written The Amethyst Box and The Filigree Ball. A series page calls this a tale of unexpected fortunes. The title story fills four chapters. An Open Door is the first of them. A second tale, The Ruby and the Caldron, stands behind it. Chapter one opens on a night to drive any man indoors. Mist wraps hill and valley in raw darkness. The narrator, a young fortune seeker, walks the road. A light shimmers through the murk at his right. He makes for the shelter it promises.

The house stands long and low, doors and windows open to the mist. One lit casement shows candles on a mahogany table. The seeming emptiness makes him pause.
35355-the-childrens-story-of-the-war-vol:
Sir Edward Parrott wrote this tale of the war for the young, in the third book of a set of ten. He held chairs of letters and wrote books on Britain past the sea and on the stage of English letters. This book runs from the first fight at Ypres to the end of the year 1914. It was printed in 1916, while the war still raged. A cut at its front shows a bold deed of the air of those first months.

Three planes of Britain flew from France across the hills into Germany, a span of 250 miles. They cast their bombs on the works at Friedrichshafen where the great air ships were made, by the shore of Lake Constance. Great harm was done, and all the men of the air but one came home safe.
35415-jewish-immigration-to-the-united-s:
Jewish Immigration to the United States studies the movement of Jews from 1881 to 1910. Samuel Joseph wrote the study. It appeared in 1914 in a Columbia University series. The series covers history, economics, and public law. Joseph dedicated the work to his father and mother.

The first chapter sets out the character of the immigration. It describes the Jews of Eastern Europe and their distribution. A second chapter surveys their homelands in depth. Russia receives the longest treatment. It covers serfdom's end and the reaction under Alexander the Third. Romania and Austria-Hungary follow. A third chapter treats the Jews' economic and social position. The study builds toward the migration itself.
35419-wood-and-forest:
Wood and Forest, a textbook by William Noyes, was copyrighted in 1912 and issued in a fifth edition in 1921 by the Manual Arts Press of Peoria, Illinois. Noyes taught industrial arts at Teachers College, Columbia University. Experts from the Forest Service and Teachers College revised parts of it. The book grew out of his lectures there.

Early chapters cover the structure and properties of wood. A key chapter names and maps the chief species. Later parts treat the working and use of timber. Forest Service photographs, maps, and a key for naming woods support the text. The book served students of handwork in wood and of forestry alike.
35439-canada-west:
Canada West is a government pamphlet issued at Ottawa in 1914 by direction of the minister of the interior. Its cover promises one hundred and sixty acre farms in western Canada, free. The Dominion needed settlers for Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta, and print was its recruiter.

The pamphlet explains the land regulations in plain order. Townships are surveyed six miles square and cut into homestead blocks. A settler who lives on his claim and makes the required improvements earns a crown deed in time. Plans of a township show the grid that still marks the prairie map. Such pamphlets crossed the Atlantic by the bale, and whole districts of the west filled with the families they persuaded.
3547-see-america-first:
Orville Hiestand, working with Charles Herr, offers wayside sketches of American scenery in this outdoor book. The dedication thanks the Herr family, whose love of the great out of doors made the sketches possible. The introduction quotes Emerson on morning light, cloud bars like golden fishes, and nature as medicine for bodies cramped by work.

Hiestand urges readers to see America first, rather than crossing the sea for famous views. His sketches follow hilltops at sunrise, woods, and open horizons, arguing that a day outdoors restores tone to mind and body. The book suits travelers, nature lovers, and readers who enjoy early twentieth century praise for the American landscape.
35562-a-rational-theology-as-taught-by-t:
A Rational Theology, by John Widtsoe, was published in 1915 for the use of the Melchizedek Priesthood. The General Priesthood Committee issued the course of lessons. Its full title ties the teaching to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Fundamentals and the pre-existent state open the contents.

The meaning of theology is the subject of the first chapter. Man in the universe, a man’s religion, and the gospel are treated there. How knowledge is gained fills the second chapter of the course. The senses, a sixth sense, and transmitted knowledge are weighed in it. The use of reason stands as the foundation of rational theology there. Widtsoe, a scientist and apostle, argues that faith and reason agree.
35652-rick-dale-a-story-of-the-northwest:
Kirk Munroe wrote Rick Dale, a story of the Northwest Coast, for Harper's boys' list, with pictures by Rogers. The hero is Alaric Todd, called Allie against his will, a rich boy who runs away to sea. The contents take him aboard the Empress, where he loses his berth, then under Captain Duff of the sloop Fancy. Puget Sound smugglers, a revenue cutter, and capture fill the early chapters.

A little Indigenous boy saves Alaric's life, and he lives for a time in Skookum John's camp. The tale then climbs: Bonny Brooks commands the scene, and the party makes for Mount Rainier, which the contents promise will be placed underfoot. A blast from the crater rim, a song that saves a life, and a logging camp close the run. Munroe knew the wild coasts he wrote, and boys got real seamanship and woodcraft inside the adventure.
35883-war-inconsistent-with-the-religion:
War Inconsistent with the Religion of Jesus Christ is a peace tract by David Low Dodge, published at Boston by Ginn and Company in 1905 for the International Union. Edwin Mead wrote the opening words. The contents lay out the case in order: war is inhuman, war is unwise, and more heads follow. A portrait of Dodge stands at the front.

Under the first head, Dodge argues that war hardens the heart and dulls tender feeling. It wrongs God's animal creation, presses on the poor, and spreads terror and distress. It brings fatigue, famine, and maimed bodies, kills the young, and fills the land with widows and orphans. Mead's praise notes that Dodge wrote the first American pamphlets aimed straight at the war system, and founded the first peace society.
36066-hermann-stieffel-soldier-artist-of:
Edgar M Howell, curator of military history at the United States National Museum, wrote a study of Hermann Stieffel as paper twelve in a museum series. Stieffel was a German born private in the United States Infantry for twenty four years. He served with Company K of the Fifth Infantry from 1858 to 1882. While in Indian country in the 1860s and 1870s he painted water colors.

Howell says Stieffel was untutored and could never be called talented. Yet his canny eye for the colorful and his minute attention to detail give value. His pictures form records of the West during the Indian wars. Howell contrasts him with famed artists like Catlin and Remington, none of them soldiers.
36162-living-for-the-best:
Living for the Best is a devotional book by James McClure, published by Revell in 1903. McClure had written A Mighty Means of Usefulness and Possibilities before this volume. A preface quotes a great newspaper publisher on how to enforce truth on readers. Truth should always be vivified through illustration and story, that editor told him.

Everyday intelligence rejoices to have truth put before it in living form, he adds. McClure follows that rule with short chapters built on anecdote and example. The book speaks to ordinary Christians aiming at a useful, earnest daily life. Revell list of practical devotion found a steady buyer in such titles.
36264-a-harmony-of-the-gospels-for-stude:
A T Robertson built a harmony of the Gospels for students of the life of Christ. Harper and Brothers held the rights in 1922 in New York and London. Robertson taught New Testament study at a seminary in Louisville, Kentucky. The work rests on the Broadus Harmony in the Revised Version.

The four Gospels are laid side by side in one clear order of events. Tables help readers find any passage fast, and an outline maps the whole. Notes at the back treat hard points such as the two family lines of Christ. Lists of parables, miracles, and old quotes close a rich study aid.
36304-rambles-of-a-naturalist:
John Godman's Rambles of a Naturalist, with a memoir of the author, was published at Philadelphia in 1859 by the Association of Friends for the Diffusion of Religious and Useful Knowledge. The memoir is built from the brief lives and eulogies printed shortly after Godman's early death. A sketch from the Tract Association of Friends supplies much of it.

Godman, a Baltimore physician, wrote the first great American work on the mammals of North America. His rambles take readers into fields and woods with a young man's eager eye. Snakes, birds, and quadrupeds fill the essays, written before illness cut his career short at thirty six. The Friends republished him as science in a moral frame. The rambles remain fresh for their close looking. Godman is a founding figure of American natural history.
36599-golden-face-a-tale-of-the-wild-wes:
Bertram Mitford wrote Golden Face, a tale of the wild west issued by Trischler and Company in London. The copy shown dates to eighteen hundred ninety two. Mitford warns at the start that his book is a tale, not a history. He touches real strife as light as he can.

Two men sit in a winter log cabin as a storm howls past. One swears he hears a war whoop in the wind. Both reach for their Winchester rifles at once. Fire light glints on the guns in the gloom. The scout holds that scalp work goes on down on the plain. His mate heard no such sound at all. Cold, fear, and old frontier hate spark the tale from its first page.
3660-out-of-the-triangle-a-story-of-the-:
Mary Bamford writes a collection of stories from far places, opening in Alexandria, Egypt. A voice rings through a street, crying that sinners should keep their eyes to the ground, while Heraklas walks by Lake Mareotis, mourning his brother Timokles lost in the desert. Other stories in the book include The Squash of the Esvidos, Comale's Revenge, At the Panaderia, Miss Stratton's Paper, and The Victory of Quang Po.

Bamford writes for young readers, with clear morals and vivid foreign settings, from Egyptian lakes to Chinese villages and Arctic igloos. Her tales mix adventure with lessons in honesty, courage, and kindness. The book suits families who enjoy old fashioned story collections that travel the world in a single volume.
36617-the-ballad-of-the-quest:
Virna Sheard, a Canadian poet, issued The Ballad of the Quest in Toronto in 1922 and gave the book to the memory of her mother. The long title poem tells of a man who vows to shut his house door and rove the world in search of his lost faith and soul. He owns he traded truth for a lie in the market place of life.

He hopes to earn his bread on out bound ships, sleep under thorn hedges, and dine on berries red as wine. Short lyrics fill the rest of the book, on poppies, winds, dreams, ships, and the crosses of war. Songs for April, June, and October give the set a calm, fond close.
36678-the-puddleford-papers-or-humors-of:
The Puddleford Papers, or Humors of the West, is a comic story collection by H H Riley, published at Boston in eighteen seventy five. Original illustrations appear in the book, as the title page states. A frontispiece shows characters named Ike Turtle and Aunt Graves in a marriage joke. Copyright was entered the year before publication, its page records.

Puddleford is a western town of Riley's invention, and its folk supply the humour. Dialect, courtship, brag, and small town pride drive the sketches in the southwestern humour line. Such papers let eastern readers laugh at frontier types from a safe distance. Riley's preface opens with a joke on authors in general.
36726-america-first:
America First is a patriotic novel by Frances Nimmo Greene, published by Scribner's in New York in 1918. Thulstrup drew its pictures. The book holds three tales: Called to the Colors, Under the Flag, and America First. The frontispiece shows a tenderfoot refusing a dare, then going for his country instead.

Another picture cries that Rudolph is under the flag and cannot be touched. A third shows a handshake for an American hero named Riego Yañez. Written in the last year of the First World War, the tales plead that immigrant and native alike owe one loyalty. Greene aimed the book at young readers of a nation at war.
37137-a-hind-let-loose-or-an-historical-:
Alexander Shiels, a minister at St Andrews, wrote this history of the Church of Scotland's testimonies, printed at Glasgow in 1797. The title comes from Genesis: a hind let loose. Shiels defends the persecuted remnant of Presbyterians against popish, prelatical, and malignant enemies.

The book asks the hard questions of the killing times. May a man hear the curates? May he own the present tyranny, or take ensnaring oaths and bonds? May congregations meet in the fields, and may the oppressed resist violence with arms? Shiels clears each controversy in some measure, from Scripture and the church's past. The work is a monument of Covenanter thought, fierce and learned.
37168-norston-s-rest:
Norston's Rest is a novel by Ann Stephens, published at Philadelphia in 1877. Peterson and Brothers issued it from their Chestnut Street house. Stephens had written some two dozen popular novels before it. Fashion and Famine and The Old Homestead stand among her earlier titles. A set of verses on love's free choice fronts the book. Why the breeze kisses violets over magnolias, the poem asks.

Love, it answers, takes a pebble from the spring as often as a gem. His reasons are as vague as winds that blow. The publisher's list shows each work complete in one volume. Stephens belonged to the bestselling American storytellers of her century. Her fiction mixed domestic feeling with high melodrama. Norston's Rest came late in a long and successful career.
37244-kitty-s-conquest:
Charles King tells a soldier's courtship in Kitty's Conquest, from J B Lippincott Company of Philadelphia in 1890, copyrighted in 1884. King had written The Colonel's Daughter. A short preface confesses that the incidents occurred some twelve years before, and the story was mainly written then.

The tale opens just after Christmas, with the narrator leaving his cosy New Orleans home on a business trip through the counties where Tennessee meets northern Mississippi and Alabama. On the slow train toward Iuka he marks his fellow passengers, six in all, and one young lady, girlish and pretty, worth a second glance. His glances repeat themselves.
37261-the-bigamist:
Bigamist is a novel by Mills Young, printed by John Lane in nineteen sixteen. The tale opens in a handsome room lit by shaded electric lamps. A man sits low in a chair, legs stretched out, brow on his hand. For a full half hour he has not stirred from that pose of thought.

A tall, slender woman with golden hair stands at the open window. Five years of happy married life lie behind her in that house. A tiny child of four sleeps in the nursery overhead that night. She had near forgotten the man presence in her own sweet reverie. The strange quiet rouses her like a sudden sound in the room.
37262-the-shadow-of-the-past:
The Shadow of the Past is a novel by Mills Young, in an edition dated 1919. Its first chapter opens on a beach at Three Anchor Bay, under a wall that splits the sand from the road above. Two men sit playing cards in the blaze of morning sun. The heat beats on their bare heads and on the hot sand sloping to a rocky shore.

Long blue waves roll in slowly from the Atlantic beyond them. The writer likens the waves to a line of hooded serpents, rearing with slow grace and folding over. Spray streams from their crests like the tail of a comet. Far out the sea glitters, save where it meets the sky in mirror calm. That lush, heavy light sets the scene before the past of the title casts its shadow.
3727-maurice-guest:
Henry Handel Richardson sets this long novel among the music students of Leipzig in the 1890s. Maurice Guest, a young man from abroad, stands before the new Gewandhaus as crowds pour out of a rehearsal, and soon he is caught in a love affair that unmakes him. He adores Louise, a gifted and restless fellow student, who in turn loves the brilliant violinist Schilsky and waits in vain for his letters.

Practice rooms, concerts, boarding houses, and long walks frame a study of obsession, as Maurice watches Louise pine, excuse, and hope against all sense. Richardson writes with close care for mood and music, and the novel grows darker as pride and longing wear the hero down. Readers who like serious fiction about art and passion will find a demanding book that earns its length.
37696-arguments-of-celsus-porphyry-and-t:
Thomas Taylor collected the Arguments of Celsus, Porphyry, and the Emperor Julian against the Christians, printed in 1830. The volume adds extracts from Diodorus Siculus, Josephus, and Tacitus relating to the Jews. An appendix gives the oration of Libanius in defence of the heathen temples, in Lardner's translation, and extracts from Bingham's Antiquities of the Christian Church.

The introduction quotes a letter of Warburton from 1749. Warburton had wished for a hand able to gather all the fragments of Porphyry, Celsus, Hierocles, and Julian, with a just comment, as a defy to infidelity. Taylor says he has partly done the gathering, though as no divine he will not confute Celsus. He confines his notes to explaining the meaning, with parallel passages from other ancient authors.
37707-a-night-on-the-borders-of-the-blac:
A Night on the Borders of the Black Forest is a tale set by Amelia Edwards. A Stokes house of New York brought it out in eighteen ninety. Edwards wrote Barbara History and Debenham Vow in past years. Six more tales stand with the name tale in the scheme at front. Salome tale, in the priest room, and a palazzo dread fill that list.

The four fifteen fast train, Sister Johanna tale, and All Saints Eve close it. The name tale is a slice of the tale voice own young life at start. Young, sound, gay, and flush with a snug new wealth, he sets out then. Time is three of a hot, clear September day in that scene set. A dust road in Wurtemberg, twelve miles north of Heilbronn, frames it.
37714-birket-foster-r-w-s-sixteen-exampl:
Birket Foster presents sixteen examples in colour of the work of the English watercolour painter Birket Foster. H M Cundall wrote the introduction. A and C Black of London published the volume in 1910, in their British Artists series beside George Morland, John Pettie, and Kate Greenaway.

The plates open with Gleaners, and each names the owner of the original painting. Foster, a member of the Royal Watercolour Society, was loved for English rural scenes. Harvest fields, village lanes, and children gleaning fill his typical subjects. Sixteen colour plates made such work available to buyers who could never own the originals. The series served the Edwardian art book trade: sound short criticism, good colour printing, and a painter praised for the charm of the English countryside.
37732-the-emigrant-s-lost-son-or-life-al:
An unnamed author tells this tale, edited by George Henry Wall in an edition printed at London in 1860 with pictures by Corbould. The frontispiece shows Frank Osborne alarmed at finding a bow and quiver hanging in the forest. The first chapter tells why the family left England and reached the forest. In the second, the boy is lost in the forest and describes his plight.

He builds himself a hut, meets a bear, hears a strange echo, and falls ill with fever. A great convulsion of nature nearly kills him before Indians rescue him at the last moment. Later he reaches his father's farm at Brompton. The tale is a boy's Robinson Crusoe set in the emigrant woods of North America.
37734-some-jewish-witnesses-for-christ:
The Reverend Bernstein gathered lives of Hebrew Christians in Some Jewish Witnesses for Christ, printed in London in 1909 at the Operative Jewish Converts' Institution. The book grew far past its first plan, from a small pamphlet to a large volume, and Bernstein says it could have grown more, so many witnesses there were. He rushed it out for the centenary year of the London Society for Promoting Christianity amongst the Jews.

The preface makes the book's twin aim clear. Converts set out the arguments that convinced them Jesus is the Messiah, hoping to lead others the same way. But their writing ranged far past argument, into almost every field of learning, and Bernstein delights in showing that range. The lives form a companion to the Society's own history, showing the human results of a century of mission work.
37782-life-in-an-indian-outpost:
Life in an Indian Outpost is a soldier's memoir by Major Gordon Casserly of the Indian Army, author of The Land of the Boxers. Werner Laurie published it at London, with pictures. The first chapter, A Frontier Post, opens with the writer's first view of the Himalayas and a ride across India in a troop train.

The chapter heads sketch the march: a scattered regiment, an elephant-haunted railway, and the peak of Kinchinjunga. The great Terai jungle, Rajabhatkawa in the days of Warren Hastings, and hillmen and roving Chinese follow. The party reaches Buxa Road and marches through forest to Buxa Duar, a lonely station. The labors of an Indian Army officer fill the lonely days that follow.
37954-maid-of-the-mist:
John Oxenham wrote Maid of the Mist, a tale told in five short books. Hodder and Stoughton issued the book in London, printed in nineteen hundred seventeen. Oxenham gave it to Frederick Caesar de Sumichrast of Harvard. A map of Sable Island fronts the whole seafaring tale.

For a Woman’s Sake, No Man’s Land, and Bone of Contention head its parts. Love in a Mist and Garden of Eden close the five part arc. A fox hunt at full stretch opens the tale in high style. The Old Roman Road, a sunk trench of a track, waits at its end. More than one horse has died on that leap in past seasons. The wily fox makes for it when pressed, and beats the hounds there. Two bold riders dare the leap as the field sits and fears. Huntsman Job and his son watch with held breath and curses.
38013-animals-of-the-past:
Animals of the Past is a palaeontology book by Frederic Lucas, curator at the United States National Museum. McClure, Phillips of New York printed it in 1901 in a series called Science for Everybody. A drawing by Charles Knight of the Phororhacos, a Patagonian giant bird of the Miocene, serves as frontispiece. Knight's restorations are a noted feature of the work.

The contents open with fossils and how they are formed. Casts and impressions, the enemies of bones, and the rarity of fossils get their explanations. Dinosaurs take the long middle: their remains, their nearest relatives, their brains, and their relation to birds. A parallel between dinosaurs and marsupials is drawn along the way. Lucas writes for the plain reader, and his book carried museum science into the home at the height of the dinosaur discoveries.
38019-an-oregon-girl-a-tale-of-american-:
An Oregon Girl, a tale of American life in the new west, is a novel in dramatic form by Alfred Ernest Rice. The title page dates it 1914 and sets the scenes in Portland, Oregon, and environs. A personae list introduces the cast before the story. John Thorpe directs an investment company. His sister Virginia is the Oregon girl of the title. Sam Harris is named the hero.

The introductory chapter exposes the founding fraud. Philip Rutley and Jack Shore promoted the Securities Investment Association on Third street. Social standing won them two wealthy directors as window dressing. When the business failed, the promoters manipulated bond transactions. The directors had to make good the losses. Prosecution was suspended when the offenders promised to leave the city at once. Three years later one of them broods in a Bay City flat over his past career.
38032-game-birds-and-game-fishes-of-the-:
Game Birds and Game Fishes of the Pacific Coast is a field guide for sportsmen who hunt and fish on the western shore. The bird half opens with the calls of quail, from the whistle of the bobwhite to the sharp cry of the valley quail. Rather than give a full scientific system, the book states just enough of it to order the kinds. Orders, families, and genera frame the accounts that follow.

Six orders of birds hold all the game kinds of North America, the writer notes. Chicken like birds come first, with quail, grouse, turkeys, and pheasants, then the ducks, geese, and swans. Fresh water ducks and salt water ducks get their own groups. For each kind the reader can expect habits, haunts, and the marks that tell it from its kin. The fish half serves the angler in the same plain, useful way.
38036-electricity-for-the-4-h-scientist:
The Idaho Agricultural Extension Service issued this bulletin in June 1962 as a guide for the 4-H Electric project. It is bulletin 396 of the University of Idaho College of Agriculture. The cover names its three themes: safety, uses, and economy.

The project is built on credit points. Each lesson carries points, and a member's yearly total must match a table set by age and by years in the project. An eleven-year-old needs thirteen points the first year; a fourteen-year-old needs seventeen. The book tells members to start with the first lesson and work through to the back. It is a plain record of how farm youth once learned the new power in their homes.
38066-the-adventures-of-a-grain-of-dust:
The Adventures of a Grain of Dust, by Hallam Hawksworth, was published by Scribner in 1922 as a companion to his Strange Adventures of a Pebble. The grain itself tells the story. It opens by boasting, modestly, that it may be one of the greatest travelers that ever was.

The grain explains how waves that smash cliffs spare the sand, cushioning each particle in water. It muses on the age of a hickory-nut pebble, and on the still older heart of a grain of dust. Hawksworth turns geology into autobiography for young readers, wandering through Nature's wonderlands in the first person. The method makes deep time friendly, and the book remains a charming piece of early nature writing for children.
38069-northwest:
Northwest is a novel by Harold Bindloss, printed at New York in 1922 and published in England under the title The Mountaineers. Bindloss also wrote The Man from the Wilds and The Lure of the North. The first chapter is called Jimmy Signs a Note. A small room at a Canadian hotel is hot and smells of cigar smoke and liquor.

Stannard puts down his cards, shrugs, and opens the window. Deering smiles and pulls a pile of paper money across the table. The chapters move to Kelshope Ranch, a cayuse pony, and Deering owning a debt. An insurable interest, a game reserve, and a deserted homestead follow. A shot in the dark and Trooper Simpson's prisoners raise the stakes. Jimmy holds fast and Stannard fronts a crisis before the gully and the camp-fire. Bindloss sets his tale of notes, debts, and ranches in the Canadian northwest he knew well.
38266-the-memoirs-of-count-carlo-gozzi-v:
John Addington Symonds translated The Memoirs of Count Carlo Gozzi into English, and volume one appeared in eighteen ninety. Scribner and Welford issued it in New York in a small, numbered run. Only five hundred twenty copies were printed for England, and two hundred sixty for America. Portraits and etchings add to its splendour.

Symonds adds essays of his own on stage comedy done without a script. He writes on Gozzi's life, on his dramatic fables, and on the painter Pietro Longhi. Hand-coloured plates show the stock masks of the Italian stage. Gozzi, a Venetian count, fought for the old comic forms against new tastes. His memoirs mix stage lore with a sharp self-portrait.
38299-under-canvas-or-the-hunt-for-the-c:
Captain Alan Douglas, a scout-master, wrote Under Canvas, or The Hunt for the Cartaret Ghost, in his Hickory Ridge Boy Scouts series. The series list at the front sums up its companion books, in which scouts camp, track, and clear up mysteries. One earlier tale has a boy from the north-west woods amaze all with his camp craft.

In this book, the hunt for a ghost takes the patrol under canvas, where their scout skills meet a spooky task. Douglas writes clean, wholesome adventure for boys, full of woodcraft and pluck. The series sold scouting itself as much as story: learn the skills, keep your head, and work as a patrol, and no ghost will scare you off.
38377-the-character-of-a-priest:
Character of a Priest is a radical pamphlet by a writer signing as Philanthropos, printed in 1821. Carlile published it in London from Fleet Street at the price of twopence. It opens with a doctrine of nature and of the equality of men in its first lines. Nature, pregnant with equality, justice, and generosity, has given all men the same organisation, it says.

She has neither created higher nor lower, superior nor inferior, master nor slave, the pamphlet argues. Inequality would imply monopoly, and monopoly partiality, and partiality divine injustice in its chain. Against that standard the priest of the title is measured and found a monopolist of heaven in the tract. Carlile, the great publisher of forbidden radical print, sold such twopenny works to the artisans of London in the years after Peterloo, when every pulpit had its answer in a pamphlet.
38384-hawkins-electrical-guide-v-01-of-1:
Hawkins Electrical Guide number one is a course of study in question and answer form, by Hawkins and staff. It was copyrighted in nineteen fourteen by a New York house. Its motto says the thought is in the question and the information is in the answer. The course aims at engineers, electricians, and students.

Its goal is a working knowledge of electricity and its uses. Pictures run through the text to aid the lessons. The preface notes that several guides exist, each on one phase of the broad subject. They lead the reader step by step, it says. Answers are kept short and direct, in plain language, so that no wrong sense can be taken from them.
38421-a-little-boy-lost:
W H Hudson wrote a children's story copyrighted in 1920, with pictures by Dorothy P Lathrop, issued again in a later printing. Martin lives on the great plain before he is lost. A spoonbill and a cloud, and a flying figure he chases, draw him away. A deaf old man finds him.

Chapters carry Martin among the people of the mirage and savages. He is alone in the great forest and meets the black people of the sky. A troop of wild horses, a lady of the hills, and little people underground follow. The great blue water and the old man of the sea close his wanderings. Hudson blends nature lore with dream.
38429-frank-merriwell-s-alarm-or-doing-h:
Frank Merriwell's Alarm, or Doing His Best, is one of the Merriwell series of boys' books, by Burt Standish. The publisher's front matter boasts that for three generations the adventures of Frank and Dick Merriwell have been an inspiration to thousands of American boys. Frank and Dick are lads of high ideals, it says, and their examples in dealing with parents, friends, and enemies are sure to make better boys of their readers.

These stories teem with fun and adventure in all branches of sports and athletics, the blurb promises. The list opens with Frank Merriwell's School Days, Chums, and Foes. Merriwell, clean-living Yale athlete, was the dime novel's schoolboy superman.
38450-the-six-river-motor-boat-boys-on-t:
Harry Gordon wrote The Six River Motor Boat Boys on the St Lawrence, or The Lost Channel, issued by A L Burt Company in New York in nineteen thirteen. Gordon had written mate books on the Mississippi, the Colorado, the Amazon, and other great rivers. Twenty three chapters fill the tale. A plate shows a wave catching the Rambler broadside and beaching her high and dry on a bar.

Chapter one brings a mysterious visitor on a dark night on the St Lawrence at nine o clock. A treacherous guest, an arrest for piracy, and talk of a lost channel follow. Teddy gives an exhibition, Captain Joe takes a prisoner, and Max is discovered. A busy night in Quebec, a run through famed rapids, and wreckers add pace. The lost charter is found at the end. Boys got river craft, Canada, and peril in one fast tale.
38532-woman-and-artist:
Woman and Artist is a novel by Max O'Rell, issued in London by Frederick Warne. O'Rell, a French writer long based in England, also wrote John Bull and His Island. He dedicates this volume to his wife, and the tale opens with French and English homes set side by side.

Early chapters bring a house in Elm Avenue, a portrait, and a woman named Dora. Later heads name an inventor, a confession, and a chapter called The Husband, the Wife, and the Other. A separation and a return close the list of chapters. Readers get a story of art, marriage, and two nations' ways of home life.
38552-select-list-of-books-relating-to-t:
Select List of Books Relating to the Far East is a guide to print works, made at the Library of Congress in nineteen four. Appleton Prentiss Clark Griffin, chief list man of that hall, led the work. The list deals with the new state of the Far East in its day. State craft and trade are its main themes.

Titles stand in set parts by land and theme, from Russia and its growth to Tibet, Japan, and China. Short notes weigh the chief works, as when one past of Russia is set past a more broad one. Press works stand in the list next to books. The guide served men who had to read fast on a hot theme of the age.
38879-the-seven-periods-of-english-archi:
Edmund Sharpe, an architect, wrote The Seven Periods of English Architecture, Defined and Illustrated. The third edition appeared in 1888 from Spon in London and New York. The book carries twenty steel engravings and woodcuts. Sharpe sets out his own scheme for dividing English building into seven periods, with the marks that define each one.

In his preface Sharpe faces a difficulty head on. English readers had long used the terms and divisions handed down by Rickman. Those names were familiar and nearly universal, so changing them needed strong reasons. Sharpe argues that his scheme serves students better. Rickman's guide had remained the standard text for nearly half a century, and most popular works drew on it. Sharpe's book offers a fresh order for studying churches and other buildings, with pictures to fix each period in the reader's mind.
38941-nooks-and-corners-of-the-new-engla:
Samuel Adams Drake wrote Nooks and Corners of the New England Coast, entered for rights in eighteen seventy-five, with many drawings. Drake, who had written on old Boston landmarks, gave the book to Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. The first part treats New England of the ancients, the lost city of Norumbega, and early maps. It asks, among other things, whether Friday is unlucky.

Later parts walk the coast place by place, from Mount Desert Island to Castine and Pemaquid Point. Drake tells of Champlain, shell heaps, sea walls, and spouting caves. He gives tales of Fort George, the Penobscot raid, and General Wadsworth's bold escape. Lobsters, mackerel, and fish oil works fill out a coast he knew and loved, told for readers who would roam it with him.
39102-the-auto-boys-quest:
James Braden wrote The Auto Boys' Quest, printed under copyright in 1910 by the Saalfield Publishing Company, with pictures by Arthur DeBebian. Braden also wrote The Auto Boys and The Auto Boys' Outing, plus tales of the frontier. A front picture shows Phil holding a yellow envelope and reading a frantic wire, that friends have gone and no one knows where.

The Auto Boys were a gang of lads with a motor car, at a time when cars were still new and thrilling. A quest plot sends them on the road to find the lost and right a wrong. Young readers got speed, teamwork, and mystery, in a series that sold the romance of the auto age.
39131-the-book-of-the-little-past:
The Book of the Little Past is a collection of poems by Josephine Preston Peabody. Elizabeth Shippen Green illustrated it, and Houghton Mifflin published it at Boston in 1910. It is dedicated to Alison, and to older children.

A note says many poems are new in this gathering. Some came from The Singing Leaves of 1903, and others from Harper's Magazine. Titles include Making a House, The Busy Child, Cakes and Ale, and I Was Lost. Others are The Polite Visitor, The Mystic, The Christmas Tree, and Candle-Light. The first poem watches a child draw: smoke trailing up the sky, then the chimney beneath it. Birds flying by come next, and then the house itself, with all its windows.
39258-fredericksburg-and-its-many-points:
Fredericksburg and Its Many Points of Interest is a guidebook printed at Fredericksburg, Virginia, with copyright in 1912. Kishpaugh published it. A bird's-eye view from Stafford Heights fronts the book. Its motto boasts that the country's history cannot be written without the name of Fredericksburg.

The historical sketch opens with the town a visitor finds today. A new place has risen from the ruins of war, with modern streets and buildings. The book aims to give travellers the town's history and sights, and a welcome besides. Captain John Smith, it says, came to the falls of the Rappahannock in 1608 with twelve men and an Indian guide. He fought the Rappahannocks there, the most courageous savages he had yet met.
39718-the-wanderings-of-a-spiritualist:
The Wanderings of a Spiritualist is a book by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, printed in London by Hodder and Stoughton. Doyle, known for his confession of faith in The New Revelation, here reports his travels as a speaker for the spiritualist cause. A frontispiece photograph shows him on the warpath in Australia in 1920 and 1921.

A motto from Theodore Roosevelt heads the title page: aggressive fighting for the right is the noblest sport the world affords. Reviews quoted by the publisher call the earlier book frank, courageous, and resolute. The title joins the two halves of the work. Doyle wanders the world, and at each stop he argues for his belief that the dead survive and can be reached. The book is part travel record and part mission report from the creator of Sherlock Holmes.
40234-the-early-introduction-of-bogus-fr:
The Early Introduction of Bogus Freemasonry in the United States of America and Texas Among Colored Masons is a polemical history compiled by Mitchell. He was grand master of the King Solomon Grand Lodge of Texas and held high posts in Scottish Rite bodies. The Armstrong Company printed it at San Antonio in 1909, at twenty five cents. His full titles crowd the title page.

Mitchell writes so that members of the fraternity may understand the origin of irregular lodges among Black masons. He traces what he calls bogus masonry from the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, whose record he calls the blackest page in masonic history. From that source, he argues, Texas masonry among coloured men first came. The book is one side of a fierce quarrel over legitimacy in Black Freemasonry.
40271-london-before-the-conquest:
W R Lethaby wrote a history of London before the Norman Conquest, published in 1902. A front picture shows London and the Thames from Speed's map of 1610. The first chapter covers origins, the legend of London, the British church, and Alfred's London. Later chapters take up rivers and fords, then roads and the bridge.

Walls, gates, and quays get a chapter, as do the citadel and Southwark. Wards and parishes, streets, craft guilds, schools, and churches follow. Lethaby ends with the government of early London and a chapter on Londinium. An appendix tells how maps of early London can be built from the surviving evidence.
40283-rudy-and-babette-or-the-capture-of:
Rudy and Babette, or The Capture of the Eagle's Nest, is a tale by Hans Christian Andersen, issued in New York with twenty illustrations by Helen Stratton. A contents list traces Rudy from childhood to a new home and an uncle's house. Babette enters in the fourth chapter, and a visit to a mill follows. The eagle's nest gives the tale its adventure peak.

The Ice Maiden enters late, with a godmother, powers of evil, and visions in the night after her. Andersen sets love in high Swiss valleys, under glaciers that can kill. Two other tales, The Fellow Traveller and The Garden of Paradise among them, fill out the volume. Mountain peril and a cold spirit haunt a love story.
40285-the-syrian-christ:
Abraham Mitrie Rihbany wrote The Syrian Christ, issued by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in nineteen sixteen. Parts had run in the Atlantic Monthly. Six parts fill the book. Rihbany, a Syrian in America, reads the life of Jesus through Syrian eyes and ways. Part one is called The Syrian Christ, and part two treats the oriental manner of speech.

Chapter one, Son of the East, calls Jesus a seer and teacher of the truths of the spiritual life. Rihbany then treats his birth, the star, and filial obedience. Later parts treat bread and salt, sacred hospitality, and delaying a parting guest. Markets, housetops, vineyards, and shepherds fill part four. A last part treats women in East and West, Paul and woman, and Jesus and his mother. Bible readers get fresh light from a native guide.
40389-the-life-of-john-marshall-volume-2:
Albert J Beveridge tells the middle years of the great Chief Justice in volume two of a four-volume life. Houghton Mifflin issued it at Boston and New York. Copyright dates run 1916 to 1919. The volume covers 1789 to 1801.

Its first chapter weighs the French Revolution's pull on America. France and the new Constitution began their courses at the same hour. All Americans at first cheered the French rising as reform. Lafayette sent Washington the key of the Bastille. Then the reign of blood in Paris won applause at home, and conservatives began to doubt. Burke's Reflections met Paine's Rights of Man in print. The younger Adams answered in the Publicola essays. Beveridge, a senator and historian, built Marshall's life from letters and state papers.
40396-jack-harvey-s-adventures-or-the-ri:
Ruel Perley Smith sends his rival campers to Chesapeake Bay in a 1908 series volume. L C Page and Company issued it at Boston. Louis D Gowing drew the pictures.

Jack Harvey falls in with oyster pirates, the dredgers who steal from guarded beds. The contents name the law of the bay, and how that law works. A night's poaching follows. Flight ends in disaster, yet Harvey gets a message to shore. The tale builds to the Battle of Nanticoke River and a pursuit of the Brandt. Smith's campers were meant to trade the woods for new ground in each book. Here the ground is mud, sail, and shot. The oyster wars of the bay were real, and boys of the day knew the stakes.
40453-tom-ossington-s-ghost:
Tom Ossington's Ghost is a tale by Richard Marsh, the author of The Beetle. It came out in London in 1898 from James Bowden, with pictures by Harold Piffard. The list of chapters gives the shape of the tale. It opens with a new pupil and moves to a matter of conscience. A chapter is set in the dead of night, and one brings in a man of law and order.

Later chapters name Madge and a panel, and a thing that was hidden. One chapter is called The Long Arm of Coincidence, and one turns on Bruce Graham's first client. The front picture shows a cry to listen for a weeping ghost. The tale is a work of mystery and the supernatural from the close of the Victorian age, as its chapter heads and its title show.
40565-a-yankee-in-the-far-east:
George Hoyt Allen wrote a funny travel book about a trip through the Pacific and Asia. The full title is A Yankee in the Far East, first held under copyright in 1914. Allen travels with companions who gain nicknames like Missouri, and he tells the trip as a string of comic scenes. Sketches by the artist Weller add to the light tone.

Ports and places roll by in short chapters. Hawaii, Japan, and the islands ruled by Spain and then the United States come first. Later chapters reach Singapore, Penang, Burma, and India. Allen jokes about food, guides, priests, prices, and odd turns of speech. Readers get a bright, dated view of how one American saw Asia on the eve of war.
40605-the-motor-boat-club-at-nantucket-o:
Hancock wrote this Motor Boat Club adventure, printed by Altemus at Philadelphia with a copyright of 1909. Two men in a railway coach talk of the Meteor, a rich man's speed boat that made nearly twenty-eight miles an hour on her trial trip. Something, one hints, could be made to happen to that boat.

Two American boys in the seat behind hear every word. Tom and his club mates take the case to Nantucket. Chapters promise a pirate sighted, a joke on the enemy, and the quickest way of walking the plank. Tom discovers the heir the title promises. A message under a rock, an attic light, and blind man's buff in earnest raise the pace. Jed runs a naval bombardment near the end. Hancock writes clean, fast boys' adventure on salt water.
40701-the-book-of-the-aquarium-and-water:
Shirley Hibberd wrote this practical guide to keeping collections of fresh water and marine life, published by Groombridge and Sons at London in 1856. Hibberd, author of Rustic Adornments for Homes of Taste, gives instructions for forming, stocking, and managing such collections in all seasons. A cabinet aquarium serves as frontispiece.

The book divides into three parts. The fresh-water tank comes first, with chapters on vessels, rockwork, plants, and fishes, then reptiles, mollusks, and insects, and general care such as feeding and cleansing. The marine tank follows, covering artificial sea water, collecting specimens, sea plants, and anemones. The water cabinet closes the volume, a smaller arrangement for pond life, with nets, jars, and the keeping of larvae such as the dragon fly.
40734-the-socialist:
Socialist is a novel by Guy Thorne, author of When It Was Dark, published in nineteen oh nine. Advertisements for the author's other books stand at the front of the hosted copy. The contents open with a chapter on a duke, called His Grace the Duke of Paddington.

Later heads promise a most surprising day and a man with a mustard coloured beard. A chapter vows to inaugurate a revolution, and the next sets out a great new plan. Kidnapping on scientific principles follows, then a heroine's initiation. News arrives at Oxford, a discovery is made, and scenes shift to a bishop's town house and a theatre. Love enters in due course, troubled waters follow, and the duke knows at last. The heads give the novel a clear conspiratorial spine.
4081-the-alchemist:
Ben Jonson's comedy The Alchemist follows three rogues who run a fake philosopher's stone business from a London house while its master is away. Face, Subtle, and Dol Common promise dupes gold, love, and long life, with chants of hum and buz to sharpen the five senses.

A gull named Dapper must bathe his fingers, wash his eyes, and pay twenty nobles among her grace's servants, dressed in a clean shirt for luck. Jonson's plot spins through greed and gulling at a furious pace. Readers who enjoy sharp, crowded comedy will find a masterpiece of trickery and talk.
40941-the-wreck-of-the-red-bird-a-story-:
The Wreck of the Red Bird is a boys' story of the Carolina coast. George Cary Eggleston wrote it, and Putnam issued it in 1882. The dedication carries a grief. Eggleston meant the book for his son Guilford. The boy, nine years old, helped plan every incident. He even gave the story its title. He died before it appeared.

The tale itself is salt and adventure. Boys sail the Red Bird, meet odd fish, and find an enemy in camp. Ned adds science, and Jack makes a discovery. Maum Sally opens the book with warm manners. A father's memorial, wrapped in a sea story.
41184-whither-thou-goest:
Whither Thou Goest is a thrill tale by William Le Queux, out in a nineteen twenty form. The Earl of Saxham hates that his son Guy loves a poor no name girl. He plots to split the pair by a state post trick in Madrid. A Foreign Office friend wins Guy a post at the legation there. The earl knows not that Madrid seeths with bomb creed plots in the tale.

A spite full woman bent on harm dogs the steps of young Guy. Tight scrapes and thrill turns crowd his days in that hot bed. Rich love strain runs through the plot web, the front words add. The first scene sets a hot July eve on the Biscay shore of Spain. Sardine boats in gay hues wait for wind in the still bay.
41586-the-red-dust:
Murray Leinster returned to his mad planet in The Red Dust, a sequel to The Mad Planet printed in Amazing Stories in January 1927. Far in the future, Earth has grown strange: huge insects stalk mushroom forests, fireflies four feet long light the night, and tiny mankind fights to fit itself to the changed world. Burl, the hero of the first tale, hunts again, and the opening picture shows him driving his spear at a great meat-eating beetle.

The beetles, though, are not the worst of it. A deadly red dust now threatens the whole human race, a terror beside which the insects seem small. Leinster builds his future from scale and dread: ant hills a hundred feet high, fungus hills, and men dwarfed by the life around them. The tale moves fast, in the bold manner of the early science fiction magazines.
41730-dixie-after-the-war-an-exposition-:
Dixie After the War, published at New York in 1906, is Myrta Lockett Avary's account of the South in the twelve years after Richmond fell. Avary had written A Virginia Girl in the Civil War. General Evans supplied the introduction. Old paintings, daguerreotypes and rare photographs illustrate the book. A portrait shows Jefferson Davis after his prison life.

Chapters run from the fall of the capital to the chaining of Davis. The counsel of Lee and the wrath of the North both appear. Tournaments and starvation parties show how a beaten people kept up heart. New fashions get a chapter of their own. Avary aims at conciliation, closing with Davis's plea to young men to drop all rancor.
42017-tom-burnaby-a-story-of-uganda-and-:
Herbert Strang wrote this boys' adventure of Uganda and the great Congo forest, reprinted in 1922. A front plate called 'A Warm Reception' points to danger early in the tale. Strang opens with a letter to a boy named Jack, whose birthday brings another book for his shelf.

No mailed knights this time, the letter promises, since the story is of the present day. Yet fierce foes in plenty await, and chivalry too, though not spelled with a capital letter. Strang holds that the spirit of chivalry lives as strongly now as ever, and Tom Burnaby's African journey tests that claim.
42057-bill-biddon-trapper-or-life-in-the:
Edward Ellis wrote Bill Biddon, Trapper, or Life in the Northwest, printed in New York with rights held in 1916. Ellis was known for Nathan Todd, a life of Pontiac, and more. A print of the trapper's home fronts the book.

Out late at night opens the tale, then a new friend and the trapper's own story. Trapping grounds, a canoe in the dark, and life alone in the wilds fill the mid part. A buffalo hunt, an awful waking, and a brigade bring old friends back. Young readers get a full tale of furs, camps, and peril in the great northwest of old days.
42066-the-young-marooners-on-the-florida:
Young Marooners on the Florida Coast is a boys' adventure tale by F R Goulding. Joel Chandler Harris, the Uncle Remus author, wrote an introduction. The New York edition of nineteen twenty seven carries copyrights reaching back to eighteen sixty two. A prefatory history tells how the book came to be written. Boys and girls used to gather round the author on a southern piazza, it says.

There they heard the varied story of his early years on summer evenings. As they grew, he wove facts of nature and practical expedients into a tale, he explains. The result is a book about two boys, Robert and Harold, cast away on the Florida coast. The story is not all story, he owns. The fiction lies mostly in the arrangement.
42115-the-trail-hunter-a-tale-of-the-far:
Gustave Aimard's The Trail Hunter, a tale of the far West, was published in London in 1861 by Ward and Lock of Fleet Street. Lascelles Wraxall, who made the English version, writes the preface and thanks the press for its kindness to the earlier books. The volume gives the earlier adventures of hunters met in the series before.

Part one is named for Red Cedar, part two for El Presidio de Santa Fe. Don Miguel Zarate, the sachem of the Coras, Fray Ambrosio, and Father Seraphin walk its pages, with Sunbeam and Nathan among the named figures. Wraxall vouches that many scenes are so startling they must come from the writer's own watching of desert and prairie life.
42183-queen-of-the-black-coast:
Robert Howard wrote Queen of the Black Coast, a Conan story first published in Weird Tales in May 1934. It opens with a verse from the Song of Bêlit, the pirate queen Conan will meet. Conan begins the tale on the run, riding a black stallion down a street that slopes to the wharfs.

He leaps aboard a galley just casting off, his broadsword wet with blood. The master protests that the ship is bound for the coasts of Kush. Conan answers that he pays his way with steel, and tells him to push off as horsemen and archers come up behind. The story launches one of Howard's best-known tales: Conan the pirate, a queen of the black coast, and plunder on a haunted shore.
42361-the-mystic-mid-region-the-deserts-:
Arthur Burdick wrote a book of the deserts of the Southwest that Putnam published in 1904. Fifty four photographs go with it. A long poem in praise and dread of the desert stands at the front. Teamsters in Death Valley form the frontispiece.

The chapters begin with the desert itself and the land of thirst. Queer plants that live there come next, then the strange dwellers of the sand. A chapter treats the men of the desert, and one a funeral in the region of death. Basket makers, and the ships of the desert, follow. Borax mines take a chapter. Death Valley itself, and the mouth of Hades, fill the heart of the book. Journalism below sea level is the odd close.
42706-across-america-or-the-great-west-a:
James Rusling, late a brevet brigadier-general, made this inspection tour of the West in 1866 and published his account with Sheldon and Company at New York in 1874. His orders from Quartermaster-General Meigs, dated July 10, 1866, sent him from Fort Leavenworth by Denver City and Salt Lake City to the Pacific Coast. He was to inspect every post on the way and weigh the cost of the great depots. General Grant's headquarters endorsed the orders, directing commanders to furnish escorts.

From San Francisco he was to work through California, Oregon, Nevada, and the territories of Washington and Arizona. Then he would return by the Isthmus and report in person. The general object was economy: to examine the bases and routes of supply and cut the enormous expenditures of the postwar army. Yosemite Falls fronts the volume.
42707-a-source-book-for-medi-val-history:
A Source Book for Medieval History, edited by Oliver J Thatcher and Edgar Holmes McNeal, was published by Scribner's in 1905. The editors gather documents that show the history of Europe in the Middle Ages in the words of the time. The first section, on the Germans and the empire to 1073, opens with Tacitus on Germany and Procopius on the Vandal and Gothic wars. The Salic law follows, then Gregory of Tours, the coronation of Pippin, and Einhard's life of Charlemagne.

Capitularies, letters about comets, the Strassburg oaths, and the treaty of Verdun carry the section forward. Such source books changed the teaching of history: students read the evidence instead of a summary. Thatcher and McNeal made the medieval world speak Latin, law, and chronicle in English dress. The volume served college classrooms for decades.
42759-distributive-justice-the-right-and:
John Ryan wrote Distributive Justice, published by Macmillan at New York in 1916. His subtitle asks after the right and wrong of our present distribution of wealth. Ryan taught political science at the Catholic University of America and economics at a college in Washington. His earlier book had argued for a living wage.

The church's marks of approval stand in the front, with the archbishop of New York's imprimatur. Ryan builds a Catholic case on wages, rent, interest, and the claims of the poor. He wrote against both the socialist remedy and the doctrine that the market settles all questions of justice. Few American books have carried so far: preachers, labor men, and lawmakers quoted Ryan for a generation. His living wage argument, set out here in full legal and moral dress, later fed the programs of the New Deal.
4277-two-years-before-the-mast:
Richard Henry Dana wrote this classic of sea life from his own time before the mast. A Harvard student who shipped as a common sailor, Dana sailed from Boston around Cape Horn to California in the 1830s. He worked aloft, handled hides on the coast, and lived under harsh captains and harder weather.

The book made its mark by telling the sailor's life plainly, without romance. Readers learn how a ship was worked, how crews were fed and punished, and what the California hide trade meant in daily labor. It remains a firsthand record of the forecastle, and a text that later reformers quoted for the sailor's cause.
4298-the-paying-guest:
George Gissing built this short novel on a simple domestic idea. Mumford sees an advertisement and suggests taking a paying guest, to keep his wife company during the day. Emmeline, startled, weighs the plan: the rent is heavy, and so is the cost of Clarence's season ticket, but their house at Sutton has room to spare.

The air at Sutton has improved mother and child since they left London, and the guest promises company as well as income. Gissing then shows how a stranger in the house changes a marriage, a household, and its small economies. It is a compact study of suburban life, told with Gissing's dry, watchful humor.
43340-the-fair-god-or-the-last-of-the-tz:
Lew Wallace's The Fair God, or The Last of the Tzins, is a tale of the conquest of Mexico. Copyrighted in 1873, it is issued here by Grosset and Dunlap with illustrations by Eric Pape. Wallace's note explains his device: personal experience told by its hero holds readers as second-hand history cannot. So he writes as translator of a native account, attributed to a real litterateur of the valley where the story lies.

The epigraph from Draper laments that Spain crushed a civilization that might have instructed Europe. Wallace, later famous for Ben-Hur, spent years on the Mexican materials. The frontispiece shows horsemen galloping over bridges. The romance follows the last of the Tzins through the Spanish invasion, giving the conquered side the narrator's voice by the translator fiction.
43675-ned-in-the-block-house-a-tale-of-e:
Edward S Ellis wrote a tale of early days in the West for young readers. Henry T Coates and Company issued it at Philadelphia, with rights held in 1883. Ned hunts in a Kentucky forest as the tale opens, rifle set on a fine buck. Deerfoot, a Shawanoe friend, soon joins the young pioneer.

Twenty-one chapters move through trackless woods, a strong block-house, and night attacks. Flaming shafts, secret guests, and a fiery foe test the small band. A North American Review note at the front praises Ellis for true, human Indian figures. Boys of the time got thrills mixed with woodcraft and grit.
43786-a-gentleman-at-arms-being-passages:
A Gentleman-at-Arms is a tale of adventure set forth by Herbert Strang, first printed in 1914. It claims to be passages in the life of Sir Christopher Rudd, knight, as told by himself in the year 1641. Pictures by Cyrus Cuneo and Robinson illustrate it. The frontispiece shows Spaniards rushing through musket smoke toward Rudd's party.

The book falls into five parts. Rudd's adventure in Hispaniola brings the strange story of Captain Q. In France he borrows the white plume of Henry of Navarre. In the Low Countries he works a quaint device of the silver shot. In Spain he plays the part of a physician. In Ireland he wins a wife, and a postscript closes the soldier's memoir of a wandering life.
43854-the-blossoms-of-morality-intended-:
The Blossoms of Morality came out in London in a fourth edition in 1806, printed for Harris and a row of partner booksellers. Forty-seven cuts, designed and engraved by Bewick, picture the tales. The editor had made the Looking-Glass for the Mind before it.

That earlier book freely translated tales by Berquin and other foreign writers for the young. This one leans more on original matter. The editor aims to be useful to the rising generation. Tales here step one level higher than the last book, mixing amusement with graver subjects. Young ladies and gentlemen, the title promises, get both pleasure and instruction. The book is a small garden of moral tales, cut in wood.
43994-caleb-wright-a-story-of-the-west:
John Habberton, author of Helen's Babies, tells a story of the West in a novel issued by the Lothrop Publishing Company at Boston in 1901. The hero's name stands as the title.

Chapter one opens with a young man of taste and little money. Philip Somerton strayed from a far-western town to New York. He wants to make his fortune and enjoy the great city. The contents map his rise and the store he joins. Chapters treat taking possession, home-making, and business ways. A pork-house, a western spectre, and fun with a camera vary the tale. Decoration Day and the railway bring it toward its close. Habberton mixes humour with a plain tale of trade, land, and marriage in the new West.
44166-life-of-abraham-lincoln-sixteenth-:
Life of Abraham Lincoln, sixteenth president of the United States, opens with a page of Lincoln's own sayings in place of a preface. At Independence Hall in February 1861 he declared he would rather be assassinated on the spot than surrender the principle of liberty. At Springfield in June 1858 he warned that the government could not endure half slave and half free.

More sayings follow: the trust renewed in his message of July 1861, and the claim that freeing the slaves assures freedom to the free. The Gettysburg words appear, that the world can never forget what the brave men did there. A letter of April 1864 confesses that events had controlled him. A biography that fronts its subject's own voice lets Lincoln frame the life that follows.
44224-old-judge-priest:
Old Judge Priest, by Irvin S Cobb, gathers stories of a kindly Kentucky judge and his home town in the years after the Civil War. The book was published in New York in 1918.

The first story, The Lord Provides, opens in the judge's chambers at the old courthouse. Cobb pictures the high, cracked room in loving detail: law books in spotted leather, a water bucket with a gourd dipper, and a steel print of President Davis. In the middle sits the judge himself, broad, stooped, and tangled in papers behind his desk. Cobb hints that the story will end where it began, with the judge still at that desk. Earlier Priest tales had already made the judge a favourite with readers.
44419-the-arch-satirist:
The Arch Satirist is a society novel by Frances De Wolfe Fenwick, published in Boston in 1910. Its title comes from a line of Thomas Hardy printed on the title page. Justice had been done, Hardy wrote, and Time, the Arch Satirist, had had his joke out. Fenwick takes that idea as the key to her story of fashionable people and their slow comeuppance.

Charles Copeland illustrated the book. The chapters promise a brilliant match, rejected addresses, a fancy dress ball, and whispering tongues. Agatha, one of the central women, does her duty and is rewarded, says one chapter title. Two women pay their debts in another. The shadows fall at the end, over a world of visits, scandals, and twins seen under a new aspect.
44909-the-new-forest:
Elizabeth Godfrey described The New Forest for the Beautiful England series, with pictures by Haslehust, in a volume printed in 1912. Gypsies at Coldharbour face the title page. Her opening praises the forest as a sanctuary in a corner of Hampshire. It has kept its own laws and customs for over eight centuries, while towns spread on every side. School lessons, she notes, taught children to curse Norman William for making it.

Godfrey corrects the old legend with modern history, then walks the ground. Brockenhurst, Boldre Bridge, Beaulieu, and Buckler's Hard all get their chapters. Minstead church, Burley Moor, and the forest's own cathedral of trees fill the plates. The book is a pocket tour of a royal forest that outlived the kings who hunted it.
45047-the-red-river-half-breed-a-tale-of:
