Gustave Aimard tells a tale of the wild northwest in a novel Englished by Henry Llewellyn Williams. The London edition gathers Aimard's novels of the years 1860 to 1885 into print. Aimard was known for Prairie Flower and Pirates of the Prairies.

The tale opens on the crest of the continent, atop the Big Wind River Mountains in November cold. Chapter titles promise a false pilot, a mountaineer's cabin, Cherokee Bill recruiting, and gold grabbers on the move. A beautiful prisoner, a nest of traitors, and a late visitor to the ladies raise the stakes in turn. The half-breed of the title dies game, as one chapter plainly warns. Readers get French frontier romance in full color, with passes, plots, and last stands.
45050-the-lady-of-pleasure-a-comedie-as-:
James Shirley wrote The Lady of Pleasure, a comedy printed in London in sixteen thirty-seven. The title page says the King's servants acted it at a private house in Drury Lane. Shirley gave the play to Richard, Lord Lovelace of Hurley, as its patron.

Aretina, wife of Sir Thomas Bornwell, has come to town for pleasure and scorns dull country talk. Around her move her steward, the young widow Celestina, and a set of suitors and gallants. The scene is the Strand, a smart part of London. Sharp talk drives the plot, as town manners and country ways clash on stage.
45198-tales-of-our-coast:
Tales of Our Coast gathers sea stories by five hands in one volume. Crockett, Frederic, Parker, Russell, and Q wrote the five long tales inside. Dodd, Mead issued it at New York in 1898 with Brangwyn plates. The Smugglers of the Clone, by Crockett, leads the set in Scots voice.

A boy is roused at two in the morning for his first smuggling run. Partans on the sands is the cry; brandy and rum wait below the hill. His mother prays, his father counsels quiet chains and a lowered head. There Is Sorrow on the Sea and The Path of Murtogh follow in the book. The Roll Call of the Reef closes the coast set.
452-lavengro-the-scholar-the-gypsy-the-p:
George Borrow tells his own wandering youth in this partly true, partly fancied memoir. Lavengro, scholar and would-be writer, roams England, learns tongues, meets gypsies, and talks with priests, tinkers, and horse dealers. Isopel Berners, a tall gypsy girl, stands out among his roadside friends.

Borrow writes in careless, vivid prose, full of talk, quarrel, and sudden charm. An introduction by Augustine Birrell praises the book's elixir of life and motion. The memoir charms as a picaresque portrait of England on foot, where learning and vagabond freedom share the same road.
45262-the-bungalow-boys-in-the-great-nor:
Dexter Forrester wrote this boys' adventure, copyrighted in 1911 by Hurst and Company. A front plate shows Jack leaping forward and outward, landing right on a sloop's deck. Forrester had earlier written 'The Bungalow Boys' and 'The Bungalow Boys Marooned in the Tropics' for the same readers.

In the valley opens the contents, and a blow-up follows as the second chapter. An involuntary hay-ride, a schooner owned by Bully Banjo and a night of mystery build the Northwest trip. Dacre sustains an accident in chapter six, in a tale of boats, woods and bold boys far from home.
45341-wager-of-battle-a-tale-of-saxon-sl:
Herbert's Wager of Battle, a tale of Saxon slavery in Sherwood Forest, was published by Mason Brothers of New York in 1855. Its author, Henry Herbert, signs his preface at The Cedars in July of that year and gives the book to Israel De Wolf Andrews of Eastport, Maine. He calls it a history-based romance of Saxon and Norman ways.

Herbert owns at once that his scene and age match Sir Walter Scott's Ivanhoe, the grand romance of the same ground. His stress falls on Saxon serfdom in the twelfth century, before the two races fused into one English people. The clash of manners between Saxon and Norman drives the tale, as it drives Scott's.
45382-the-blue-and-the-gray-or-the-civil:
A R White wrote The Blue and the Gray, or The Civil War as Seen by a Boy. K T Boland published it in eighteen ninety-eight. Frank Beard illustrated the book. More than one hundred fifty war photographs join his drawings. A verse by Fred A Palmer fronts the tale.

White calls his book a story of patriotism and adventure in the war for the Union. He dedicates it to the sons and daughters of the veterans. Those who fought, and lived to teach its lessons, share the honour. So does the memory of the heroes of North and South alike. A boy's eyes carry the reader through marches and camps. The photographs ground the tale in the war's real faces.
45419-the-religio-medical-masquerade-a-c:
Frederick Peabody, a lawyer, wrote The Religio-Medical Masquerade as a full attack on Christian Science and its founder. His title page calls the book a complete exposure of the movement. Peabody argues that the faith and its healing claims rest wholly on Mary Baker Eddy herself. If her claims about herself are false, he says, the whole system falls with them.

Chapter heads charge Eddy with fraud, greed, and a ban on marriage among her followers, and one calls her system witchcraft. Peabody writes with open scorn and says he will judge an old woman harshly because her sway over thousands makes her a public force. The book is a period piece from the fiercest years of the fight over Christian Science. It shows how strong the pushback was while the new church was still growing fast.
45483-the-story-of-my-mind-or-how-i-beca:
M M Mangasarian wrote The Story of My Mind in 1909. Its subtitle tells how he became a rationalist. The book is given to his children. They had asked him how his change came. He was raised a Calvinist by his parents. He served as pastor of a Philadelphia church.

His daughter Zabelle was baptized in that church. His son Armand and daughter Christine came later. They were born after he left the Presbyterians. He held off writing till they grew old enough. The fight with each dogma fills the tale, he says. Hand to hand, he grappled his way out. He writes so his grandchildren may read it too. A minister's farewell to orthodoxy, told as a letter home, the book stands as a freethought classic of its day.
45545-the-staying-guest:
Carolyn Wells wrote this story for girls, printed by the Century Company in New York in 1904. Smith drew the pictures. Primrose Hall, a white colonial house on a hill, belongs to two prim maiden sisters, Priscilla and Dorinda Flint. Into their ordered life walks a small whirlwind.

The frontispiece gives her entrance line: I am Ladybird, and I have come to stay. Chapters follow her through school, up a tree, and into a civil war of manners. An earl arrives; a rival, Lavinia Lovell, appears; half sisters are revealed. Ladybird works like a small lawyer for the people she loves. The tale ends with a wedding in the orchard. Wells writes bright, funny scenes, and her heroine rules every room she enters.
4589-all-s-for-the-best:
T. S. Arthur published All's for the Best in 1869, gathering twelve sketches. Their titles run from Faith and Patience and Is He a Christian? through Rich and Rare Were the Gems She Wore, Not as a Child, and Angels in the Heart, to Cast Down but Not Destroyed, Good Ground, and Giving That Doth Not Impoverish. Later pieces ask Was It Murder, or Suicide? They add The Nursery Maid, My Father, and The Christian Gentleman.

The opening sketch meets a doubter who trusted human prudence, walked by his own light, and lost his way, confessing he has no faith in anything. A gentleman answers that he has faith in God, though the doubter shakes his head in bewilderment. Readers get a set of earnest Victorian tales about faith, patience, and conduct. Each is short enough to read alone, and each aims to steady a reader in doubt or sorrow.
45930-the-romance-of-plant-life-interest:
The Romance of Plant Life, tales of the strange and curious in the plant world, is a book by G F Scott Elliot, printed in 1907. Elliot was a naturalist and the author of A Naturalist in Mid Africa. His first chapter treats the activity of plants: plants that move, the work of green leaves, and the power of sunshine.

The contents range widely over the plant kingdom. One chapter tells how early peoples and doctors used plants, from quinine to the wars of the spice trade. Others treat hemlock, spruce, and pine forests, the struggles of a pine seedling, and bark beetles. Tall trees, giant seaweeds, and old sequoias and oaks fill later pages. The frontispiece shows a living bridge of roots in the Himalayas. Elliot wrote botany as adventure for general readers, full of odd facts and travellers' tales.
46045-the-boy-allies-on-the-north-sea-pa:
Ensign Robert Drake's The Boy Allies on the North Sea Patrol, or Striking the First Blow at the German Fleet, was published by Burt of New York in 1915. Drake had written three Boy Allies books before it, under two flags, with the terror of the seas, and with the flying squadron. A frontispiece catches the series' tone: Great Scott, it's a girl.

Chapter one is called Shanghaied. Frank Chadwick, strolling the Naples waterfront, hears a cry of help in English from a dirty sailors' boarding house. Inside, a little American in a red sweater is fighting for his life against two men with gleaming knives. Frank charges in, the men flee, and the rescued sailor presses a drink on him at the table. Frank refuses, and turns to go, glad to have been of assistance; the chapter's title warns that the kindness is a trap.
46208-a-voice-from-jerusalem-or-a-sketch:
A sketch tells of Orson Hyde's long trip as a church man to Jerusalem. Hyde was a missionary of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints. His road ran through Germany and Constantinople to the Holy Land. The book came out in Liverpool from Pratt's Star Office. His last note dates to Bavaria on January 18, 1842.

Mount Zion and the Pool of Siloam are drawn from his sight. East ways and dress are told as light on Bible texts. Talks with Jews' church men fill parts of the tale. News of lands and of Israel's rise to come close it. Saints get a prized first-hand road tale.
46250-the-thorn-in-the-nest:
The Thorn in the Nest is a novel by Martha Finley, printed at New York by Dodd, Mead and Company with copyright of 1886. Finley was the author of the Elsie books and the Mildred series. Her epigraph gives the title its sense: he puts a thorn in our nest to drive us to the wing, that we may not be grovellers forever. Thirty-three chapters tell the tale.

The story opens in the spring of 1797, in a sequestered valley in western Pennsylvania. Orchard, meadow and wheat and corn fields stretch away on either hand, shut in by forests. Beyond tower the Alleghenies, their summits still white from the storms of the past winter. Finley sets her tale of faith and affliction in the early republic's backcountry.
46328-in-the-old-west:
In the Old West is a set of mountain man narratives by George Frederick Ruxton, edited by Horace Kephart. The Outing Publishing Company copyrighted the edition in 1915 at New York. Its subtitle promises the West as it was in the days of Kit Carson and the mountain men. Chapter one camps a band of trappers on Bijou creek in the Platte country.

It is October in that opening, when early frosts have crisped the leaves of the cherry and ash along the brooks. The ridges and peaks of the Rockies are already covered with a glittering mantle of snow in the scene. The camp has all the appearance of permanency in the telling of that first page. Ruxton, an English officer who hunted and trapped in the Rockies in the 1840s, wrote the classic account of the mountain men.
46458-laughing-last:
Jane Abbott wrote Laughing Last, a girls' novel published by Grosset and Dunlap at New York. Lippincott held the copyright of 1924. Abbott had written Highacres, Keineth, and Red Robin. Corinne Pauli drew the pictures, and a front caption quotes a girl calling a boat a pirate's ship.

Abbott dedicates the book to Frances Stanton Smith, whose loyal interest was an unfailing help. The chapters open with an egg and a rebellion. Pola lifts a curtain, and Sidney digs for cousins. A chapter promises that the summer will tell who laughs last. Later come dreams come true, an explanation by a Mr. Dugald, and Sidney finding where she belongs. Abbott's girls are lively and modern, and her books were standbys of the girls' shelf between the wars.
46600-by-the-world-forgot-a-double-roman:
By the World Forgot is a double romance of the east and west by Cyrus Townsend Brady, issued in September 1917. A front picture shows a man named Beekman crying out as he stares into white mist, appalled by what he sees. Brady dedicates the book to a kinsman he calls a good friend. Each of its two books opens under a Kipling verse.

The first book opens with a clash of wills and hearts, and a stubborn heroine named Stephanie. A wedding that was not, and the mystery of some last words, carry its plot. A triangle becomes a four sided figure before the book ends. The second book turns to the hardest of confessions and a search resolved upon. East and west thus trade scenes in one linked tale of love.
4676-outpost:
J. G. Austin, author of Dora Darling, or The Daughter of the Regiment, published Outpost at Boston in 1867. Its contents open with sunshine, the little wife, Cherrytoe, and the children of Merrigoland. They go on to a runaway, Mother Winch, Teddy's little sister, the Fayver, and the night-watch. An empty nest, a trace and a search, Teddy's temptation, and the Cachuco follow.

Later chapters bring Giovanni and Pantalon, a pink-silk dress, beginning a new life, wholesale murder, and Dora Darling herself. A chamber of memories, a letter and an offer, Giovanni's room, and a confession lead to Teddy losing and finding his home. Burroughs' business, man versus dog, a visitor for Mrs. Ginniss, a new patron, and welcome home close the tale. Readers get a long Victorian domestic adventure, full of children, secrets, and second chances.
4701-the-ethics-of-the-dust:
John Ruskin, Slade Professor of Fine Art, wrote The Ethics of the Dust as ten lectures to little housewives on the elements of crystallisation. He dedicates the book, at Christmas 1875, to the real little housewives whose gentle listening and thoughtful questioning enabled him to write it. An old lecturer, of incalculable age, talks with girls named Florrie, Isabel, May, Lily, Kathleen, Lucilla, Violet, Dora, and Egypt.

Lectures run from the valley of diamonds and the pyramid builders, through crystal life, orders, virtues, quarrels, caprice, and sorrows, to home virtues and the crystal rest. Ruskin uses crystals to teach order, patience, and moral conduct, mixing science with fable. Readers get a charming, unusual Ruskin book, where geology becomes a lesson in character, for young readers and for adults who like science told as story.
4702-the-flaming-forest:
James Oliver Curwood opens The Flaming Forest with David Carrigan, sergeant in the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, humming softly under a blue northern sky and thanking God he is alive. He blesses McVane, superintendent of N Division at Athabasca Landing, for detailing him to his mission. Glad to travel alone in deep forest, he expects weeks carrying him deeper into his beloved north.

Making noonday tea over a fire at a river's edge, Carrigan concludes for the hundredth time that it is nice to be alone in the world. Green forest crowds like an inundation on three sides of him. His comrades call his task a bad assignment, and danger waits ahead. Readers get a northern police adventure of forest fire, pursuit, and romance, with Curwood's usual snow, rivers, and lonely trails, and a hero who loves the wild he polices.
47262-old-times-on-the-upper-mississippi:
George Byron Merrick wrote this memoir of river life, Old Times on the Upper Mississippi, published at Cleveland in 1909. The catalog title is a piece of the subtitle; the book gives the recollections of a steamboat pilot from 1854 to 1863. A picture of the mouth of the Wisconsin River, the ancient highway between the lakes and the great river, stands at the front.

Merrick dedicated the book to his old chiefs: an engineer, a clerk, and a pilot, masters each of his trade, from whom he learned what made these memories possible. He tells of the boats, the islands, the towns, and the trade of the upper river in the years before the railways took its place. It is first hand river history.
47518-the-tempest:
The Tempest is Shakespeare's comedy, presented here in an illustrated edition. Hodder and Stoughton published it in New York and London. The text follows the Oxford Edition by permission. Edmund Dulac supplied the illustrations.

The plates follow the action in order. Prospero tells Miranda he acted only in care of her. Caliban offers water with berries. Antonio plots beside the sleeping king. Stephano makes Trinculo kiss the book, his bottle. Ariel, as harpy, denounces three men of sin. The masque brings Iris, Ceres, and Juno in act four. Prospero's speech on the stuff our dreams are made on is pictured. The dramatis personae list Alonso, Sebastian, Antonio, and Ferdinand. Caliban, Trinculo, Stephano, Miranda, and Ariel complete the island company. The scene is a ship at sea, then the island.
47633-copper-coleson-s-ghost:
Copper Coleson's Ghost is a boys' mystery novel by Edward Hendrick. Page published the book at Boston in 1930, with pictures by Harold Cue. Hendrick dedicates the tale to his sons Bob and Jack. The contents run to twenty five chapters.

The story opens at the Blake homestead in the town of Truesdell. A great apple tree behind the cottage shades the yard. Ned Blake has rigged its branches into an open air gymnasium. School friends, a big game, and a summer plan fill the early chapters. Then a haunted mine and a note from a ghost take over. A light on a wall, a mystery ship, and a dance apparition raise the stakes. The boys end trapped in the mine before the chase and capture.
47648-geology-the-science-of-the-earth-s:
Geology: The Science of the Earth's Crust is the third volume of the Popular Science Library, written by William Miller, professor of geology at Smith College. Collier printed the set at New York with copyright of 1922. Garrett Serviss was editor in chief of the sixteen volume library. A captioned photograph opens the book: a great ledge in Ogden Canyon, Utah, where Cambrian strata were buried, hardened to quartzite, tilted nearly vertical and laid bare by erosion.

The chapters march through the making of the landscape. The action of wind and the instability of the earth's crust follow. Tables set the eras beside their characteristic life and their estimated millions of years. The volume is popular science between the wars, teaching deep time to the general reader.
47750-wanderlust:
Robert Reynolds wrote Wanderlust, a memoir of tramp travel printed in New York in 1913 by the Broadway Publishing Company. A front picture shows the author making one grand plunge to grab the rail of a baggage car. Reynolds gave the book to two comrades in many of the adventures told in it, Gardner and Conlon.

Chapter one recalls his first escapade, with thrilling scenes in the pine fields and sand hills of Florida. From there the road life rolls on, with freight trains, odd jobs, and close calls. Reynolds writes as a man who loved the road for its own sake. Readers get a firsthand tale of hobo life in the early 1900s, told with gusto.
47811-abe-lincoln-s-anecdotes-and-storie:
Abe Lincoln's Anecdotes and Stories is a collection of the best stories told by Abraham Lincoln, compiled by R D Wordsworth. It was compiled in nineteen hundred eight for a Boston publisher and bills Lincoln as America's best story teller. An opening sketch calls him a fun loving and humour loving man. Shakespeare is brought in as a parallel case.

The strain of four years of civil war might have overcome Lincoln's reason without his humour, the sketch argues. His jokes and tales are thus presented as a safety valve for a great mind. Readers get the tall tales, courtroom wit, and frontier humour that built the Lincoln legend. Anecdote, not archive, is the method throughout.
47871-james-geikie-the-man-and-the-geolo:
Marion Newbigin and Flett wrote James Geikie, the Man and the Geologist, printed at Edinburgh in 1917. Geikie, who died in 1915, was Scotland's great student of the ice age, the man who read the drift and boulder clay for the story of glaciers. A portrait from his later years faces the title page.

Newbigin tells the life and prints the letters, from boyhood in 1839 through his first years on the geological survey. Flett and others weigh the science: the mapping of Scotland, the case for land ice, and the interglacial controversies that fill the last chapters. A list of his publications closes the book. It is a full life of a genial, combative Victorian scientist.
47900-the-splendid-outcast:
The Splendid Outcast is a novel by George Gibbs, published by Appleton in New York in 1920. Gibbs wrote and also drew the pictures for the book. It first appeared in the Red Book magazine in 1919. The frontispiece shows a woman crouched, watching, breathless and uncertain.

The contents open with a convalescent and a deepening mystery, then a character cast out. Piquette appears, and youth triumphs in turn. A night attack, green eyes, and a small blue letter drive the middle chapters. Escape and a clue carry the tale to its conclusion. Gibbs fills the story with wartime colour and a hero who must win his way back.
48249-signing-the-contract-and-what-it-c:
Signing the Contract and What It Cost is a novel in forty one chapters. A wanderer and a rescue open the tale, then one for life follows. A strange revelation and a betrothal come before the search begins. Floy resolve, love and pride, and a lost lost lost chapter build it.

Mrs Alden plays abettor, and Espy speaks his mind on the matter midway. Hetty comes to the rescue before a cruel blow and a great surprise land. A long lost deed, solicitors, and gilded misery fill the later chapters. The madame confesses, ghosts of the past rise, and lovers reunite at last. Found found found answers the lost cry near the overflowing cup close.
48371-a-spring-harvest:
A Spring Harvest is a book of poems by Geoffrey Bache Smith. Smith was a young Oxford man who went to war as an officer. He died of wounds in France in December 1916, aged twenty-two. The book came out in London in June 1918, after his death.

The poems were written at many times, one as early as 1910. A friend who saw the book through the press set their order. The last part holds only poems written once the war had begun. Some were made at Oxford, some in Wales, and many in France. Smith spent a year there from late 1915 to his death. The long poem at the end, on the burial of Sophocles, was sent from the trenches.
48524-motor-matt-s-queer-find-or-the-sec:
Motor Matt Queer Find, or The Secret of the Iron Chest, is number thirteen of the Motor Stories dime series. Street and Smith issued it at New York on 22 May 1909 for five cents. Weekly tales of thrilling adventure motor fiction formed the brand of the line. An illustration shows Matt tying a rope to the handles of an iron chest.

Chapter heads run from a hut by the bayou to an attack on the car. Smoke pictures, foul play, and dried frogs for luck fill the middle chapters. Plotters, a trail, and a black mystery raise the stakes for the boy hero. At close quarters come a night ride, a wreck, and the secret of the chest itself. Such weeklies gave young readers speed, machines, and peril in a cheap weekly dose.
48644-the-heart-of-the-red-firs-a-story-:
Ada Woodruff Anderson wrote The Heart of the Red Firs, a story of the Pacific Northwest put out in Boston in 1908. Charles Grunwald drew the pictures. Anderson gave the book to the few pioneers left who knew the Nisqually Trail before logging roads cut the Puget Sound hills.

The tale opens in a new school house, where a bold man walks in on the class. Camps at the headwaters, salmon boats, a house-raising, and a rockslide crowd the chapters. Loggers, teachers, and settlers test each other in the big fir woods. Anderson mixes love, pride, and rough work in a land still wild. Her book keeps the feel of the old trail days as the town builders close in.
48674-a-hundred-years-hence-the-expectat:
A Hundred Years Hence, The Expectations of an Optimist, is a book of forecasts by T Baron Russell, published in London in nineteen hundred five. Russell had written on poor law guardians and other public topics, as the title page notes. A Shakespeare motto argues that a man may prophesy from the seeds of his own time. Chapters start with the rate of progress itself.

Housing, travel, and population questions come next, followed by the man of business in the world to come. Russell projects the trends of Edwardian Britain a full century forward, in an optimist's key. Trade, towns, and daily life are all recast. The book is an early specimen of popular futurology.
48846-hawkins-electrical-guide-v-02-of-1:
Hawkins Electrical Guide, Number Two is a self-study manual on electricity, published by Theo Audel in 1914. The series motto runs: the thought is in the question, the information is in the answer. The guides offer a progressive course in question-and-answer form for engineers, electricians and students.

Volume two is devoted to the armature, the heart of the dynamo. Its contents run from the definition of the armature, through ring and drum windings, to commutation, brushes and construction. The contents are written as a study syllabus, naming the points each section settles.
48865-the-family-among-the-australian-ab:
B Malinowski studies kinship in The Family Among the Australian Aborigines, a sociological study from the University of London Press in 1913. It stands as volume two of the Monographs on Sociology, edited by L T Hobhouse and E A Westermarck. Malinowski took his doctorate at Cracow.

The first chapter sets out the problem and his method. Contradictions and obscurities about family and kinship in Australia, he argues, demand a careful account of the individual family itself. He explains how the evidence must be criticized: the writer's material, his way of getting it, and his purpose all weighed.
48880-rough-beast:
Roger Dee wrote "Rough Beast," a science fiction story of an escaped alien animal. The most dangerous, utterly vicious carnivore the Galactics knew had escaped to Earth. Because contact with Earth was forbidden, they knew little of it, which led to certain false conclusions. A picture by Barbereis illustrates the tale.

The beast is a Morid, fleeing a Federation ship in a stolen lifeboat. The field of an experimental thought reading station in the Florida Keys catches its attention, as a dark cave with a lamb inside might catch a wolf's. The lifeboat crashes in the mangroves near Dutchman's Key, seconds before its power plant explodes. The Morid emerges in snarling haste and vanishes, magenta furred, into the moonlit vegetation.
49252-hawkins-electrical-guide-v-06-of-1:
Hawkins Electrical Guide, number six of ten, is a course of study for engineers, electricians, and students, copyrighted in 1914 in New York. Its motto runs: the thought is in the question, the information is in the answer. The whole set teaches electricity by question and answer, with many illustrations.

This volume treats alternating current motors, from their classes and main parts to how they start and run. It weighs the faults and merits of the synchronous motor, its speed, its load changes, and its field strength. Such guides let working men study at home and gain a working knowledge of a new trade. Number six serves those already past the basics of the craft.
49253-hawkins-electrical-guide-v-07-of-1:
Hawkins and his staff wrote this electrical guide, copyrighted by Audel of New York in 1915. Guide number seven of ten teaches by questions, answers and illustrations, as its cover states. The thought is in the question and the information is in the answer, runs the motto at the front.

The course serves engineers, electricians and students who want a working knowledge of electricity. Alternating current systems fill this volume, from page 1531 onward in the contents. Advantages of alternating current, kinds of systems and vector summation open the lessons, with series and parallel circuits and transformer systems treated in question-and-answer form.
49371-the-waterways-of-the-pacific-north:
A historical paper by Clarence B Bagley, reprinted at Seattle in 1917. Macmillan had published it in a volume on the Pacific Ocean in history. Bagley spent his life gathering the region's written history. He disclaims being a professional writer of it. His subject is the Columbia, Puget Sound, and the Fraser. Only the Columbia and Fraser pierce the mountain wall, he notes.

Most exploration, he observes, came from the east. Mackenzie reached the great river's upper waters in 1793. Lewis and Clark followed in 1805, and Fraser and Thompson after them. Missionaries, fur men, and Fremont all travelled overland and downriver. Astoria alone was founded from the sea. Canoes, bateaux, and prairie schooners ruled transport for seventy years. Bagley's sketch maps how waterways built the Northwest.
49512-hawkins-electrical-guide-v-04-of-1:
Hawkins Electrical Guide Number Four is a study book for engineers, electricians, and students. Hawkins and his staff wrote it, and Theo Audel and Company of New York copyrighted it in 1914. The whole guide teaches by question and answer. Its motto says the thought is in the question and the information is in the answer.

This volume treats distribution systems first. It explains series and parallel wiring, feeders and mains, and the Edison three-wire system in its many forms. A long section then covers wires and wire calculation. It compares copper, iron, and other metals and gives rules for covered conductors. The book aims at a working knowledge a man could use on the job, not mere theory.
49675-hawkins-electrical-guide-v-05-of-1:
Hawkins and staff compiled an electrical guide in question and answer form, number five of ten, copyrighted in 1914 by Theo Audel of New York. Its motto runs: the thought is in the question, the information is in the answer. The course serves engineers, electricians, students, and any reader wanting a working knowledge of electricity. Guide five treats alternating currents across some seventy pages of the set.

Contents begin with the word alternating itself and the advantages of alternating current. Direct and alternating apparatus are compared. Principles follow in catechism form. Audel's guides taught tradesmen by self study for decades. The question format lets a reader drill exactly the point he missed.
49769-hawkins-electrical-guide-v-03-of-1:
Hawkins Electrical Guide Number Three is a study book on electricity, written by Hawkins and staff in question and answer form. Theo Audel printed it in New York, with a copyright of 1914. The motto at the front says the thought is in the question and the information is in the answer.

The third guide treats measuring tools and testing gear. Long sections explain the galvanometer in its many forms, from simple compass tools to mirrored types. Later pages cover standard cells, the volt and the ampere, and Ohm's law. Resistance boxes and the Wheatstone bridge get full treatment. The course was made for engineers, electricians, and students who needed working knowledge, learned step by step.
50015-on-the-edge-of-the-primeval-forest:
Albert Schweitzer wrote On the Edge of the Primeval Forest, first published in English in 1922 and reprinted many times since. Schweitzer, trained in theology, philosophy, and medicine, tells how he came to work as a doctor in equatorial Africa. C T Campion translated the book, and photographs show the Ogowe river country and the hospital at Lambarene.

Chapters mix the journey out and first impressions with dated journals from July 1913 through 1915. Others treat the lumbermen and raftsmen of the forest, its social problems, and two wartime Christmases at the station. The mission closes the account. Schweitzer wrote to win friends for his hospital, and the book made Lambarene known across Europe and America.
50036-my-country-tis-of-thee-or-the-unit:
Willis Fletcher Johnson, a journalist and historian, wrote this big popular book on the United States, past, present, and future. It is keyed to the Columbian Exhibition at Chicago of 1892 and 1893. A bird's eye view of the fair grounds opens the volume. Johnson had written lives of Sherman and accounts of Stanley in Africa and of the Johnstown flood.

The book adds the views of the country's leading men on the great issues of the future. A president and an ex president speak, along with senators, a cardinal, bishops, and generals, gathered by John Habberton. It is history and prophecy in one fat illustrated volume, sold to a nation admiring itself at a fair. The fair gives the book its frame and its pride.
50068-hawkins-electrical-guide-v-08-of-1:
Hawkins Electrical Guide Number Eight is one volume of a ten part course on electricity, built as questions and answers with many pictures. Its motto runs: the thought is in the question, the information is in the answer. The course was made for engineers, electricians, and students who wanted a working grasp of the field.

By the eighth volume the lessons reach advanced plant work, including the gains from heating feed water for boilers, with tables of pressures and heat values. Plain questions lead the student step by step, and each answer gives the rule or fact in direct terms. The set served self taught workers who kept the power plants, street railways, and lighting systems of the early electric age running.
50453-the-pest:
Teignmouth Shore wrote The Pest, a novel published at New York in 1909. Shore also wrote The Talking Master and Egomet, and shared The Fruit of the Tree with another hand. The catalog lists him as Shore, and the year as 1909.

Chapter one opens on a November afternoon in London: pavements slippery with greasy black mud and air yellow with evil tasting fog. George Maddison, tall, erect, and dark, walks slowly along. His eyes, ever ready to seize on any striking effect of color, note the mingled lights of the street. A painter in the fog is a fine start for a tale of London life. The pest of the title waits somewhere in the murk ahead of him. Shore writes Edwardian London with a journalist's eye.
50636-reports-of-trials-for-murder-by-po:
Reports of Trials for Murder by Poisoning is a law and science volume. Lathom Browne, a barrister of the Midland Circuit, shaped the reports. Stewart of Saint Thomas's Hospital laboratory added the chemical learning. Stevens and Sons, law publishers of London, brought it out in 1883. The poisons named are prussic acid, strychnia, antimony, arsenic, and aconitia.

Trials of Tawell, Palmer, Dove, and Madeline Smith fill the case list. Pritchard, Smethurst, and Lamson stand among the famed names tried here. A chemical introduction and notes on each poison frame the reports. The preface hopes the book will serve doctors and lawyers alike. Medical and chemical witness words stand in full where experts clashed. Townsend's form for grouping witness words by head guided the work. Science and moral proof stand split apart for the reader's eye.
50933-finding-the-worth-while-in-the-sou:
Finding the Worth While in the Southwest is a roam book by Charles Saunders, out in nineteen eighteen. A McBride house of New York brought the book out that spring. Saunders wrote a like book on California finds in past years. Parts run from Santa Fe through the Rio Grande towns and cliff homes. Dead towns of the salt flats and Acoma rock town fill next parts.

Zuni, called the core of the earth, and El Morro writ rock stand mid scheme. Navajo storied land and Hopi homes of peace fill more parts. Stone wood, Flagstaff base, and the Grand Canyon crown the scheme in rank. New Mexico is sun, hush, and adobe in the words of Lummis he quotes. Adobe is wall, fence, and crop ground of that land in one.
51008-two-weeks-in-august:
Frank Robinson wrote this science fiction story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in February 1951, with pictures by Elizabeth MacIntyre. The narrator works in an office with a man named McCleary, whom nobody can stand. McCleary tops every story: your child's bright remark, your new car's mileage, all fall before his bragging. Vacation time brings out the worst of it.

The narrator warns that the humblest events can spring from grand beginnings, and that space travel started just this way. Robinson builds a tall tale from office rivalry and holiday talk. The title's two weeks in August hold the key to the joke. It is an early work by a writer who later won fame for bigger novels.
51068-agatized-rainbows-a-story-of-the-p:
Agatized Rainbows is a guide to the Petrified Forest in stone hues. Its full title adds a story of that strange park in Arizona. Photos by park hands show the logs in their red and gold bands. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

Three woods of stone logs stand in the park in set tour stops. A log bridge spans a cut in the rock, held now by a beam for strength. The great log near the house of finds has the widest base of all. Flaked and shined bits in that house show the stone in full glow. The book aims to draw route folk to the parks of the north state.
51113-plays-written-by-sir-john-vanbrugh:
Plays Written by Sir John Vanbrugh, volume the first of two, collects the stage works of the Restoration dramatist. A London booksellers' group printed the set in 1776. This volume contains The Relapse, or Virtue in Danger; The Provok'd Wife, with a new scene; Aesop, in two parts; and The False Friend.

The front matter gives an account of the author's life and writings. Vanbrugh, an eminent dramatic writer, was the son of Giles Vanbrugh, a London merchant, and was born in the parish of Saint Stephen, Wallbrook, in 1666. The family had been merchants of great credit at Antwerp and came to England under Queen Elizabeth, fleeing persecution for religion. At nineteen Vanbrugh was sent to France for some years. The account notes drily that The Relapse was the first of his plays produced, though not the first he had written.
51126-the-princess-and-the-physicist:
The Princess and the Physicist is a science fiction story by Evelyn E Smith, taken from Galaxy Science Fiction for June 1955, with art by Kossin. A blurb says Zen the Omnipotent, elected a god, longed for real powers, for he was also Zen the All Put Upon, a galactic sucker.

Zen the Terrible lay quiet in the secret retreat that housed his body. He was glad he had had the forethought to demand a weekly holiday when godhood was first thrust upon him, hundreds of centuries before. It took some little time to find the drawbacks, and by then it was too late, for he had become the established church. Then a tendril of curiosity brings news of an Earth ship arrived unannounced. Space tale fans get a tired god and an Earth visit.
51136-nothing-but-the-best:
Nothing But the Best is a science fiction story by Alan Cogan, first printed in Galaxy magazine in September nineteen fifty six. Its hero, Charles Mead, stands on Hobson's Hill above his town. Four black metal boxes hide in the bushes behind him on the hill. Their antennae curve in to form an arch where light shimmers and shakes.

Mead steps into that arch and is smothered at once by darkness. He feels weightless, falling, with nothing to push against in the black spin. Then he stands on another Hobson's Hill, in a town much like his own. One proof of the switch is that a lumber firm from his world is gone. Each world he visits holds such small and large changes, he notes. He walks into town and rings the bell of a small brick house.
51448-the-border-and-the-buffalo-an-unto:
The Border and the Buffalo, an untold story of the Southwest plains, by John R Cook, was printed at Topeka, Kansas, by Crane and Company in 1907. Cook gives the book to his crippled wife, who patiently helped and encouraged him to write it. A portrait of Cook stands at the front.

He gives it also to Sol Rees, to Mortimer N Kress, called Wild Bill, and to the buffalo hunters who stood shoulder to shoulder in 1877. They fought Kiowas, Comanches, and Staked Plains Apaches during the summer of 1877 on the Llano Estacado. The title promises the bloody border of Missouri and Kansas and the story of the slaughter of the buffalo. Cook calls himself an uneducated man of sixty three, with no pretensions to literary attainments. West fans get the last buffalo years.
51737-wau-bun-the-early-day-of-the-north:
Wau-Bun recounts the early day of the North-West on the American frontier. Juliette Kinzie wrote the memoir. The Caxton Club issued this edition at Chicago in 1901. Reuben Thwaites added an introduction and notes. A portrait of the author faces the title page.

The contents trace a journey and a residence. Chapters begin with departure from Detroit. They pass Mackinac and the fur trade. The party reaches Green Bay and travels the Fox River. Fort Winnebago becomes the centre of the tale. Garrison life and Indian payments fill the middle chapters. Winter journeys in canoes follow. Names of chiefs, traders, and officers crowd the pages. The edition was limited to a few hundred copies on handmade paper.
51772-the-brighton-boys-in-the-argonne-f:
The Brighton Boys in the Argonne Forest is a boys' war novel by Lieutenant James R Driscoll, published in Philadelphia by the John C Winston Company in 1920. It belongs to the Brighton Boys series. Sister volumes put the boys with the flying corps, in the trenches, with the battle fleet, and in the radio service.

Later titles take them to Cantigny, Chateau-Thierry, and Saint Mihiel, and across the Atlantic by air. This volume opens with Going In Again and To the Front. Starting a Big Job and Into the Jaws of Death promise the Argonne fighting. A frontispiece shows a soldier shouting to keep cool because the enemy must never reach them. Such series turned the Great War into schoolboy adventure within two years of the armistice. Driscoll's boys learn soldiering the way other series heroes learned football.
51800-wild-sports-in-the-far-west:
Gerstaecker, a German traveler, wrote this hunting diary of the American West, and Crosby and Nichols printed the translation at Boston in 1859. Weir designed its eight crayon drawings. Gerstaecker kept the diary for his family, then revised it when extracts in a German paper drew notice.

His preface warns sportsmen honestly. The West is not the plenty of the guidebooks. A settler may win independence faster than at home, but he pays in solitude, mosquitoes, and hunger. Chapters follow the voyage out, the march through the states, the swamps of Arkansas, and a hunting trip in the Ozarks. Deer tracks lead for days without a shot. Wet, cold, and alone, the hunter learns the price of freedom. The social picture is as sharp as the sport.
51931-how-to-bring-men-to-christ:
R A Torrey, superintendent of the Chicago Bible Institute, wrote this handbook for personal evangelism, entered for copyright in 1893. The front pages advertise his vest pocket companion of texts, arranged like medicine for the malady of each soul. Torrey's preface gives the motto: not every soul needs the same dose.

The first chapter treats the general conditions of success in bringing men to Christ. Then come how to begin, and dealing with the various classes of sinners. The book is a practical manual of the Moody school: texts classified for use, arguments made plain, and the worker sent out with a method. It went through many printings among evangelical churches.
52203-the-comic-almanack-volume-1-an-eph:
Chatto and Windus bound up nine years of a famous comic yearly in one volume at London. The first series of The Comic Almanack covers 1835 to 1843. George Cruikshank supplied many hundred cuts.

The title page names the writing team. Thackeray stands first. Albert Smith, Gilbert A Beckett, and the brothers Mayhew join him. Robert Brough and Tom Hood the elder also had a hand. The notice praises Cruikshank's run of nineteen years on the yearly. Thackeray's Stubbs' Calendar, the tale of the fatal boots, first saw print here. Each year mixes merry tales, comic verse, and quips with the calendar. The preface calls these almanacks among Cruikshank's finest work. They catch London humour in the years when Dickens was rising.
52204-the-comic-almanack-volume-2-an-eph:
The Comic Almanack, second series, gathers the yearly issues from 1844 to 1853 of an ephemeris in jest and earnest. Chatto and Windus published the collected volume in London. Its writers include Thackeray, Albert Smith, Gilbert Beckett, and the brothers Mayhew, with hundreds of illustrations by George Cruikshank and other artists.

A notice for the first series boasts nearly a thousand woodcuts and steel engravings. The almanack for 1844 opens with simple rules for interpreting acts of Parliament, advising readers to avoid the preamble, which confuses rather than enlightens. Each year mixed merry tales, humorous poetry, quips, and oddities with the calendar. The Comic Almanack was a Victorian institution, carrying the best comic writing and drawing of its day into a cheap yearly.
52562-the-unbidden-guest:
The Unbidden Guest, by Ernest William Hornung, is a novel set in Australia. Longmans, Green issued it at New York in 1894 in full. Arabella Teesdale opens the tale, reading while her father drives home from Melbourne. The farm parlour, fly proofed and stuffy, sets the colonial scene at once.

Chapter titles promise a bad beginning and a matter of twenty pounds. A watch and a pipe, moonlight sport, and the saving of Arabella follow. Two Miriams and a day of reckoning drive the plot to its close. Face to face scenes and a last encounter end the twenty one chapters. Bush life and English ties cross through the story of the guest.
52939-life-of-john-knox-fifth-edition-vo:
A fifth form of the life of John Knox fills two books, this being the first. Knox was the great voice of the Scots church reform. The book's full title notes its plates of his world. Old spell forms stand as they were first set in print. Page marks from the old book are kept in this text for aid.

Knox's youth, school years, and first faith steps lead the tale. His clash with queens and priests builds through the book. Calls, flights, and bold speech mark his road year by year. The life is told from the reform side with warm zeal. Church past fans get the core tale in full dress. Volume two holds the rest of his road.
52940-life-of-john-knox-fifth-edition-vo:
Thomas McCrie wrote this life of John Knox. It carries illustrations of the history of the Reformation in Scotland, with notices of the reformers and sketches of Scottish literature in the sixteenth century. Blackwood at Edinburgh and Cadell at London published the fifth edition in 1831, and this is the second volume, fronted by a portrait of James Stuart, Earl of Murray.

The contents open with the seventh period: Knox back in Edinburgh, urging the settlement of church polity against the nobles' dislike. He was employed in compiling the Book of Discipline, approved by the General Assembly and subscribed by the Privy Council. McCrie sketches the form of the reformed church, its attention to education, and the avarice of the nobility. He treats the Reformation's influence on literature, the introduction of Hebrew into Scotland, the return of Buchanan, and answers Hume on the rudeness of the Scots.
52996-selected-articles-on-the-parcels-p:
Selected Articles on the Parcels Post is a debaters’ handbook of readings on a live question of its day. The Debaters’ Hand Book Series put such volumes into schools and clubs. Kindred titles in the series treated capital punishment and direct primaries. Income tax, woman suffrage, and child labor had volumes of their own.

A parcels post meant letting the post office carry packages like the express companies. Farmers and small towns backed the plan with heat. Express firms and their friends fought it in print and in Congress. A handbook gathers the best articles on both sides of such a fight. Debaters could then arm themselves for the school hall contest. Spelling varies in the book, as the editor left each writer his own style.
5301-the-imperialist:
Sara Jeannette Duncan's Imperialist, published in 1904, is set in the Canadian town of Elgin. Old Mother Beggarlegs presides like a venerable stooping hawk over a market stall of gingerbread horses, round cookies, and brown sticky taffy. Children speculate about her past, but she will never tell, and only children have time to wonder.

From that small-town opening, Duncan builds a novel of Canadian politics, imperial loyalty, and the pull of Britain against the United States. The book offers a sharp, witty portrait of a young dominion arguing about its future, through characters rooted in a single Ontario town.
5315-told-in-the-east:
Talbot Mundy's Told in the East, published by Bobbs-Merrill in 1920. It was reprinted in the omnibus Romances of India, and gathers three stories: Hookum Hai, For the Salt Which He Had Eaten, and Machassan Ah. Hookum Hai opens with a blood-red sun resting on a low mud wall, above dried acacia trees, in a landscape of heat and dust.

Mundy writes of India with the colour and pace of popular adventure, following soldiers, traders, and local rulers through loyalty, salt, and honour. Readers get three linked tales of British India, in which oaths and debts matter. Desert roads shape the action, from a writer who knew the region's stories well.
53551-sarita-the-carlist:
Marchmont, author of By Right of Sword, wrote Sarita, the Carlist. McLeod and Allen entered the novel at Toronto in 1902, under Canada's copyright act.

Ferdinand Carbonnell tells the tale, and calls himself the victim of a woman's preference. A marriage refused sets exile and intrigue in motion. The plot runs through Carlist plotters in Spain and scenes in London. Sarita Castelar stands at its heart. Chapters promise an abduction, a rescue, a fight, and war to the knife. Quesada gives his own version of events, and Sarita at last hears the truth. Marchmont piles twist on twist in his brisk, romantic style.
53821-julius-the-street-boy-or-out-west:
Horatio Alger wrote Julius, the Street Boy, or Out West, for Donohue of Chicago and New York. Julius, a New York bootblack, tells his mate Patrick Riley that he has retired from business. His uncle, he jokes, has gone up the river to Sing Sing for his health. Julius himself will go west in a few days, for his own health, he says. He will travel with a man named O'Connor and a lot of other boys.

Julius means to live on a farm or in a store, and grow up respectable. Pat doubts the country can match the city for life. Alger builds his tale on that move, from street trade to a fresh start. Young readers get city slang, pluck, and a boy's bid for a clean life.
53918-the-woman-the-priest:
The Woman and the Priest is a novel by Grazia Deledda, translated from the Italian by Mary Steegmann and first published in London by Jonathan Cape in 1922. Deledda sets her story in a remote Sardinian hill village. The translator's note calls the village half civilized and superstitious.

The chief interest, the note says, is psychological. Two figures, a woman and a priest named Paul in the text, carry the drama. All the action runs within the space of two days, and the drama between the two is woven through it. Fourteen chapters hold the short, intense tale. Deledda's Sardinian novels made her Italy's best-known woman novelist of the day. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
53940-haw-ho-noo-or-records-of-a-tourist:
Haw-Ho-Noo, or Records of a Tourist, is a travel and lore book by Charles Lanman, author of Letters from the Alleghany Mountains. Lippincott, Grambo of Philadelphia published it in 1850. Lanman inscribes it affectionately to William Cullen Bryant, in whom, he writes, are blended the exalted attributes of the poet and the man. His address to the public is combative.

The title and contents, he says, contain all he has to say of the book's character. His only apology for appearing again is the kindness of the critics toward his former productions. One exception, the North American Review, he attacks as cruel and undeserved. The title itself comes from Native tradition. A passage preserved in the copy explains the phrase as the country upheld on the back of a turtle. A portion of the volume, he adds, is devoted to the traditionary lore of the Aborigines.
54022-dorothy-dale-in-the-west:
Margaret Penrose was the pen name of Lilian Garis, who wrote the Dorothy Dale books for Cupples and Leon. Dorothy Dale in the West appeared in 1915, tenth in a series that began with Dorothy Dale: A Girl of To-day. A picture shows Dorothy walking right up to a pony's head.

Garis also wrote the Motor Girls series under the same name, and her girls travel, camp, and motor through every volume. Out west, Dorothy meets ranch life with the same pluck she used at Glenwood School. The series sold at sixty cents a volume to girls who wanted motion in their stories. Garis, one of the Stratemeyer syndicate's fastest hands, kept Dorothy in print for two decades.
54075-windmills-picturesque-and-historic:
F H Shelton of Philadelphia wrote Windmills, Picturesque and Historic: The Motors of the Past. The piece is reprinted from the Journal of the Franklin Institute for February 1919, printed by Lippincott. Shelton opens with two doctrines of invention. The pessimist calls man a lazy animal who invents machines to save work. The optimist calls him industrious, inventing to accomplish more. Either way, no contrivance beats the windmill for beauty and use.

The windmill was the world's principal motor for some eight hundred years, Shelton says. Steam, electricity, and gasoline came later; the windmill harnessed the wind first. Steam came in early in the nineteenth century, and by 1825 the great English cities had it. Before steam, power meant men, beasts, wind, or water. Water needed falls and leveled country was shut out, but the wind blew everywhere.
54480-the-tell-tale-an-original-collecti:
The Tell-Tale, printed in London by Harris and Son in 1823, calls itself an original collection of moral and amusing stories. The book was made for young readers, with pictures. Its plates carry the date April 20, 1823, and the name of the firm by St Paul's churchyard.

The first tale, Arphu, or The Fairy Kitten, opens with a boy, William Dormer, in talk with his mother. From there the book moves through short tales meant to amuse and to teach at once. Such mixed fare was the stock of the early children's book trade. Readers now meet the plain, earnest style that London shops sold to families in the 1820s, lessons and all.
55093-life-in-the-far-west:
George Frederick Ruxton, a young British officer, wrote these sketches of life in the far west. They first ran in Blackwood's Magazine and were published in book form at Edinburgh in 1849. The head carries his death notice. The London papers of October 1848 told of his death at Saint Louis, at the early age of twenty-eight. He had been a lieutenant of the Eighty-ninth regiment.

Ruxton had traveled Mexico and then the Rocky Mountain fur country, hunting and trapping with the mountain men. His sketches of their speech, camps, and dangers are among the truest ever written. He died on his way home with the book unfinished. Few writers packed so much seeing into so short a life.
55297-hazelhurst:
Hazelhurst is a novel by Enid Leigh Hunt, published in London in 1908. Hunt also wrote The Advent of Arthur. A picture shows Gerald carving the mutton while Teddie serves the vegetables. The prologue introduces the Le Mesurier family, owners of Hazelhurst for three or four hundred years.

The great house now stands stripped bare: rooms empty of furniture, hangings gone, floors uncovered. The family's strong voices ring through the hollow galleries. The prologue sets a tale of an old house and a family in decline. The novel follows the present generation of Le Mesuriers in their emptied home.
55332-the-republic-of-ragusa-an-episode-:
Luigi Villari wrote a history of the republic of Ragusa, printed at London in 1904 with many illustrations by William Hulton. Marino Caboga stands at the front. Various accounts of Dalmatia have been written in English, the preface says. Many of them include a historical survey of Ragusa, but the only special histories of the town itself are in German or Italian, and even those are not by any means complete.

The best is Professor Gelcich's little book on the civil development of Ragusa, a perfect mine of information, he says. But it treats internal growth, archaeology, and architecture, and does not dwell on the town's international position, which for foreign readers is its most important aspect. Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik, held its freedom for ages between Venice and the Turks. Villari tells how the small republic traded, bribed, and endured.
55374-frank-reade-jr-fighting-the-terror:
Frank Reade Junior Fighting the Terror of the Coast is a dime tale by Noname. It ran as sheet forty nine of the Frank Reade Weekly on October second, nineteen three. Five cents bought that sheet from the Tousey house of New York. Its cuts show the air ship Jove sweep past a schooner in flight. Frank climbs a lad rope while shot flies at him in that scene.

Part names run from an air ship chase to a pirate hoard end. A hard fall, a tip in the air, and Pomp flight fill first parts. Coast fear, land gun fire, and mud stuck turns crowd mid parts. Pirate den raid and one ship end lead to the save part close. A swarthy ride man bursts in town with word of the air ship trial.
560-mr-standfast:
John Buchan returns Richard Hannay to war work in this sequel to Greenmantle, dedicated to South African troops. Hannay, cured of dyspepsia yet restless, hunts a German spy ring through English villages, Picardy chateaus, and Alpine passes. Andrew Amos, Blenkiron, and a cage of wild birds mark the chase.

Buchan writes with warm, steady vigor, mixing spy craft with Bunyan echoes in chapter titles. The tale ends with an exile's return and a summons for Mr. Standfast himself. The novel stands as a strong wartime adventure, where duty, friendship, and faith carry a man through.
56169-billy-to-morrow-stands-the-test:
Sarah Pratt Carr wrote this school and home novel for young readers, issued in 1911. It is a later book in her Billy To-morrow series. Billy Bennett, called Billy To-morrow, is a high school boy who keeps putting things off. His friend Erminie and a teacher named Pop Streeter play large parts in his life.

The chapters move from class-room stir to games, a scout, a fight, and a night of trouble. Billy must speak up, stand by his word, and face the results of delay. Erminie's own doubts and choices are woven through his tests. The tale ends with Billy winning through, not by luck, but by learning to act when action is due.
56262-when-we-were-strolling-players-in-:
Louise Jordan Miln wrote When We Were Strolling Players in the East, published in New York in 1896. Miln travelled with a theatre company through India, Burma, China, and nearby lands. Her book first appeared in part in the Pall Mall Gazette and the Pall Mall Budget. She thanks editors and photographers in Calcutta, Colombo, and Rangoon for help and pictures.

Chapters recall her first glimpse of the Orient, a rickshaw ride, and the Burra Bazaar in Calcutta. She describes a Christmas dinner on a roof, Hindu weddings and funerals, and Burmese burials and bridals. King Theebaw's state barge, an opium den in Shanghai, Hong Kong, and Canton follow. The book blends stage life with travel writing.
56391-the-little-london-directory-of-167:
A small book printed in 1863 reproduces the oldest printed list of London names and addresses, a catalogue first published in 1677. The 1863 editor kept the errors and odd spellings of the old book, and he called it almost a facsimile. Only spacing has been condensed in this transcription, and the introduction explains the deliberate faithfulness of the reprint.

Directories began with such lists of merchants and tradesmen, and the 1677 catalogue is a landmark of London topography and genealogy. Names, trades, and streets of Restoration London fill its pages, and historians mine it for the business geography of the city. The reprint served Victorian antiquaries tracing old London families, and it served them as they traced those families.
56571-the-birth-of-civilization-in-the-n:
The Birth of Civilization in the Near East is a work of archaeology by Henri Frankfort, first published by Indiana University Press in 1951 and reissued in Doubleday's Anchor Books. Frankfort was born in 1897 in Holland and studied history at Amsterdam. His main field project was the Oriental Institute of Chicago's excavations in Iraq, from 1929 to 1937, which he organized and headed.

Those digs yielded much new information on the early history of Babylonia, from 4000 to 2000 before Christ. In 1938 he went to Chicago to teach, and in 1949 he became director of the Warburg Institute in London. He died in 1954. The plates preserved in the copy reach further back than Babylonia. One shows a bone sickle haft with its end carved as a goat's head, grooved for flints, from a Natufian cave site.
56742-survey-of-the-high-roads-of-englan:
Survey of the High Roads of England and Wales, part one, was arranged by Edward Mogg. Mogg published it in London in 1817. He gives the work to the Prince Regent. The maps are planned at one inch to a mile. Counties covered run from Kent and Surrey to Devon and Cornwall. Part of Buckingham and Middlesex is added. The sheets show the seats of nobles and gentry near each road.

Branch roads, towns, rivers, and canals are marked. Railways and turnpike gates appear as well. Indexes give topographical and descriptive notes. Mogg claims the roads of England had never been drawn on so large a scale. He hopes to fill that gap for travellers. The atlas blends map, guide, and gazetteer in one grand plan.
56895-a-yankee-flier-in-the-far-east:
Al Avery wrote a boys' war tale of a Yankee flyer in the Far East. The book came out in New York in 1942. Paul Laune drew the pictures for it. Stan Wilson is the flyer at its core. A front plate shows Stan as he strafes a car from the air.

Stan rests in Singapore, then joins the China air arm. The Flying Tigers take him in for scout and rescue work. Attack, jail at Kula, and a shrine with a red roof fill the mid parts. A jungle trail and a glory trail close the book. Young war fans get fast flight and brave deeds. The tale moves at full speed.
57017-the-heritage-of-unrest:
The Heritage of Unrest is a novel of the southwestern frontier by Gwendolen Overton, published by Macmillan in 1901 and reprinted several times within the year. The story follows soldiers of a cavalry troop in the desert country, among them a private named Cabot and his lieutenant, Landor, a friend from boyhood in the East.

The opening is a small essay on sacrifice: to fill a ditch for others is one thing, to die unavailingly, an obstacle in the way, is another. Cabot faces the second fate as his horse dies under him in the white dust. Cabot, beside himself with fear of the burning desert, jerks the bridle and kicks the dying horse. Landor rides back and looks down in silence. The scene sets the novel's terms of fear, rank and wasted youth in the cavalry.
57033-the-harmonicon-part-the-first:
The Harmonicon, Part the First, is a music journal volume for 1833, printed at London for Longman and partners. Its title page promises essays, criticisms, biography, foreign reports, and miscellaneous correspondence. The contents run to pieces on composers and singers of the day, from Vincenzo Righini to the tenor Rubini and the bass Tamburini.

An index of names lists Kircher and Mersenne among the old writers on music, and Metastasio among the poets. The transcriber's notes to this text warn that some foreign musical reports in the contents match no passage in the text. Numbering in some tables is kept as printed, since the source of the error cannot be told. The Harmonicon was a leading musical magazine of its decade. Its pages record the concert life, opera, and criticism of London and Europe in the year 1833. Part the First gathers the first half of that year.
57276-yellow-star-a-story-of-east-and-we:
Elaine Goodale Eastman wrote this novel, published at Boston in 1911, and called it a story of East and West. Eastman knew both worlds: she taught in Indian schools in Dakota and married a Sioux doctor. Her heroine is a girl from Dakota who comes east to school. The dedication verse praises a child of the prairie with fires from native kings and Pilgrim sires in one breast.

Chapters move from Laurel folks to a lesson in history, a wild west performance, and Indian hospitality. Angel De Cora and William Lone Star, both Native artists, drew the pictures. The tale turns on what the girl's mixed heritage means in an eastern school world. It speaks to young readers about pride, belonging, and two Americas meeting.
57473-the-yellow-pearl-a-story-of-the-ea:
The Yellow Pearl, a Story of the East and the West, is a novel by Adeline M Teskey. Hodder and Stoughton and the George H Doran Company of New York published it in 1911. Teskey had written Where the Sugar Maple Grows before it. The tale is told in the first person, as a young woman's own record, opening with a dated entry of the first of March.

The narrator is the daughter of an American man and a Chinese woman. Her father was a Commissioner of Customs in China who fell in love with her mother there and married her. Arriving in her father's country, the girl overhears her Aunt Gwendolin call the marriage a monstrous thing, above all because the bride was a heathen Chinese. The novel works out that prejudice from inside the family it wounds.
57476-philip-the-story-of-a-boy-violinis:
Philip, the story of a boy violinist, by an author who signs with initials only, was published in Boston, New York, and London in 1898. Twenty chapters follow Philip from his home to a concert and a fire near the end. Heads name his mother, his father, a mining tragedy, Aunt Delia's secret, Lord Ashden's plan, and a trip to Italy.

Philip's days are spent in a place of great heights and depths, long halls and galleries, with people passing to and fro. Not a grand hotel, the narrator says, but a deep, dark mine, where Philip and his mother pass sun-bright days in a sort of living death, with no grass, flowers, or sky. Music becomes the boy's path out of the pit toward light and fame.
57509-the-mercer-boys-at-woodcrest:
Capwell Wyckoff wrote The Mercer Boys at Woodcrest, a boys' adventure book printed in 1948. Don and Jim Mercer reach Woodcrest, a school for cadets, with their friend Terry Mackson. An old empty house on the grounds, Clanhammer Hall, draws their eye at once.

Soon a bigger puzzle takes over: Colonel Morrell, the head of the school whom the boys have never seen, has vanished. With help from Cadet Vench, the boys do their own sleuth work and dig up a wild tale of crime. Chapters move through a sunlit message, a man with a key, a night trip, and a fight on the ice before the truth comes out.
57564-hall-caine-the-man-and-the-novelis:
Hall Caine: The Man and the Novelist is a critical biography by Fred Kenyon, published by Greening of London in 1901. It is number four in the series English Writers of To-day. Kenyon writes of a living man much in the light of public opinion and still a subject of controversy. He takes every responsibility himself for errors of judgment or taste in the work.

The chapters run from an introduction to Caine's childhood and youth, then to the years 1879 to 1884. His novels follow one by one: The Shadow of a Crime and A Son of Hagar, then The Deemster. Caine as dramatist, short-story writer, poet, and critic gets a chapter. The Bondman, The Scapegoat, The Manxman, The Christian, and The Eternal City close the survey.
57707-the-great-war-of-189-a-forecast:
A team of soldiers and war writers produced The Great War of 189, a forecast first printed in the magazine Black and White. Heinemann issued the second edition in London in 1895. Sketches made for the magazine fill the book.

Admiral Colomb, officers Maurice and Maude, Forbes, Lowe, Murray, and Scudamore planned the tale together. It begins with an attempt on the life of Prince Ferdinand of Bulgaria. Russian troops move on the Austrian frontier, and the first clash with German troops follows. A Russian balloon bombs Varna in the front picture, its load bursting above the tallest buildings. Paris seethes with warlike excitement in the contents. The book imagines the great war a generation before it came.
5772-ae-in-the-irish-theosophist:
George William Russell, known as AE, writes on theosophy and mysticism in AE in the Irish Theosophist. Contents include a word on the objects of the Theosophical Society. The Twilight Hour, The Mask of Apollo, and The Secret of Power follow. The Priestess of the Woods, A Tragedy in the Temple, and essays on waking, dreaming, and deep sleep complete the set. Verse by AE closes the collection.

Readers meet Irish mysticism at its most poetic, where myth, vision, and spiritual practice blend. Russell treats consciousness as a landscape to explore, with gods and symbols as guides rather than dogmas. The book suits readers of Yeats's circle, Irish literature, and esoteric thought, offering short, luminous pieces that reward slow, reflective reading.
57823-twenty-four-discourses-on-some-of-:
Twenty-Four Discourses gathers sermons preached to a church in Hartford, Connecticut, around the year 1795. The transcriber of this copy notes that the church was most likely Congregational. The minister's name is not given in the front pages of this copy.

The sermons take up what the title calls important and interesting subjects of religion. They were likely written down from the minister's notes or by hearers as he spoke. The dedication at the front gives the reason the book was printed. The printing itself was done by several hands of mixed skill, the transcriber notes, with the tight spacing of old shop work. Sermon books like this one were how a noted local preacher's voice outlived his pulpit, and they show plain American preaching of the early republic.
57854-what-norman-saw-in-the-west:
What Norman Saw in the West was written by the author of Four Days in July and A Winter at Woodlawn. Carlton and Porter published it at New York for the Sunday School Union in 1859. Eight pictures illustrate it, among them the Falls of Minnehaha and the Falls of Saint Anthony. A line from Margaret Fuller heads the book, on a life enriched by Niagara, the great lakes, and the prairie scenes.

Norman's road runs by railway to Niagara, then to the Queen City of the lake, the Rock River, and the Mississippi. Indian stories, a picnic, a camp meeting, and a Sunday in Dubuque fill the river days. Chicago, Mackinaw, Toronto, and Niagara once more bring him home. It is a western tour told for young Sunday school readers.
58068-wagner-as-man-artist:
Ernest Newman set out in 1914 to judge Richard Wagner whole, as man and as artist, in this London study. The contents show his method. First comes a long look at the man: childhood, marriages, loves, temper, and egoism in friendship. Then a second part takes up the artist in theory. A front picture shows Richard and Cosima Wagner together.

Newman tests Wagner's own life-story, Mein Leben, for trust, and takes up famous quarrels case by case. Then he turns to the writings, Art and Revolution, The Art-Work of the Future, and Opera and Drama, and to Wagner and Beethoven. Newman became the standard English writer on Wagner, and this book shows why: clear-eyed about the man's faults, and serious about the music's claims.
58456-the-south-devon-coast:
Charles Harper wrote The South Devon Coast, a guide to the shore of south Devon, printed in London in 1907. The catalog lists no author, but the title page names Harper, who wrote many books on old roads and coasts. His route runs west past small ports, cliffs, and bathing towns.

Town by town he mixes place lore, past tales, and notes on what the eye can see. Early stops take in a great landslip, the port of Seaton, smuggler tales at Beer, and Sidmouth. Walkers and armchair guests alike get a rich, slow tour of a loved shore in the years before cars filled the lanes.
58589-the-boys-and-girls-pliny-being-par:
John S White edited The Boys' and Girls' Pliny for Putnam's Sons, with copyright in eighteen eighty-five. White was headmaster of the Berkeley School. He had edited like volumes of Plutarch and Herodotus for the young. Fifty-two pictures fill this one.

The book gives parts of Pliny's Natural History in a form for boys and girls. It opens with Pliny's own dedication to his friend Titus Vespasian. Book two takes up the world and its elements. Stars, comets, and the teachings of Hipparchus follow in short chapters. White trims the vast Roman work to a size young readers can carry. Wonder at nature is its whole aim.
58775-the-north-devon-coast:
The North Devon Coast, by Charles Harper, surveys a famed stretch of English shore. Harper wrote road books by the shelf, as the front list shows for him. The Portsmouth Road, The Dover Road, and The Bath Road stand in that roll. The Exeter Road and The Great North Road follow in the same advertisement.

The Norwich Road, The Holyhead Road, and the Cambridge road fill out his list. Each volume mixes history, fashion, and frivolity of an old highway in his manner. Cliffs, combes, and fishing towns of north Devon give this volume its matter. Smugglers, wreckers, and poets of the coast walk through its local tales. Road and coast lore for the motor age fills the Harper tour books.
58800-the-girl-of-the-golden-west:
David Belasco novelized his own play as The Girl of the Golden West, printed in New York under copyright in 1911, with pictures by Marchand. A front quote sets the scene in strange days, when people came from all over to the gold country of California. The play had been a stage hit, and the novel let readers keep the tale at home.

The Girl runs a saloon in a mining camp, and a road agent under a false name wins her heart. Belasco loads the plot with pursuit, loyalty, and a famous poker game for a man's life. Readers get a ripe western melodrama, the same tale that soon served as the base for a famed opera.
58892-the-kentish-coast:
Charles Harper, whose road books covered the Portsmouth, Dover, Bath, and Brighton roads, turned to the Kentish coast in this volume, published by Chapman and Hall at London in 1914. A motto from the Second Part of Henry the Sixth praises Kent as the civilest place of all the isle, full of riches, its people liberal, valiant, active, wealthy.

Harper begins at Deptford, with Peter the Great's stay there, and moves to Greenwich, its royal naval hospital, the Fubbs yacht, and the Greenwich whitebait dinners. Woolwich follows, with the Princess Alice disaster, Lesnes Abbey, Erith, and Dartford. Later chapters run down the shore past the white cliffs to Dover Castle, pictured at the front. The book mixes history, anecdote, and description in Harper's road-book manner, treating each town as a stage in a journey along the Channel coast of Kent.
58934-the-somerset-coast:
The Somerset Coast is a topographical travel book by Charles Harper, published by Chapman and Hall in 1909. Harper had written the standard road books of England. This volume walks the Somerset shore from the Avon to Exmoor.

Harper opens with a joke against himself. When he confided to friends and journalists that he meant to write on the Somerset coast, they assured him with disconcerting unanimity that there is no coast of Somerset. The contents answer them: Clifton suspension bridge, Clevedon with its Coleridge and Tennyson associations, Weston-super-Mare, the Holms in the channel, Brent Knoll and Burnham. The book is Harper's method entire, history, literature and gossip gathered at walking pace along a shore his critics said did not exist.
58973-shackleton-s-last-voyage-the-story:
Shackleton Last Voyage, the story of the Quest, was written by Commander Frank Wild and printed in London in 1923. Wild drew on the official journal and the private diary of Dr A H Macklin. More than one hundred photos and maps fill the book.

Wild gives the book to the Boss, as the crew called Sir Ernest Shackleton, with a verse by Gerald Gould on ships that sail away. Plates show Shackleton in polar clothing, John Quiller Rowett who paid for the trip, and views of the small ship Quest. The voyage was Shackleton last, and he died on the way south. His men tell the tale of the ship, the seas, and the loss of their chief. Polar readers get a loyal, first hand final chapter.
59315-the-periodical-cicada-the-17-year-:
The Periodical Cicada is a farm leaflet from the agriculture office of the United States. Its number in that leaflet set is three hundred and ten. The text came from scans held by a large web archive group. It tells of an insect found in the east half of the land and no place else.

Broods sleep in the soil for years, then rise by the million in spring. The north broods take seventeen years, and the south broods take thirteen. Adults sing from dawn to dusk, mate, lay eggs, and die in weeks. The adult is black with red eyes and veins of orange in clear wings. First white settlers took the swarms for the locust plagues of the Bible.
59420-use-of-mines-in-trench-warfare-fro:
Use of Mines in Trench Warfare, from the French School of St Cyr, was translated and edited at the Army War College. The Government Printing Office at Washington printed it in July 1917, as War Department document 635. It is marked confidential, for official use only. It is not to be taken into front line trenches. The adjutant general's note publishes the French notes for the American army then training for France.

Trench mining meant digging tunnels under enemy lines and blowing them up: slow, terrifying work. The French had two years of it to teach. This manual passes on their galleries, charges, and listening methods.
5952-the-bobbsey-twins-in-the-great-west:
Laura Lee Hope takes the Bobbsey family west for a new round of holiday adventures. Bert and his small brother Freddie appear early, full of plans for snowmen and snowball games, while Flossie and the rest of the household share the trip. The book stands late in a long series of Bobbsey tales.

The western setting gives the children fresh ground to explore and fresh scrapes to get out of. As in the houseboat book, the pleasure lies in family company and small, lively incidents. Young readers follow a familiar set of siblings through unfamiliar country.
59601-mary-louise-stands-the-test:
Edith Van Dyne wrote Mary Louise Stands the Test, a girls' book published by Reilly and Lee at Chicago in 1921. It belongs to the Bluebird Books, the Mary Louise series. The frontispiece, by Harry Armstrong, shows Josie and Mary Louise together. Van Dyne was the pen name under which Baum, the author of Oz, wrote for older girls.

Earlier volumes had taken Mary Louise through the country, a mystery, and the war years with her Liberty Girls. This one opens with a small cloud on her sky. A visit to the Higgledy Piggledy Shop follows, and the test of the title builds from there.
