The series mixed schoolgirl life with detection, since Josie O'Gorman, Mary Louise's friend, was a detective's daughter with a bent for solving things.
59920-the-little-gods-a-masque-of-the-fa:
The Little Gods, a masque of the Far East, is a book of tales by Rowland Thomas. Little, Brown published it at Boston in 1909, with pictures by Charles Sarka. The stories had first appeared in Collier's and Everybody's Magazine. A prologue named The Little Gods frames chapters on Fagan, God's little devils, and the little man.

Later tales treat a ripple of patriotism, the superfluous man, and the valley of sunshine and shadow. What Okimi Learned and McGennis's Promotion close the set, with an epilogue. The front picture shows a deputy supervisor revealing the thrilling difference between a peach and an apple. Thomas wrote of the Philippines and the East as an American who had served there. His tales mix colonial officers, native folk, humour, and pathos. The prologue opens in a quiet New England house, seeking in vain for inspiration for his pen.
60214-ernesto-garcia-cabral-a-mexican-ca:
Ernesto Garcia Cabral, a Mexican Cartoonist is a small tribute book by Conway, printed in Mexico City in 1923. Only one hundred and fifty copies were made, for private circulation among friends. Each copy was to be inscribed at Christmas 1923, the front pages show.

A biographical foreword of some pages opens the book. Plates follow, showing Cabral's caricatures of Mexican public men. A former American president, Taft, stands late in the list of sitters. A noted artist called Dr Atl appears among them too. Conway asks readers to admire the genius and forgive the compiler's faults. Readers get a scarce keepsake on Mexico's great caricaturist.
60239-stories-of-the-east:
Leonard Woolf wrote the three tales in Stories of the East, printed and published in 1921 by Leonard and Virginia Woolf at their Hogarth Press in Richmond. The tales are A Tale Told by Moonlight, Pearls and Swine, and The Two Brahmans. The first opens at a country house on a hot June night, after dinner, in bright moonlight.

There a hard, blunt man named Jessop tells of battle, murder, and sudden death as plain facts of life. Guests who dislike his bluntness still find his grim tales hard to put down. Woolf draws on his years in the east for stories of force, faith, and fate.
60369-illustrated-history-of-furniture-f:
An Illustrated History of Furniture, first printed in 1892 and here in its fifth edition, traces chairs, beds, and tables from the earliest times to the end of the eighteenth century. Editions came fast, a second in 1892 and a third in 1893, which proves the hunger for the subject. The book is packed with drawings of real pieces in museums and great houses.

Furniture history teaches taste by showing how each age built for its life. Egypt, Greece, the Gothic hall, the French court, and the English home pass in carved review. Collectors, dealers, and makers all used the book as a pattern guide. Readers get a clear path through five thousand years of the maker's art.
60395-going-west:
Going West, by Basil King, was published by Harper and Brothers in June 1919, just after the Great War. Its hero Lester is no born fighter but a broker of old American stock: his father fought Spain, his grandfather in the Civil War, and his forebears the French and Indians. Duty, not taste, takes him to the border and then to France.

The first chapter jumps ahead to a trench, where Lester faces a burly German swinging a rifle while he fumbles to recall his bayonet drill. Then the book goes back to trace how a civilian came there. King wrote the home front's question: what does a peaceful man owe?
60590-dardistan-in-1866-1886-and-1893-be:
G W Leitner wrote Dardistan in 1866, 1886 and 1893. The Manjusri Publishing House issued it at New Delhi. The book supplements his Hunza and Nagyr Handbook. It also distills his Languages and Races of Dardistan. Gilgit, Chilas, and Kandia fill its scope. Yasin, Chitral, Hunza, and Nagyr join them.

History, religions, customs, and songs fill the work. Legends and fables of the Hindukush crowd it. A map of Dardistan and the Pamirs fronts it. Demons called Yatsh open the legends part. Fairies and wizards follow in their turn. A legend tells of Gilgit's founding there. The Feast of Firs and its songs come next. Riddles, proverbs, and fables fill a section. Polo and dances stand among its amusements. Birth, marriage, and funeral rites get full records. A scholar-administrator's vast notebook preserves the high valleys' lore between empire and the modern age.
6067-the-pony-rider-boys-in-the-rockies-:
Frank Gee Patchin opens with love of a horse, as Tad Butler begs Walter Perkins for two minutes on his pony. Walter hesitates, Tad insists he knows how to ride, and Chunky, whose well-rounded cheeks earned his nickname, backs him up with tales of Texas ponies and a broncho barely saddled once.

The Pony Rider Boys ride the Rockies in search of a lost secret, with Stacy Brown, Ned Rector, and Professor Zepplin along. Patchin writes brisk boy adventure, where riding skill, camp talk, and mountain trails matter most. The boys' pride in the saddle carries them into country that tests it.
60686-archibald-marshall-a-realistic-nov:
William Lyon Phelps, a Yale professor of English literature, wrote this study of the novelist Archibald Marshall, published at New York in 1919. A portrait of Marshall fronts it. Phelps dedicates the book to Chicago's English department, notable for scholars, teachers, and two creative artists. His first chapter is dated Tuesday, May 21, 1918, and begins with a memory. On a mellow autumn day in 1900 he sat on a bench in Dorchester talking with Thomas Hardy.

Hardy said, without emphasis beyond the weight of the words, that the basis of every novel should be a story. Phelps turns the remark over: what seems self-evident is often belied by most instances. Marshall, the realistic novelist of English country life, is his proof case. The book is appreciative criticism from the age when professors championed living novelists in print.
60710-the-geology-of-groton-state-forest:
Robert Christman wrote The Geology of Groton State Forest, published in 1956 by the Vermont Geological Survey. The state forester and the Vermont Development Commission joined in issuing it. Christman, working under the state geologist Charles Doll, describes the rocks of a public forest in northern Vermont. A cover picture looks south along Groton Pond from near Stillwater Brook.

Granite and its related rocks come first. Light ledges of granite crown most of the hills, on Owlshead, Little Deer, Big Deer, and other summits. Smaller outcrops appear along brooks, the railroad, and the outlet of Groton Pond. Christman argues that all these ledges belong to one great mass of granite running deep below the surface. Soil and glacial rubble hide most of it, so its full extent can only be guessed. The survey gives walkers and foresters a clear account of what lies under the trees of Groton.
6102-from-jest-to-earnest:
E. P. Roe dedicates From Jest to Earnest to his friend of youth and maturer years, Reverend A. Moss Merwin, a missionary in a foreign land who left every earthly ambition open at home. The novel begins with a practical joke and its victim, puzzled and interested, then a little pagan and plain talk.

A sleigh ride and something more, another spell than beauty's, finding one's level, and the other set follow. Midnight vigils, a preacher taught by the pagan, and the dawning light carry Hemstead toward earnestness. Roe turns jest into conversion, showing how a joke can open a life to serious faith.
61025-on-the-track-of-ulysses-together-w:
On the Track of Ulysses is a book of travels by Stillman, issued at Boston and New York in 1888, with copyright in 1887. Its subtitle calls it two studies in archaeology made during a cruise among the Greek islands. The catalog title here is the start of that long subtitle.

One study follows Ulysses' wanderings across the real seas. The other goes in quest of the so called Venus of Melos and its story. Stillman dedicates the book to Wendell Phillips Garrison with warm praise. His rectitude in an age of scramble renews faith in humanity, he writes. Readers get a scholar sailor's hunt for Homer's world among the islands.
61195-diversions-of-a-naturalist:
Sir Ray Lankester gathered his short pieces as Diversions of a Naturalist, first published in nineteen fifteen. Lankester was a senior British man of science, and the book carries forty-four pictures. The pieces range far from the lab bench to shore, field, and fjord.

Chapters treat seals, grouse, sand, amber, and the small life of the sea beach. Sea worms, anemones, crabs, and barnacles each get close study. Later pieces turn to courtship in beasts and men, then to apes and man. Skeletons, brains, and minds are set side by side. The style stays light while the facts stay firm.
61385-the-last-chance-a-tale-of-the-gold:
The Last Chance, a tale of the golden West, is an Australian novel by Rolf Boldrewood, author of Robbery Under Arms, published by Macmillan at London and New York in 1905.

Its opening chapter presents Arnold Banneret, a commissioner of goldfields and police magistrate in New South Wales whose pay barely passes the necessaries of life. The necessaries are catalogued with dry humour: horses and a buggy, clothes and books, and bread and butter for half a dozen growing children. Seaside trips and a recurring doctor's bill complete the catalogue. Banneret leans at the police barrack after a long official ride with Inspector Falcon, turning over ways and means. He has sunk his spare money in a promising mining claim that proved worthless, and his tradespeople have suddenly pressed for payment.
61391-the-iowa-ornithologist-volume-2-no:
The Iowa Ornithologist, volume two, number two, is a state bird journal dated at Salem, Iowa, in January 1896. A pintail duck fronts the number. Its lead paper, read before the first congress of the Iowa association, treats the sea birds that visit Iowa. Frank Shoemaker of Hampton wrote it, grouping four orders of water birds under that heading.

Shoemaker owns that his list is mostly a gathering from others, since his home lay far from lakes and rivers. His chief source is a report on bird migration in the Mississippi Valley for 1884 and 1885. He also uses Allen's list of Iowa birds from the state survey of 1870. The loons open his account: the common loon nests in the north and passes on migration, while the red throated loon comes only in winter. Such state journals built bird knowledge county by county.
61400-the-geology-of-calvin-coolidge-sta:
The Geology of Calvin Coolidge State Forest is a park geology booklet by Harry Dodge, issued in 1959 by the Vermont Geological Survey with the state's Department of Forests and Parks. A cover photograph shows the entrance to the forest park, looking north along the state highway. Charles Doll was state geologist, and Perry Merrill directed the department.

Dodge opens by inviting the visitor to wonder. Have you ever asked why the mountains and valleys are where they are, and how and when they got there? The rocks underfoot, he says, have a definite story to tell. The geologist reads the rock layers as others read the pages of a history book, rebuilding ancient lands and seas from the record. The booklet then reads that record for one Vermont forest: the hills of the Coolidge park explained for the camper and hiker.
61494-the-modern-clock-a-study-of-time-k:
Ward Goodrich wrote a full guide to how clocks work, how they are built, and how they are fixed. The book came out in Chicago in 1905. Goodrich had also written on the watchmaker lathe. His first chapter says clockmakers need more skill than many of them show in their daily work.

Later chapters cover the laws that rule pendulums, ways to make pendulums keep time in heat and cold, and many kinds of escapement. The book goes on to springs, weights, striking trains, cuckoo clocks, calendars, bells, and electric clocks. Clear drawings help a worker follow each part and each step of repair.
61535-frank-merriwell-in-maine-or-the-lu:
Burt Standish wrote Frank Merriwell in Maine, one of the cheap Merriwell tales sold for fifteen cents a copy. Frank Merriwell, the clean-living Yale athlete, was the hero of hundreds of these stories, followed by half a million young fans. This one takes Frank and his party to Maine, the land the ads call way down east.

The Merriwell books mixed sport, travel, and adventure, and this trip offers woods, water, and tests of pluck far from the playing field. Frank plays fair with himself and with all he meets, as the series promised. The tale is a fine sample of the dime-novel style that trained a generation of American boys to prize grit and fair play.
62053-the-geology-of-mt-mansfield-state-:
Robert Christman, a geologist with the Vermont Geological Survey, wrote this account of the rocks of Mount Mansfield State Forest, issued in 1956. Mount Mansfield is Vermont's highest peak, and its cliffs at Smugglers Notch draw many visitors. The cover shows the notch looking northeast from the summit.

Christman reports that nearly all the rock in the forest is a mica-albite-quartz schist, a metamorphic rock. It forms the cliffs of the notch and the bare faces along the crests. He explains how ancient sediments were squeezed and heated in an age of mountain-making until they recrystallized into schist. The booklet maps the rock for foresters, students, and hikers who want to read the mountain.
62093-rick-and-ruddy-out-west:
Howard R Garis wrote Rick and Ruddy Out West, issued in Springfield in nineteen twenty-three. Rick is a boy, and Ruddy is his dog. Earlier books took the pair to camp and afloat on a cruise. W B King drew the pictures for this western outing.

A strange message opens the tale, and then Uncle Tod goes missing. A telegram sends Rick off for the West, with Ruddy giving warning on the way. A wild ride, a lonely cabin, and a chase fill the middle chapters. A picture caption has Rick boast that they found Lost River and can turn it back again. Garis keeps the tale brisk, warm, and safe for young readers.
62180-an-irish-crazy-quilt-smiles-and-te:
Arthur Forrester, an Irish born writer in Boston, stitched songs and tales into a volume called An Irish Crazy Quilt, printed in Boston in 1891. He gave the book to the felons of Ireland, men exiled, jailed, or killed for love of their land. The contents mix smiles and tears, as the sub title says, in song and story.

Ballads praise the Irish Brigade, the green flag at Fredericksburg, and the graves of martyrs, and they mock landlords and state men. Tales such as Ryan's Revenge, Taming a Tiger, and Exploits of an Irish Reporter sit between the songs. Fenian hopes, boycotts, and police courts give the book its heat and local bite.
62244-galactic-ghost:
Galactic Ghost is a tale of a death ship in space by Walter Kubilius. It first ran in a planet tale magazine in the winter of nineteen forty two. A tag line calls its ghost craft the Flying Dutchman of the void. One man named Willard has seen the ghost and lived to tell it.

His sole friend in space lies dying in their ship at the start. Black dust tips mar the hands that once worked the ships board. Willard lies of Earth near at hand to calm the mans last hours. Drift on the suns pull is their thin hope in the cold dark. Grief and dread tune the short pulp tale of the far lanes.
63257-an-apology-for-the-colouring-of-th:
An Apology for the Colouring of the Greek Court in the Crystal Palace, by Owen Jones, defends the decision to paint the Greek court of the rebuilt Crystal Palace at Sydenham. Bradbury and Evans published the pamphlet in 1854 for the Crystal Palace Library.

Jones argues that Greek temples and statues were coloured like those of the lands before and after them. He cites the painted ornaments that Stuart and Revett had found on the mouldings of Greek temples long before. Supporting arguments come from GH Lewes and W Watkiss Lloyd. An extract from the 1836 committee report on the Elgin Marbles is included. A fragment on the origin of colouring in building, by Professor Semper, closes the case. The pamphlet is a key paper in the great Victorian quarrel over painted antiquity.
63289-the-ring-of-amethyst:
The Ring of Amethyst is a volume of poems by Alice Wellington Rollins, published by Putnam's in New York in 1878. The book opens with a pair of sonnets, The Ring addressed to George Eliot and The Book to a friend, that frame the whole collection as an offering. Some eighty short poems follow, under headings such as Joy, Pain, Charm, Doubt, Faith in Works, Longing and Indian Summer.

The Eliot sonnet takes its image from Dorothea in Middlemarch, who would not wear her amethysts and emeralds as careless ornament. Turning a key by chance, she finds the jewels sending out glowing rays and lifts them lovingly in her white hands. Rollins offers her own ring the same way: a small thing held out to a great writer. The poems that follow work the same vein of devotional love poetry, closing with a piece called Last, an Amethyst.
63307-the-untamed-range-life-in-the-sout:
George Pattullo's stories of range life in the southwest were gathered in Toronto in nineteen eleven, after appearing in the Saturday Evening Post, McClure's, and the American Magazine. Pattullo, a cowman turned writer, tells them through animals, and the contents introduces each tale by its beast.

Ol' Sam is a mule, the glutton of the chuck wagon team, locked in a feud with the cook who once fed him bread. The Marauder is a coyote, Corazón a roping horse, The Outlaw a steer, and Shiela a wolfhound whose three days with the wild reawaken her blood. Molly is a range cow, the Mankiller a jack, and Neutria a mountain cowhorse. A trail ballad stands at the front as the book's creed: coffee boiled unground, books that are brooks, and sermons that are stones. Pattullo writes the cattle country from inside its work.
63323-a-funeral-sermon-for-the-rev-josep:
John Alexander preached this funeral sermon for Joseph Kinghorn at Norwich in 1832. Kinghorn had been minister of the Baptist meeting house of Saint Mary in that city. The sermon was given on Sunday afternoon, September the ninth, a few days after his death. Wilkin and Fletcher published it at Norwich the same year.

The sermon's other title calls the congregation to be reminded of the work of their deceased minister. Alexander takes his text from the second letter of Peter. The apostle speaks of stirring hearers up by putting them in remembrance, while he is still in this tabernacle. A line at the head runs: the memory of the just is blessed. Funeral sermons were printed by the thousand in that age, part tribute, part teaching, and this one keeps a noted Norfolk preacher's name alive.
63369-the-sense-of-the-past:
An unfinished novel by Henry James, published at London in 1917. W Collins Sons issued it after James's death. Percy Lubbock's preface explains its history. James began the book years before, then set it aside. The war's first winter drove him back to it. He re-dictated the early books and continued into autumn 1915.

His last illness struck that December before he could resume. The later chapters stand unrevised beyond verbal touches. Full notes dictate the course the novel was to follow. Ralph Pendrel, the hero, has known mostly loss by thirty. Father, sisters, brother, and mother all died before him. An inherited London house and a swap of centuries drive the ghostly plot. James's notes complete what his hand could not.
63473-dust-unto-dust:
Dust Unto Dust is a science fiction story by Lyman D Hinckley, taken from Planet Stories for summer 1955. A blurb calls the find alien, yet asks if it was dead, a towering, sinister city of metal. Three space scouts advance on it with care.

Martin sets the lifeboat down with close attention and stares with his two companions at the city a quarter mile off. Black walls shoulder into the twilight sky, and a sheared edge marks where the metal city ends and bare earth begins. The too strict geometry of the whole build struck him even before they landed. Wass, blond and slight, unbuckles his belt and asks if they shall go in. A return flight window of thirteen hours ticks down. Readers get a tense first look at a dead alien city.
63632-formula-for-conquest:
James Adams wrote Formula for Conquest, a science fiction story printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1945. The blurb gives its three movers: August Twilken had a formula, the freebooter Tod Mulhane had a nose for adventure, and Mon Pordo had an urge for interworld domination. When those three got together, hell had to explode.

The narrator is Mulhane himself, a soldier of fortune drinking in a Martian musk-parlor. A little man with milky-blue eyes and a bedraggled mustache seeks him out by name and announces, too loudly, that he has a formula. Mulhane hustles him to a back room before the mangy crew can slit his throat for the credits it might bring. The tale runs on pulp fuel: secrets, strongmen, and a bid to rule worlds.
63741-the-galactic-ghost:
The Galactic Ghost is a science fiction story by Mack Reynolds, taken from Planet Stories for March 1954. A spaceship comes gracefully and quietly down on a deserted New Jersey field. Wonder and fear strike the earth-people, not for the ship itself but for its strange message. Radar posts and jet squadrons miss the landing until the ship has settled.

The first extras reach New York streets half an hour later, and the news buzzes through the Kremlin in forty minutes. Then the alien takes a hand, sending its message into the mind of every human on earth. The tale is a first-contact puzzle in the pulp manner. Its copyright was never renewed.
6384-that-printer-of-udell-s-a-story-of-:
A dying mother prays in broken dialect for Dick, fearing a tough time for him when she is gone. She has had no show and has kept scratching to provide for herself and her boy. Her man is mostly no count and trifling, except when he drinks, and then, she says, God knows how he uses them. Dick, a hollow cheeked wisp of a boy crouching like a frightened animal, creeps to the bed and touches her wasted hand.

Harold Bell Wright's middle western story follows that printer's boy from such a start into print shop life at Udell. A body viewed for identification, a disfigured hand, and a missing little finger raise questions of letters and papers hidden. Dick asks in a whisper whether search was thorough, for people hide important documents. Wright writes uplift through work, faith, and a friend who hoped when others lost hope.
63917-lorelei-of-the-red-mist:
Leigh Brackett and Ray Bradbury together wrote "Lorelei of the Red Mist," a fantasy story printed in Planet Stories in the summer of 1946. Bradbury was then at the start of his career, and Brackett was already a name in the pulps. The blurb gives the plot in one breath: a man dies, then wakes in a new body.

Hugh Starke, a small stringy thief, flees the company police across the night sky of Venus. His ship is failing, and this time he may not get away. Death takes him, and he wakes rich and powerful on the strange world of Falga. But his new body is hated by all, and his soul belongs to Rann, the devil goddess of that planet. She means to use him for her own gain, and the red mist of the title hides her designs.
63990-palimpsest:
Palimpsest is a science fiction story by Roger Dee, drawn from Planet Stories of November 1951. Its pitch sends readers to Venus with the crew of the Terra the Fourth. That ship is named as the sole craft to escape a demolished Earth behind it. A new race is to be founded from its company on the new world.

Framing matter tells of the first Venusian ship to reach a ruined Earth later. Its crew finds one lone tribe roaming the bush of a southern island. Those Earth folk flee in dread from all bids to speak with them. Val Conna and his nine tall crewmen search the land and pass by dead cities.
64026-shannach-the-last:
Shannach, the Last is a science fiction story by Leigh Brackett, taken from Planet Stories of November 1952. Its hero is Trevor, a prospector on Mercury. He went into the Twilight Belt hunting sun-stones. One or two of those stones could turn a prospector into a rich man. He found none.

A quake brought down a whole mountain wall on Trevor's ship. He was left with a pocket torch, a handful of food tablets and a canteen of water. Rather than die in the valley, he went into the tunnels, the ancient blowholes of a cooling planet. Mercury's Twilight Belt is cut into thousands of cliff-locked pockets, like the cells of a honeycomb. The story is Brackett's planetary romance at its darkest.
64313-beneath-the-red-world-s-crust:
Beneath the Red World’s Crust, a story by Erik Fennel, ran in Planet Stories in the fall of 1947. Under a dust dry planet, an ancient leviathan heaves in a buried cavern. It pumps water upward, as it was told to do. Only the hunted Nick Tinker knows that more than water is coming to the surface.

The tale opens with a shot whining past the face of Tinker. The slug splats into the eroded grey wall beside him. He should have died then, by the odds of that shot. A sticky wetness under his feet makes him recoil, and that saves him. He crumples and falls, a trick from his war days back on Earth. Fennel writes fast pulp action with a buried monster at its heart.
64372-the-boy-s-book-of-indians-and-the-:
The Boys Book of Indians and the Wild West was writ and drawn by Williams, both pen and brush his own. Its rights were set in law at New York in the years just past. Its first part takes the red men of the deep woods.

When the white man found America, that part says, he found a vast old wild of rich vales, high hills, and deep woods. Tall trees had grown for long ages, their tops to the blue sky. They shut the sun from the gloom of the woods hush. In those deep shades the red man lived in wild free days. Skilled in wood craft and the art of rude war, he was lord of that vast land.
64400-the-workers-an-experiment-in-reali:
The Workers: An Experiment in Reality is a work of firsthand social investigation by Wyckoff, then an assistant professor at Princeton. The eastern volume, copyrighted in 1897 and issued by Scribner's in 1899, records jobs he took as an unskilled labourer. Its chapters run from day labourer to hotel porter, farm hand and logging camp.

The narrative opens in July 1891 at Highland Falls, where Wyckoff hires on for seven in the morning to help demolish the old Academic building at West Point. He boards with a woman he calls Mrs Flaherty, in a crowded town full of workingmen drawn by the new building work. The experiment's point is plain: to live the labourer's life from inside rather than study it from a lecture room, and the diary form keeps every hardship close and concrete.
64461-roraima-and-british-guiana-with-a-:
Boddam-Whetham wrote Roraima and British Guiana after a trip made in the late 1870s, put out in London in 1879. A piece in the Spectator had fired his wish to see Roraima, the great flat-topped mount of Guiana. Old tales said its top held lakes, strange fish, and giant white eagles.

He sailed by way of Bermuda and the West Indies to Georgetown. There the colony's rulers let him join their own trip toward Roraima. Rivers, falls, and deep forest fill the route through the interior. Boddam-Whetham tells what he saw of the land, its folk, and its plants. The book is a brisk, fond record of a hard trip to a place few white men had seen.
64462-the-defeat-of-varus-and-the-german:
The Defeat of Varus and the German Frontier Policy of Augustus is a study in Roman history. William Oldfather and Howard Vernon Canter, both teachers of classics at the University of Illinois, wrote the work. The university published it at Urbana in 1915 as part of its studies in the social sciences. The contents move from sources to a new reading of the question.

The authors state the common view they mean to test. Most writers hold that Augustus meant to conquer Germany as far as the Elbe. On that view, the loss of Varus's legions in the year 9 ended the plan. The study quotes German scholars and Mommsen at length in support of the old reading. Later chapters weigh the sources and attack the accepted account. A final chapter offers the authors' own new interpretation of Augustus's frontier policy.
64493-the-workers-an-experiment-in-reali:
Walter A Wyckoff, an assistant professor of political economy at Princeton, made an experiment in reality: he lived as a working man and wrote down what he found. This volume, The West, was first copyrighted in 1898 and reissued in 1909. It follows his earlier volume on the East.

The chapters begin with the army of the unemployed. Wyckoff lives by odd jobs, finds steady work, and serves as a hand-truckman in a factory. He falls in among revolutionaries, builds roads on the World's Fair grounds, and travels from Chicago to Denver and on to the Pacific. The book reports wages, hunger, and hope from inside the life it studies.
64596-the-star-beast:
The Star Beast is a science fiction story by Damon Knight. It appeared in Planet Stories in the spring of 1949. A headnote names the creature at its centre. Men called the tentacle-headed blob Oscar. They were to learn a better name.

The tale opens on the observation deck of a space liner. A dead man lies sprawled by the entrance wells. Beside him sits a black, limbless creature like a lump of mud. Phil Horitz finds the body at the ship's early morning. The dead man's throat bears a deep red line. An empty metal box hangs at his middle. Horitz calls the captain at once. Thomasson has been murdered, he reports.
64612-a-twentieth-century-idealist:
Henry Pettit published A Twentieth Century Idealist in New York in 1905. Its frontispiece looks from a cathedral roof toward the delectable mountains, captioned among the Himalayas. The peaks near Sandakphu are claimed at twenty-nine thousand feet, the highest on earth. His motto runs: under the surface of ordinary life lie great mysteries. The real part of man, he adds, is in his ideals.

Pettit writes the new century's spiritual program in the idiom of his day: part philosophy, part travel, part uplift. The Grafton Press issued the book as a handsome gift volume. Idealism had a mass market in 1905, between the churches and the New Thought parlors. Pettit's title names the customer exactly: the ordinary reader who believed his inner life was his real one.
6471-the-children-of-the-new-forest:
Captain Marryat, Royal Navy, sets The Children of the New Forest in 1647, when King Charles the First, defeated after nearly five years of civil war, lay prisoner at Hampton Court. Cavaliers were dispersed, and Cromwell's parliamentary army began to control the Commons. In November, Charles escaped with Sir John Berkely, Ashburnham, and Legg, riding fast toward Hampshire and the New Forest, hoping friends had provided a vessel to France.

No vessel waited, and disappointment followed. A mid passage shows Edward and Humphrey in the forest, laying a body in a grave from a cart before calling their sisters, then debating prayers for the dead. They are not in the Bible, Edward says, so some portion of the Bible must be read instead. Marryat writes a children's story of war, hiding, and family duty in the forest.
6479-lady-mary-and-her-nurse-or-a-peep-i:
Mrs. Traill writes Lady Mary and Her Nurse, subtitled A Peep into the Canadian Forest, as a child's guide to forest life told through a nurse's stories. The flying squirrel opens it, with its food, a story of a wolf, an Indian village, and wild rice. Sleighing, sleigh robes, fur caps, otter skins, an old snow storm, otter hunting, and otter slides follow, with Indian names and remarks on wild animals and their habits.

Lady Mary then reads Mrs. Frazer the history of the squirrel family: grey squirrels on Pine Island, their poor relations the chitmunks, and Velvet Paw at the mill by the rapids. Later chapters add Indian baskets, maple sugar, racoons, Canadian flowers, porcupine, and beaver architecture. A mid passage shows blue jays, blackbirds, field mice, squirrels, and chitmunks busy in wheat fields, filling cheeks with grain. Traill writes Canada for children, creature by creature.
65005-an-illustrated-directory-of-the-sp:
An Illustrated Directory of the Specifications of All Domestic and Foreign Motor-Cars and Motor Business Wagons is the 1907 buyer's guide of Motor magazine. Motor, the national monthly magazine of motoring, issued it from 1789 Broadway, New York. Gasoline, steam, and electric machines sold in the United States are all listed, with illustrations.

An index marches the makes from Acme and Adams-Farwell through Buick, Cadillac, Ford, and Franklin to the foreign houses: Berliet, Darracq, Delahaye, and FIAT. Electric carriages get their due with Babcock, Baker, and Columbia, and steam with the Clark and Boss steamers. Each entry gives the specifications a buyer compared: price, body style, seats, weight, wheel-base, tread, tires, steering, brakes, springs, frame, and the engine's bore and stroke. Pages 156 to 200 are reserved for business wagons and trucks. It is the whole American motor market of 1907 in one reference.
65074-the-ultimate-quest:
The Ultimate Quest, by Hal Annas, ran in Imagination in December 1950. The headnote asks if man, who has evolved slowly toward a dim goal, will regret reaching it. The hero, Art Fillmore, strides down a hall on long thin legs.

Fillmore reads the news as a beam in his mind: scientists are to wake a twentieth century man. He thins his body by concentration and walks through a twelve-foot door without opening it. In the office he talks of his forthcoming wedding to a girl he has never seen. She is a hundred and nine years old, which counts as youth in that age. The price talk turns her purchase into a joke about a glutted market in brides.
65145-essays-of-a-biologist:
Julian Huxley wrote these essays, printed by Alfred A Knopf of New York in 1923. Huxley gives the book to his colleagues and friends at the Rice Institute in Houston, Texas. The first essay, on progress in biology and beyond, opens with a poem that turns the handle of a cinema of the mind. Reel after reel runs from astronomy to the rise of life.

Other essays treat biology and sociology, the mind of birds, and sex in life and mind. Philosophic Ants offers a biologic fantasy. The last two essays take up reason and the idea of God, and religion and science as old wine in new bottles. Huxley writes as a young biologist testing his science against the big questions.
6516-the-suppressed-gospels-and-epistles:
Archbishop Wake gathers writings that early Christian groups held dear, yet later councils set aside from the New Testament as most readers know it. Mary, the infancy tales, Nicodemus, letters of Paul and Clement, Barnabas, Hermas, and the notes of Ignatius all appear here, each with its own chapters. The long title states the case plainly: these books were once prized, then barred after sharp dispute.

Wake adds notes on where each text came from and why its standing was questioned, so a reader can judge the claims for each one. The volume thus serves both as a set of old writings and as a record of how a canon took shape. It suits readers who want to see what the early church read beyond the books that stayed in.
65169-early-man-projectile-points-in-the:
Kenneth Honea wrote Early Man Projectile Points in the Southwest, a popular pamphlet from the Museum of New Mexico Press. Honea opens with a curious fact: early man in the Southwest most often made his tools of very finely textured stone. The fine flaking needed for his points, knives, and scrapers demanded such stone.

The work on many points is so good, Honea says, that early man seems to have sought a kind of beauty in his tools. Need for the best stone drove wide trading. Flint from quarries near Amarillo, in the Texas Panhandle, has been found at sites as far west as Arizona and as far north as Wyoming. The pamphlet maps that old craft and trade.
65186-beyond-the-fearful-forest:
Reynard wrote this fantasy tale for Imagination, where it ran in April 1951. Sunset Fields opens the story: a meadow where the bones of the ancient dead never decay. The people chip those bones into arrow points and needles, and their singers tell of a first murder there.

Beyond the fields run three brooks, and beyond them stands the Fearful Forest. No hunter has ever followed the great Knifetooth Bear into its shade. Past the forest lies a worse peril, the land of the Nameless. The tale is told in the voice of the bone working folk themselves. Their world is gentle, their loves are shared, and violence is a half believed legend. The forest waits as the test of that innocence.
65189-hashimura-togo-domestic-scientist:
Hashimura Togo, Domestic Scientist is a comic book by Irwin, with pictures by Strothmann. Its rights were set in law in the mid nineteen teens. A note at its front warns that the books odd words, spell, and marks are kept as first struck, by plan.

Its parts are named in the heros own bent English. An introduce word comes first. Then come his Thursdays out, his move day, and his run of a house heat box. His brush with week end guests and his swat of the fly fill the next run. The joke form of the age is plain: a Japan house boy in America, whose queer speech and sly wit turn each chore into a small war with his boss.
65382-the-crimson-west:
Alex Philip wrote The Crimson West, a novel published by Thomas Allen at Toronto and printed in Great Britain. The title page carries verses by Donald Malloch: in the East we dreamed our dreams, and in the crimson West those dreams come true. Philip dedicated the book to the native sons of Canada, in whose hands, he writes, rests the future prosperity of their birthplace.

The novel opens in a jail. A sheriff leads John McLean to a cell where his son Donald wakes from a drinking bout. The father speaks bitterly. Donald was arrested in a low gambling den and has disgraced the family name. Cast off until he can return rid of his bad habits and proven a man, Donald must make his way in the West. Philip's tale belongs to the Canadian western romance: a disgraced son, a stern father, and redemption on the frontier.
65474-mirabilia-descripta-the-wonders-of:
Friar Jordanus, who became bishop of Columbum in Greater India, wrote Mirabilia Descripta, The Wonders of the East, about the year 1330. The Hakluyt Society printed an English version at London in 1863, turned from the Latin as issued at Paris in 1839. Colonel Henry Yule added commentary. The book is given to Sir Bartle Frere, governor of Bombay, whose love for old travellers the editor trusts.

Yule grants that Jordanus, striving to speak only truth of what he saw, still retails fables from hearsay. What the friar did see struck him as so wondrous that he was ready to take in tales of lands farther from Christendom. The work holds his account of India and the East: its peoples, beasts, fruits, and faiths. It stands among the first-hand Western reports of the East before the sea road to India.
65621-report-on-the-migration-of-birds-i:
Report on the Migration of Birds in the Autumn of 1879 is a paper by Harvie-Brown and Cordeaux, printed in The Zoologist for May 1880. It is the first report of its kind in the volume. Forms of enquiry and letters of instruction went to twenty-six lighthouses on Scotland's east coast. Thirteen stations sent returns.

The rest sent none, or blank forms, owing to an unusual scarcity of birds. The report then goes coast by coast and species by species. Scotland's east coast leads, then England's east coast, then Scotland's west. Lighthouses are named from North Unst in Shetland southward, with their lights described. The paper founds the study of bird migration on lighthouse keepers' logs.
65772-once-upon-a-monbeast:
Charles E Fritch wrote Once Upon a Monbeast, a tale first printed in Imagination in March 1952. The blurb asks for pity for the poor man who writes of bug eyed beasts. His readers see them in print, but he may have to live with a few. The teller warns that the name at the top is not his true name.

He was a new hand at the craft when the tale starts, by his own word. He tells of blood, sweat, and stamps spent on each tale he sent out. Hope and waste ran hot and cold with the mail of each day. Then a note came from Donald MacDonald, a great name in the field. That note, shown in the tale, tells the young man he has no gift for the craft at all. The sting of that note sets up the strange turn the blurb hints at.
65822-prehistoric-indians-of-the-southwe:
H M Wormington, keeper of archaeology at the Denver Museum of Natural History, wrote Prehistoric Indians of the Southwest as number seven of the museum's popular series. The book first came out in 1947, and this copy is the seventh printing, of 1966. An added part at the end, by Erik Reed of the National Park Service, lists sites to visit, living pueblos, and local museums.

The chapters begin with the most ancient cultures: Sandia, Folsom, San Jon, Yuma, Gypsum Cave, and Cochise. Then come the Anasazi in their stages, from Basketmaker times through the great Pueblo age, and the Hohokam, Mogollon, Sinagua, and Patayan peoples in turn. Tree-ring dating, points, sandals, and weaving all find a place. The book gives readers a clear map of the old peoples of the Southwest and how their ways changed over long ages.
65906-my-story-that-i-like-best:
Six famous magazine writers tell, in My Story That I Like Best, which of their own tales they prize most. The book came from New York in 1925, in a fifth edition by November. Ray Long, editor of Cosmopolitan, supplies the introduction. The writers dedicate the volume to the constant readers of his magazine.

Long plays the host in his preface. He has invited six distinguished writers to relax over their coffee, he says, and talk about their work. The six are Edna Ferber, Irvin Cobb, Peter Kyne, James Oliver Curwood, Meredith Nicholson, and Witwer. Each then names a favorite story and tells how it came to be. The book is a piece of magazine promotion, but a charming one: the best paid storytellers in America, caught between editions, explaining their craft to their fans.
65936-wanderlust:
Alan E Nourse wrote Wanderlust for Imagination, a science fiction magazine, in October nineteen fifty-two. The tale opens on a farm, where young Tad Barlow has come home late. His father George has waited all day for tractor bolts and feels dread he cannot name. Tad, like many young men in the tale, looks to the spaceways for thrills.

George fears that the road Tad wants will end in ruin for his son. That clash, farm home against the pull of space, drives the short tale. Nourse sets the scene in plain farm detail before any ship appears. The result is a quiet, tense tale about youth, risk, and a father's fear.
66034-the-school-girls-in-number-40-or-p:
The School-Girls in Number 40, or Principle Put to the Test, is a tale issued at Philadelphia by the American Sunday-School Union. It was entered for copyright in 1859, and its motto warns those who think they stand to take heed lest they fall. Every book from the union had first to pass a board drawn from seven churches.

The tale opens with Carrie Stanley kneeling by an empty trunk, at a loss how to pack all her things into two. Her room is in cheerful disorder, with drawers on the floor and books strewn about. Chapter heads promise a tableaux party, a trap set, and a secret out, as the girls of room forty face their test.
66205-literary-pilgrimages-of-a-naturali:
Literary Pilgrimages of a Naturalist, by Winthrop Packard, is described in the publisher's list of his works in plain terms. The book makes visits to the haunts of Whittier, Emerson, and Hawthorne. Celia Thaxter, Webster, and Aldrich are named as well. The list names his New England Year set as well: Woodland Paths, Wild Pastures, Wood Wanderings, and Wildwood Ways, one for each season. Florida Trails stands apart in the list.

Packard's method joins two loves: walking the woods and reading the men who wrote of them. The pilgrimages take the reader to the houses, paths, and shores where New England's authors lived and worked. Photographs by the author and others illustrate the scenes. The book was sold in ornamental cloth with gilt top, boxed, in the manner of a gift volume for readers who walk.
66438-vengeance-from-the-past:
Reynard wrote "Vengeance From the Past," a science fiction story printed in Imagination in September 1954. Ray Rollins fights to save the space station, and Earth itself, from an enemy mankind had forgotten. That enemy hides, waiting for its revenge.

The tale opens in a quiet house during a television program. Little noises at the doors and windows go unnoticed at first, blamed on wind and rain. Two things are trying to get in, silent as cobras, testing each opening. The narrator feels eyes on his back and ripples run up his spine. His wife sleeps upstairs, with a baby on the way. Reynard builds the menace from those small sounds before the past's enemy shows itself.
66969-greensea-island-a-mystery-of-the-e:
Greensea Island, a mystery of the Essex coast by Victor Bridges, was printed in New York and London in 1922. Bridges held the copyright of 1921 and had written A Rogue by Compulsion before it. He gives the book to Margaret.

The narrator, Dryden, leans on the starboard railing of the Neptune in Leixoes Harbour. He has just spent five hours supervising the unloading of cargo. Ross, the ship's doctor, saunters up with a large Manilla cigar and teases him for idleness. Dryden asks if he is coming ashore at Oporto, and Ross shakes his head. More hands are due aboard at three, and he must examine their eyes. Dryden is sick to death of the ship and wants to stretch his legs. Seafaring, both men agree, is a dog's life.
67057-polly-in-the-southwest:
Polly in the Southwest, by Lillian Elizabeth Roy, is one of a shelf of Polly books. Grosset and Dunlap printed it in New York in 1925, with pictures by Barbour. Earlier volumes took Polly to New York, to South America, and on a southern cruise.

The tale picks up as the cruise ends and the yacht White Crest lands its party in New York. The din of the city grates after the trip. Eleanor stops her ears, and Jack wishes himself back in Buenos Aires. A plate shows Algy at full length upon the floor. The contents promise news from Dodo, old friends met once more, and Dodo joining the ranks. Albuquerque festivities, hold-ups along the way, and a climb on Humphrey's Peak fill the westward trip. Letters east and west and Dalky's story lead to arrivals in Los Angeles.
67171-buddhism-and-christianity-a-parall:
Archibald Scott, minister of a great Edinburgh parish, gave the Croall Lecture for 1889 and 1890 as Buddhism and Christianity: A Parallel and a Contrast. David Douglas published it at Edinburgh in 1890. His first lecture argues that comparing the faiths properly is a duty, not a curiosity.

Scott cites Schopenhauer's prediction that eastern studies would change European religion and thought. He grants Buddhism its age, its spread, and the quality of its teaching. Then he draws the parallels in history and doctrine, and the contrasts he finds decisive. Both faiths, he insists, rose independently, so likeness cannot be explained by borrowing. The lectures belong to comparative theology's first confident age, when the East arrived in Edinburgh lecture halls.
67278-a-secret-service-being-strange-tal:
A Secret Service, being Strange Tales of a Nihilist, is William Le Queux's book of Russian revolutionary stories. Ward, Lock and Company of London published this second edition in 1896 for London, New York, and Melbourne. Le Queux had written Zoraida and The Great War in England in 1897.

His preface tells how the tales were got. Writing for The Times on the Russian movement and the Siberian exiles, he came to know the original of Anton Prèhznev, whose stories these are. The preface paints the Russia behind them: protest answered by arrest without trial and the road to Siberia, prisoners knouted in the Warsaw Citadel, and dungeons under the Peter-Paul Fortress. Under Nicholas the Second, Le Queux argues, the old cruelty rules unchanged, and despair keeps making revolutionists faster than the police can bury them.
67316-the-first:
Edward Ludwig wrote The First, a tale in a science fiction magazine. The number was dated November 1955, its note states. Man will need signposts to guide the way to infinity, it quotes. Tonight the great rocket would rumble, the blurb runs. The city was enchanted on the morning of the parade.

It was a colossal music box blaring a thousand victory chants. Three spacemen sat stiffly in a blue-bannered convertible car. A hundred bands and eight hundred flowered floats escorted them. Ten thousand men marched with them to the Capitol. Captain Everson stood in the front seat, waving to the crowd. Everson was the legless man, bronzed and square-jawed, it says. His first rocketship had exploded at take-off. He lived to walk on false legs and build another. Ludwig gives the first voyage its parade before its flight.
67421-grist:
Grist is a north land tale by Murray Leinster, set in the land of frost and gold. Leinster opens not with a man but with a dog, Cheechako, a malamute pup chained by a lone cabin. The dog howls to the stars in grief.

Cheechako knows his master, who should be in the cabin, will never come out again. He knows the smoke from the chimney will die and never thicken once more. He knows the other man who fled down the river trail will never return. Yet the pup is warm, fed, and freed at times by a man named Carson. Leinster builds peril, loyalty, fear, and courage in the far north. Dog and men face tests that try the soul in snow and silence.
67486-life-of-christ:
Life of Christ is a tale of the life of Jesus by Giovanni Papini. Dorothy Fisher turned the Italian text into free English for this print. The turn takes its verse quotes from the old King James form. Rights date the work to the year nineteen twenty three.

A note owns that some quotes are made of bits from far parts of the book. Name forms in the text take the shapes most known to plain readers. The book aims at home hearts, not at schools or dig lore, it says. Scenes from the tales of the four books are retold in lush, warm prose. The work was a famed faith book of its age in two tongues.
67520-the-conquest:
Henry Bedford-Jones wrote The Conquest, a historical novel published by the David Cook Publishing Company in 1914. Bedford-Jones dedicated the book to his mother, whose picture, he says, stands behind Ruth MacDonald in these pages. The contents run from a Scottish moor to the Canadian wilderness. Chapter titles name Radisson the Great, the villages of the Crees, and Hudson's End.

The story opens in the Scottish Highlands. Davie, the narrator, goes out with his father and the dog Grim to gather sheep after a storm. By the cliffs they find something washed up that changes the boy's life. The tale follows the ship Lass o' Dee and the men of the Hudson's Bay trade. Pierre Radisson, the great French explorer of Canada, stands at the centre of the later chapters. Bedford-Jones builds a boys' adventure of the fur trade out of real history.
67604-a-peep-into-the-past:
A Peep into the Past is a piece of fancy by Max Beerbohm, privately printed in 1923. The edition was limited to three hundred copies on Japan vellum. Its subject is Oscar Wilde, treated as a forgotten old gentleman of the present day. Beerbohm wonders how many readers the jingle of that name still stirs. Once, he says, it was on all lips, and Punch made its jokes at his cost. Now his star is set in this busy, changeful city.

The old man lives on among his books, the piece goes. Keats and Shakespeare, jest books and Greek plays in plain prose, are his company. He still writes without pause, and still means to dramatise Salome. Student papers take his poems without a name. The piece is a tender and sly what-if: Wilde grown old, outliving his fame.
67632-good-hunting-in-pursuit-of-big-gam:
Theodore Roosevelt wrote Good Hunting, a set of pieces on big game in the West, issued at New York in nineteen seven. The pieces first ran in Harper's Round Table in eighteen ninety-six and ninety-seven, for younger readers. A publisher's note calls the book a field book by a true sportsman, written from his own experience. It praises Roosevelt's work for saving big game and for national parks and forest reserves.

The first part treats the wapiti, or round horned elk, with plates of a wounded bull and six point antlers. A cattle killing bear, a Christmas buck, and the timber wolf follow. Shooting the prong buck and a tame white goat fill the later parts. A closing part on ranching gives cowboy sports, tailing a bull, and hard galloping on the range.
6769-the-people-of-the-mist:
H. Rider Haggard dedicates The People of the Mist, first published in 1894, to his godsons, as a record of primeval and troglodyte imagination and barefaced, flagrant adventure. Chapters bear titles like The Sins of the Father, After Seven Years, The Last Vigil, Otter Gives Counsel, and The Tale of Soa. Leonard swears on the blood of Aca, and a midnight marriage follows.

From a yellow devil's nest to the temple of Jâl, the tale moves through vengeance, disillusion, and a people's strange rites. Haggard writes with the gusto of his African romances. The People of the Mist is a thrilling, old-style lost-world adventure, full of danger and wonder.
67714-peru-a-land-of-contrast:
Peru A Land of Contrasts is a roam book by Millicent Todd with photo cuts. A Little Brown house of Boston brought it out in nineteen eighteen. First right claim bears nineteen fourteen from the same house. Part one, In the Desert, runs from shore walk to Lima odd turns. Pica, called the bloom of the sand, gets a part in that scheme.

Pirate and gold fleet tales and old back tales fill mid desert parts. Part two climbs to the high lands and a great stone town by a saint lake. Inca and his realm and sun god rite fill that mount scheme in rank. Part three drops to the green wilds in a land of bold deeds. Dark and light beasts and green wild strife close its scheme parts.
6808-woman-on-the-american-frontier-a-va:
William Fowler argues that history, as usually told, records men's deeds in war and statecraft, while women appear only as queens or schemers for power. The story of women's work in great migrations, he says, has been told only in lines where it should fill volumes. His book aims to fill that gap, with heroism, adventures, privations, captivities, and noble lives and deaths of pioneer mothers.

Illustrated with many engravings, the history gathers tales of women on the frontier, from cabins to captivity. Fowler's tone is admiring and earnest. Woman on the American Frontier is a valuable, early tribute to pioneer women, still moving in its rescue of their stories.
68084-wild-west:
Bertrand W Sinclair wrote Wild West, issued in Boston in March nineteen twenty-six. Little, Brown published the northern novel. Contents run to twenty-five chapters of clipped titles. The Straw in the Wind opens the set, and Keep Off the Grass follows with a warning.

Machiavelli gets a chapter with a question mark. A Rider and a Lady and On With the Dance lighten the middle. A Word and a Blow turns the dance floor rough. Cornered, A Near Showdown, and Crossed Wires tighten the close. Robin Tyler rides down a spur of Chase Hill to Birch Creek in chapter one. He finds there what he had sought since sunrise. Sinclair wrote the Canadian west he had punched cows in himself.
6813-lost-in-the-backwoods-a-tale-of-the:
Mrs. Traill's tale of the Canadian forest, first called The Canadian Crusoes, returns in 1882 under a new, more descriptive title, Lost in the Backwoods. Young readers had loved it at first, and the publishers hoped it would please a new generation as well. The opening verse paints a Canadian morning, bright streamers on high, dazzling white snow, and ocean waves on shore.

Children lost in the woods must learn to live by wit, work, and courage, in a romantic adventure of the northern forest. Traill writes with a settler's knowledge and a storyteller's warmth. Lost in the Backwoods is a classic Canadian children's adventure, full of woodcraft and pluck.
68186-insect-life-souvenirs-of-a-natural:
J.-H. Fabre wrote these thoughts of a man of the fields on the life of bugs, put in English dress in a print of 1913. David Sharp wrote the word at its front. Charles Darwin called Fabre that peer-less man of watch, in words set on the title page. The first shape of the book came out in 1901. Cuts by M. Prendergast Parker go with the text.

The list of parts gives the cast of the fields. The Sacred Beetle stands at its head, the star of the author's fame. A plot of ground kept for his watch comes next. Then come the wasps of the kind Cerceris, one of which slays with skill. The wasp of the yellow wing, three strokes of a blade, and the grub and its change fill the mid parts. Deep thoughts on the kinds close the first run.
68309-address-of-president-roosevelt-at-:
President Theodore Roosevelt gave this address at Chautauqua, New York, on August 11, 1905. The Government Printing Office at Washington published it the same year. Roosevelt takes up one feature of foreign policy and one of domestic policy.

The foreign half treats the Monroe Doctrine. It is not part of international law, he says, but the root of American policy in this hemisphere. It has won respect because the nation kept it alive, adapting it to changing needs instead of letting it fossilize. A right claimed brings duties with it. The speech sets out the Roosevelt Corollary in his own words: America must police its neighborhood while guarding its sister republics from conquest.
68343-cato-the-creeper-or-the-demon-of-d:
Frederick Dewey wrote Cato, the Creeper, or The Demon of Dead-Man's Forest for Beadle and Adams of New York. The tale was entered in eighteen seventy-eight. Beadle's dime novels sold adventure by the cartload. Chapter one, Captain Downing Smiles, opens under a hot Arkansas sun.

Dead-Man's Forest spreads below that sun for thousands of acres. Swamp, glade, and hillock mix in its gloom, and the sun scarce pierces its matted branches. Indians of old held the place haunted by evil spirits, the tale says. Its name came down from them, feared by all who knew it. Into such a wood Dewey sends his creeper and his captain.
68426-two-fares-east:
Two Fares East, a western tale by Tuttle, opens on a wedding night in cattle country. The ranch house of Uncle Hozie Wheeler Flying H outfit blazes with light. Two lanterns hang on the wide veranda that nearly rings the rambling old house. More lanterns hang from the corral fence, the stable, and the big gate.

Saddle horses and buggy teams already stand tied at the fence in the yard. One stall in the stable is piled full of noise makers for the night. Empty five gallon cans, cow bells, and shotguns wait for the final words of the minister. The biggest shivaree ever pulled off on the Tumbling River range is the plan. Inside, the company sits stiffly around the room, conscious of their best clothes.
68523-pattern-for-conquest:
George Smith wrote this science fiction novel in parts for Astounding Science-Fiction in the spring of 1946. The opening is pure crisis: a signal officer tears a tape from a typer as it feeds a master transmitter, and the overload wrecks tubes, breakers, and a tuning guide. He pays no mind to the damage his grab has caused.

Smith was an engineer, and his fiction runs on gear, signals, and men who fix machines under fire. Pattern for Conquest belongs to his tales of future war, where the fight turns on who reads a signal first. The serial form keeps each part ending on a hook. It is hard, fast pulp science fiction from the camp of John Campbell's magazine.
68524-the-optimist:
E M Delafield wrote the novel The Optimist. The Macmillan Company issued it at New York in 1922. Delafield gave the book to C A Dawson-Scott. She praised that woman as novelist and friend. Part One bears the names Valeria and Owen Quentillian. A ship pulls from a wharf as it opens.

Owen recalls a long sea trip from his boyhood. His mind runs back to his arrival at Saint Gwenllian. A small, cold child rode in a pony cart, he recalls. Miss Lucilla Morchard sat beside him on that ride. She was Canon Morchard's daughter, fifteen years old. Owen tries to pick up a lapsed tie as the tale starts. A quiet English novel of family and place, it shows Delafield's cool eye for manners and hurt pride.
68564-barrier-beaches-of-the-atlantic-co:
Barrier Beaches of the Atlantic Coast, by Frederick J H Merrill, was reprinted in 1890 from the Popular Science Monthly. Merrill describes the long sand reefs that fringe the coast from Cape Cod to Cape Florida and shield the mainland from storm waves. For most of American history the barriers stood empty. Then city crowds needed breathing places, and railroads, bridges, hotels, and cottages spread across them within a few years.

Merrill compares the beaches along their whole length. Long Island's are almost barren, while New Jersey's carry oak, cedar, holly, and sassafras. The swamp magnolia appears farther south, then the palmetto in the Carolinas, blighted by frost. The paper is a geologist's tour of the shore, written just as the summer resort age was transforming it.
68616-anastasia-the-autobiography-of-h-i:
Anastasia is presented as the autobiography of the Grand Duchess Anastasia of Russia, fourth daughter of Nicholas the Second. Robert Speller and Sons published volume one in New York in nineteen sixty three. The jacket calls it the only authentic account of her life story. The dedication lists her father, mother, brother, and three elder sisters.

Six parts divide the story the book sets out to tell its readers. They run from her youthful years through the First World War at home. Arrest and exile, life at Tobolsk, and life at Ekaterinburg follow in order. A final part tells of rescue and escape to Bukovina after the killings. The preface is said to explain her long hiding and late return to view. Anecdotes and lighter events are promised beside the grave record.
68760-betrothed-for-a-day-or-queenie-tre:
Street and Smith of New York issued Betrothed for a Day, or Queenie Trevalyn's Love Test, in 1901 as number 2 of the Laura Series. Its author, Laura Jean Libbey, is billed on the title page as the greatest living novelist, and the copyright rests with Norman Munro from an earlier claim.

The story opens on the last night of the season at Newport, in the ballroom of the Ocean House. Miss Trevalyn, the belle of the ball, stands at the centre of the gay crowd in the season of 1901. A one-day betrothal is the test the title promises, and the love plot turns on how Queenie bears it.
68789-the-dead-tryst: James Grant wrote The Dead Tryst, a novel issued in London in eighteen eighty-three by George Routledge and Sons. Grant had first won readers with The Romance of War. His long list of tales, printed at the front, runs to dozens of titles. Most of them deal with soldiers, Scotland, and the wars of past times.
69014-the-prey-of-the-strongest:
Morley Roberts wrote The Prey of the Strongest, a novel published in London in 1906 by Hurst and Blackett. The book opens with a letter to a man named Baker. It recalls their work together on the Canadian Pacific Railroad in the Kicking Horse Pass and on the Shuswap. They were hustling to put the line through. Roberts says he is no longer in touch with any of those men. Some are distinguished, some have gone under, and some may lie in obscure graves beside other tracks.

The letter frames a tale of the men who built the mountain railway and what became of them. Roberts knew that world at first hand.
69148-the-eternal-quest:
The Eternal Quest is a science fiction novelette by Joseph Gilbert, first published in Astonishing Stories in October 1942. A nondescript little man stands before a five-hundred-foot spaceship. He tells two billion viewers he has come, a new Moses, to lead his people to the stars.

Watching the broadcast is Robert Lawrence of the Space Patrol, and he smiles. The speaker promises the crowds the adventure only the Patrol knows, but Lawrence's own patrol life is boredom: tight orbits round Mars, joyriding youngsters to intercept, settlers' sick calls to answer. The little prophet says mankind has died spiritually and lost hope for a hundred years. The novelette sets the prophet's promise against the patrolman's routine, and asks which of them understands the eternal quest of the title.
69393-spacemen-lost:
Smith wrote this space novel for Startling Stories, where it ran in the fall of 1954. Finlay drew the pictures. A great spaceport hall crowds the opening pages. Loudspeakers call passengers for Flight Seventy-nine, bound for Castor Three and Pollux Four.

Commodore Ted Wilson walks his sweetheart Alice to the gate, carrying her bag. He begs her not to go. She wants to see the worlds he talks of before she is sixty. At the gate he asks her to marry him. She says yes, but only when she returns, so he will be sure he asks from love, not to keep her home. The title hangs over them: spacemen lost. Smith mixes romance with the working detail of a space line.
69451-behind-the-scenes-in-a-restaurant-:
The Consumers' League of New York City published Behind the Scenes in a Restaurant in 1916, a study of one thousand seventeen women who worked in restaurants. The foreword opens with a worker's plain question: I keep hearing about laws for women; where are they? She worked twelve hours a day, in a trade the factory laws of the day left out. The League set out to count her world.

Chapters give the workers' ages, nations, and home lives, then their hours: the long day workers, night work, and the fight for one day's rest in seven. Wages, the tipping system, and slack seasons follow, with a summary and a call for new laws. A statement from the state labour office and a health study from a city clinic stand in the back. It is reform by arithmetic, the Progressive method at its most dogged.
69555-cactus-and-pine-songs-of-the-south:
Sharlot Hall wrote Cactus and Pine, songs of the Southwest, printed in Boston in 1911 with rights held from 1910. The catalog gives a short title, but the title page gives the full name. Hall knew Arizona well, and her poems sing of desert, pine woods, trails, and ranch life.

Her songs take in the Santa Fe Trail, the Colorado River, old Tucson, sheep camps, and Boot Hill graves. A set of camp fire tales in verse and a last part called Beyond the Desert close the book. Readers get the land and its folk in plain, warm song from one who lived there.
6972-lays-from-the-west:
Stella, whose full name appears as M A Nicholl, sings lays from the west in a volume dedicated with gratitude to Missus Spotiswood Ash of Bellaghy in Ireland. A prefatory verse pictures a spirit taking her songs as tiny germs and bidding them root among coming hours and grow into flowers. The opening poem, In the Northwest, sets prairie flowers, blue sky, and sweet air against love of a native land far away.

The poet dreams of broad beech shade in glens beside Lough Neagh, even while poplars quiver and the tall iris blooms by a blue lake. The lays that follow hold that double vision, of a new western home and an old Irish shore. Nicholl writes with simple feeling for exile, landscape, and memory.
69801-the-dread-apache-that-early-day-sc:
Freeman wrote The Dread Apache, a pamphlet from Tucson, Arizona, in 1915. He was a doctor there, and dates his piece November 14. Two early-day photographs recalled the frontier drama to him, he opens. The Apache was the chief actor in that bloody drama, he writes. For years he was the relentless foe of the pioneer.

A headline counts two thousand pioneers as victims of Apaches. How many breakers of the wilderness were sent to rest, who can say. Some place the number at two thousand, some say more, he writes. The soldier boy is not counted in that grim reckoning. The Apache never met you in the open, he charges of the old days. Ambush behind boulder or brush was his way, he says. A quoted voice owns the Apache was no coward at heart. Freeman gives an Arizona pioneer's view of the desert wars.
69813-go-she-must:
David Garnett builds a country novel around a clergyman's household, in a book issued by Alfred A Knopf at New York in 1927 and dedicated to Stephen Tomlin.

Sixteen chapters carry the tale from a snowbound January morning in Dry Coulter. The Reverend Charles Dunnock looks out on three inches of snow. Later chapters pass through Plough Monday, a trapeze boy, a burnt farm, and a birthday tea. Later the scene shifts to Paris, then home again for a removal, a honeymoon, and a close called Angels. Garnett writes with a light, exact touch: the snow passage lingers on how one colour can make a known world strange. The book is a quiet family tale told in set pieces, each chapter standing like a small painting.
6998-the-spanish-chest:
Edna Brown's Spanish Chest opens with a foreword comparing books to a sketch whose painted figures walked out of the picture. Brown says books grow because someone thinks hard about their characters, and her own little book grew that way. It is dedicated to Florence and Clara, who shared a winter in the Channel Islands and have since gone on a longer journey, with verses confessing lines washed in with tears.

An illustration asks what a tiny dotted line across the grounds can mean, as Win inquires into a mystery. Photographs and drawings by John Goss adorn the tale, which mixes nonsense, mocking fears, and feeling. Brown wrote not for critics but for friendly eyes, and the chest at the center holds more than old things.
70193-with-washington-in-the-west:
Edward Stratemeyer wrote With Washington in the West, a tale for boys in his Colonial Series. Its short title calls it a soldier boy tale of fights in the wilds. The book came out at Boston from Lothrop, Lee and Shepard. A plate shows Colonel Washington in the thick of a fight, at page 278.

Ads in front list the many sets Stratemeyer wrote for the young. His Old Glory set told of war in Cuba and the isles of the east. The Colonial set turns back to the birth of the land. A boy hero walks with the young Washington in the west woods. Such tales taught boys pride in the past through fights, marches, and risk. The brisk pace and brave tone mark the school of boys books of that age.
70305-torwood-s-trust:
Torwood's Trust is a novel by Evelyn Everett-Green, published in London in 1884 in three volumes. The author dedicates it to her sisters Gertrude and Constance. She calls it her first novel, given in fulfilment of a promise made in early childhood, as the dedication states.

A line from Henry the Fourth heads the book, on plucking safety from danger. Volume one opens with a prologue, then news from England. A Doctor Schneeberger, an exile's return, and Philip's sister enter in early chapters. Michael Meredith and a talk in the twilight carry the tale onward. Readers get a full Victorian three decker of family trust, exile, and return.
70306-torwood-s-trust:
Evelyn Everett-Green wrote Torwood's Trust, A Novel, shown here in Volume Two of a three volume set issued at London in 1884 by Richard Bentley and Son. A quote from Henry the Fourth heads the book on danger and safety in a plot. Fifteen chapters fill this volume. A Second Alfred Belassis leads the tale.

Mrs Belassis visits Ladywell and a paper goes missing in the early turns. Wild oats, a visit to Germany, and discomfiture follow. Betsy Long, a betrothal, and a guest from Italy build the middle. Friend or foe, an ally for Mrs Belassis, and Miss Marjory's opinions press the intrigue. Plots and counterplots, an agreeable dinner, and Maud's decision close the volume. Chapter One shows Miss Marjory's dinner a marked success, with talk of politics and science in her garden and drawing room.
70307-torwood-s-trust:
Torwood's Trust is a novel by Evelyn Everett-Green. The text here is volume three of three, printed in London in 1884. A line from Henry the Fourth stands as the motto.

The last volume opens with a chapter named Detected, and turns on an attack. Escape, a wishing well and a lost will drive the plot. Two men, Phil and Tor, face each other as the truth nears. A house named Belassis falls by the close. The chapter heads promise secrets, flight and a will that could change all. The tale ends the long family drama. Everett-Green was known for tales of faith, home and duty.
70402-dynasty-of-the-lost:
George O Smith spins a tale of stolen science in a novel drawn from a magazine of May and June 1950. Harry Vinson arrives early to test a machine built over eight years of hard work. The great hall stands empty, its racks stripped, its power switches open and its fuses pulled.

Inside, Vinson grasps that the vast machine was not wrecked but calmly taken apart and carted away in one night. Each nut sits neatly by its bare floor stud, as if a crew had all the time in the world. He staggers home in a daze and dreams of a gleaming monster and a frightened girl. Readers get a brisk mystery that asks who could steal tons of gear, and why metal doom may follow.
70445-host-and-guest:
Host and Guest is a book about dinners, dinner giving, wines, and desserts by Kirwan of the Middle Temple, printed at London by Bell and Daldy. Verses from Shakespeare and Horace, and a Spanish proverb about eating one's fowl alone, stand at the front. Kirwan is clear in his preface: the book is not a cookery book.

He writes from a life of dining out and giving dinners, and from years spent in foreign lands. He says he often felt the want of such a guide when young, and heard friends say the same. The book treats the choice and quality of foods, and the art of the table, for hosts who would do the thing well.
70559-survival-of-the-fittest:
Gene Henderson wrote a novelet that ran in Science Fiction Quarterly in November 1951. They were not robots, the blurb insists, even though people called them that. They were androids, and they wanted to be treated as rational beings. Treat machines as equals, humans scream in horror at the thought.

The tale opens in a small inner laboratory. Don steps in and unseen latches click, while a low hum marks a lethal field on the other side that would burn any non metallic object to a crisp. Doctor Stone, his superior, stands tall and dejected with three men watching. Sealed caves and tunnels lined with an impervious alloy, first thought Incan, deepen the puzzle. Fitness, pride, and survival clash.
70599-the-trumpet-in-the-dust:
Constance Holme wrote this novel of English country life, in a second edition published in London in 1921. Holme had already written The Lonely Plough, The Old Road from Spain, and other rural tales. She gives this book, with dry humor, to a lord, calling it a weed from an uncultivated garden.

The title comes from a poem about a man on his way to the temple with evening offerings. He finds a trumpet lying in the dust and wonders whether his wanderings are truly over. Holme's tales turn on farms, old houses, and the slow clash of old and new ways. Readers get a quiet, strong novel from a writer rooted in her ground.
70606-the-last-test:
The Last Test is a horror story by Adolphe de Castro, printed in Weird Tales in November 1928. De Castro had written The Monk and the Hangman's Daughter with Ambrose Bierce. An editor's note commends the tale to readers who like artistic horror. It speaks of unthinkable things from the elder world.

Few people, the story says, know the inside of the Clarendon affair. The newspapers never reached it. It was a San Francisco sensation in the days before the fire. Panic and menace kept it company, and it touched the governor of the state himself. Governor Dalton was Clarendon's best friend. The tale unfolds as a cold breeze from the tomb, by the editor's phrase, over a city scandal with a rotten heart. De Castro writes in Bierce's shadow and holds his own.
70695-bakst:
André Levinson wrote the text of Bakst, a life of the Russian stage artist Leon Bakst, issued by the Alexander Kogan Publishing Company of Berlin in its Russian Art series in 1922. Brentano's of New York sold the American edition, which ran to two hundred fifty numbered copies; this is number 247. A portrait of Bakst by Modigliani stands at the front, with a design for a decorative panel called Chastising Cupid.

Levinson opens in the yellow drawing room of Bakst's childhood home in a sober middle-class house on Sadovaia street in Petrograd. He marvels that the boy raised in that dull home became the maker of costly pageants and splendor that changed the western stage. The book tells the life of the designer of the Ballets Russes for collectors and lovers of the theatre.
7074-beauty-and-the-beast:
Marie Le Prince de Beaumont tells Beauty and the Beast as a tale for juvenile readers, ornamented with elegant engravings. A rich merchant with six children, three sons and three daughters, spares no cost for their education and gives them all kinds of masters. His daughters are extremely handsome, above all the youngest, admired from childhood as the little Beauty, a name she keeps as she grows.

Her sisters, proud because they are rich, give themselves ridiculous airs and will visit only persons of quality. The youngest, handsome as she is, proves better than her sisters in temper and heart. A frontispiece shows the Beast attacking the merchant, and the tale that follows turns pride, patience, and love into a household classic.
70791-the-highest-aim-of-the-physicist:
Professor Rowland of Johns Hopkins, America's leading physicist of his generation, gave The Highest Aim of the Physicist as an address printed in Science on December 8, 1899. He spoke to the founding gathering of the new national society of physicists. Gentlemen and fellow physicists of America, he begins: we meet on an occasion that marks an epoch.

Rowland argues that American physics must prize pure discovery over invention for profit. He had built the ruling engines that split light into its finest lines, and he spoke as the craft's elder. The address is a founding sermon for American research science: do the deep work, train students to revere truth, and the applications will follow of themselves.
70851-the-heiress-of-greenhurst:
Ann Stephens wrote this autobiography of a heroine, printed by Edward Stephens in New York in 1857. Stephens had already won readers with Fashion and Famine. She dedicated the book to her mother. Fifty-six chapters carry the heiress from a first gift to an old tower chamber.

A sibyl's cave, a weird wedding, and a gitanilla's oath open the wonders. Chaleco the gypsy plunders and triumphs by turns. Marston Court and Greenhurst, mansion and cottage, frame the tale's two worlds. A bronze coffer holds a mother's journal; a father's house waits behind a threshold. Stephens writes the domestic sensation novel at full stretch: lost friends, shadowy death chambers, and flights by night. The heiress tells her own story, tempest by tempest, as the type demanded.
70951-a-text-book-on-hygiene-and-pediatr:
A Text-Book on Hygiene and Pediatrics from a Chiropractic Standpoint, by John H Craven, was published by the author at Davenport, Iowa, in 1924.
