Craven taught hygiene and public health at the Palmer School of Chiropractic, and held its chair of philosophy in orthopedy. He dedicates the book to B J Palmer, who, he says, saved the life of his son.

Section one treats hygiene at large: housing, air, ventilation, heating, lighting, and water. School and industrial hygiene follow, then immunity, germs, disinfection, and the sick room. Food, food poisons, milk, and meat close the part. Section two turns to the child: the baby, dentition, the analysis and adjustment of infants, and the systems of the body.
70967-the-unhallowed-harvest:
Homer Greene wrote a tale of a city parish that Jacobs of Philadelphia copyrighted in 1917. Chapter one is named An Enforced Verdict. The Reverend Robert Bruce Farrar walks down the aisle of a court room and passes the rail, to his seat among the lawyers. An ordinary citizen would have stopped at the rail.

He is rector of Christ Church, the oldest and richest body of its kind in the city, and has held the post for two years. His one fault, men whisper, is that he may slight the souls of the rich to care for the bodies of the poor. The contents promise a sermon the vestry fights, a minister's crisis, a bishop's dilemma, and a final tragedy.
7107-adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chap:
This closing part of Huckleberry Finn opens at chapter thirty six, once all are reckoned asleep. Huck and Tom slip down the lightning rod, shut themselves in the lean to, and bring out fox fire to work by. They clear four or five feet along the middle of the bottom log, right behind Jim's bed, and plan to dig under it, hidden by Jim's counterpane hanging near the ground.

They dig with case knives till near midnight, hands blistered, with hardly a mark to show for it. Huck jokes this is no thirty seven year job but a thirty eight year job, while Tom sighs and falls to thinking. The closing chapters leave Tom still planning while Huck digs through the night.
71086-the-outcast:
The Outcast is a novel by Selma Lagerlof, in a translation from the Swedish by Worster. Doubleday published the English text at Garden City in 1922. A list of the author's books names Jerusalem, the Nils stories, and the Story of Gosta Berling among them. The contents divide the novel into three books.

The story opens on Grimon, an island among rocks and reefs off the west coast of Sweden. There a husband and wife, much unlike each other, sit on a flat rock one Sunday evening. Joel, the husband, is heavy, slow, and fond of his own voice. His wife stays neat and pleasant at fifty, and listens with wandering thoughts. Chapter titles promise a schoolhouse, a flight, and a sermon on the sacredness of life. A curse and its lifting frame the later books of the tale.
71133-won-at-last:
Won at Last, or Mrs Briscoe's Nephews, by Agnes Giberne, is a tale in a new edition. Shaw of Paternoster Row issued it among its tales for the young. Giberne had written The Earls of the Village and Floss Silverthorn before it.

A frontispiece shows a bank-note passed into the narrator's hands. Twenty-eight chapters chart the tale: Cherry and I opens it. Some one unexpected, what to do with her, and a packet of letters follow. Anxious thoughts and doing work mark the middle grind. A young teacher, news from America, and an excursion vary the run. Jack's trouble, measles, and the brothers come in turn. The response, the sacrifice, a telegram, and the reading of the will drive to the end. The first scene is quiet: Cherry sews, sighs, and turns to her mother, with Cress on her lips.
71224-twenty-five-years-in-the-west:
Erasmus Manford wrote a memoir of twenty five years as a traveling preacher in the West, issued in Chicago in 1867. He gave the book to the Christian friends with whom he had lived and labored for years. The contents read like a road log of the young United States, from New England school rooms to Texas battle grounds.

Manford tells of his youth, his change of heart, and his first tours and debates, where he came out second best. He preached in Maryland, crossed the Allegheny Mountains, and worked in Pittsburgh, Ohio, and Cincinnati. Steamboat talks, a sea voyage, and a tornado precede hard travel in Texas, where he slept on the ground and crossed rivers on logs. Houston and San Jacinto both appear.
71318-proceedings-of-the-expedition-to-e:
Proceedings of the Expedition to Explore the Northern Coast of Africa is the official account of a British survey of 1821 and 1822. Captain Beechey of the Royal Navy led the work, with his brother as co-author. The book was published in London by John Murray in 1828. It covers the coast from Tripoli eastward, the Greater Syrtis, and Cyrenaica.

The authors also describe the old cities of the Pentapolis, the five Greek towns of the region. Their dedication thanks the Earl Bathurst and Lord Melville for backing the voyage. The expedition mapped a little-known shore and recorded its ruins. The book stands as a record of naval survey work and early study of the Libyan coast.
71334-nancy-first-and-last:
Nancy First and Last is a novel by Amy Blanchard, printed in Philadelphia in 1917 with pictures by Will Stecher. Blanchard wrote many books for girls, among them Betty of Wye. This tale opens in a peaceful garden where a young couple walks and quarrels: Nancy speaks with passion while the man listens, half bewildered.

A ring drawn from a finger ends the first scene, and the search that follows crosses the sea. Chapters take Nancy to Spain, to a fiesta, to Barcelona, and into a cathedral, with help from England at a key point. Then war breaks out, and the tale turns to wounded men, patience, and opened eyes. It is a romantic story of loss and finding, shaped by its wartime year.
71422-the-pioneer-west:
The Pioneer West: Narratives of the Westward March of Empire is an anthology of frontier narratives, selected and edited by Joseph Lewis French. Little, Brown of Boston published it in 1923, with a foreword by Hamlin Garland and colour illustrations by Remington Schuyler. The frontispiece shows a Doctor Steele, president of the gulch, acting as judge. Bishop Berkeley's line on the westward course of empire stands as motto.

French's introduction calls these the vital pages of American history. America, he writes, is the story of trail-makers, pioneers in every sense. Before government, invention, and city building came the men and women who explored, ploughed, and planted the wilderness. Many of the starkest chronicles of the border, he notes, had passed out of print. A passage preserved in the copy adds the Great War's effect.
71522-how-to-become-a-scientist:
Frank Tousey of New York brought out How to Become a Scientist in 1900 as a book of fun science for young readers. Its full title page promises experiments in chemistry, mechanics, sound, and fireworks, plus math problems and puzzles. The tone is bright and hands-on, aimed at boys and girls who want to try things at home.

Inside, short trials show how air, heat, light, and simple mixes behave, with each effect explained in plain words. Some pieces are party tricks for friends and family, while others teach real first steps in lab work. Math puzzles sit beside the trials, so a reader can shift from doing to thinking. The book still shows how home science was sold to young people at the time.
71659-toffee-haunts-a-ghost:
Toffee Haunts a Ghost is a comic tale of the fantastic by Charles Myers, first printed in Fantastic Adventures in November 1947. Its blurb sets the snag at once. Toffee, a dream girl, is bad enough for Marc to have around. A ghost named George is too much. The hero is Marc Pillsworth, a lean man whose face will not show fear in the common way. In peril it ties itself into a prim knot. As the tale opens, a safe falls from a pulley toward him.

The safe misses him by the merest fraction of an inch. Worse, it fell as if a great hand had hurled it, clean against the laws of physics. The morning has bristled with such impossibilities for Marc. He stares at the black lump in the sidewalk and waits for it to leap at him. Myers plays the haunting for laughs and shivers both.
71725-a-summer-journey-in-the-west:
Steele, the wife of a minister and author of Heroines of Sacred History, kept a notebook of a summer tour in the west and printed it in New York in 1841. Her trip ran four thousand miles, by the Great Lakes, the plains of Illinois, and three great rivers. She says she writes what she saw.

Her notes add fares, distances, and ways to travel for those who might tour or move west after her. She checked what she heard on the road against good gazetteers to guard against error. Readers get a clear, first-hand view of travel in the young west, with costs and routes spelled out.
71888-lives-of-the-apostles-of-jesus-chr:
Lives of the Apostles of Jesus Christ was printed at New Haven in 1836. Young issued the book, entered by its author the year before. David Francis Bacon entered the copyright as author. A plate after Raphael shows Christ's charge to Peter. The preface states the book's promise plainly. Each apostle gets a distinct, plain, historical narrative of his life. Bacon drew aids from writers of former ages and other lands. Their works lay locked in dead or foreign tongues, he says. Thousands who might profit had no access to them.

His aim was to open those stores to common readers. Scripture, tradition, and old authors stand behind the lives. The book belongs to the plain, earnest religious publishing of its time. It treats the twelve as real men whose acts can be traced and told.
722-james-otis-the-pre-revolutionist:
John Clark Ridpath tells the life of James Otis, the Boston lawyer whose speeches against writs of assistance helped spark the American Revolution. Otis argued that taxation without representation broke English liberty. Otis argued against writs of assistance in 1761, a speech John Adams called the start of independence.

Ridpath follows Otis from his early career to his fiery courtroom stand and his later decline, placing him before the better-known patriots. The short life serves as an introduction to a founder whose ideas outlived his mind. Ridpath, a popular historian, wrote the life for general readers, not for scholars alone.
7237-roving-east-and-roving-west:
E. V. Lucas roves east and west in this travel book, opening in India with noiseless feet, the sahib, and the passing show. Birds, towers of silence, and garlands follow, then Delhi, Agra, Lucknow, a tiger, the sacred city, and Calcutta. Japan follows, with its little land, its rope trick, and its quiet scenes, and the contents promise a traveller's eye in both worlds.

Lucas dedicates the book to his host at Raisina and quotes Johnson on the two objects of curiosity, the Christian world and the Mahometan world, with Wordsworth close behind. His sketches favour people, streets, and small encounters over grand sights. The result reads like a notebook kept by a friendly wanderer.
72515-a-motley-jest:
Oscar Fay Adams wrote A Motley Jest, Shakespearean diversions in play form. Sherman, French and Company issued it at Boston in 1909. Adams wrote a dictionary of American authors. A life of Jane Austen bears his name too. The book goes to the Old Cambridge Shakespeare Association. Two pieces fill its pages.

A Shakespearean Fantasy opens the set at page one. The Merchant of Venice, Act Sixth follows at forty-nine. William J Rolfe adds a note to that piece. The sixth act first ran in a Cornhill booklet in 1903. The fantasy sees print here for the first time. Caliban sleeps by a cave in its first scene. Trinculo and Stephano enter quarreling over lost bottles. Prospero's isle after the master's leaving gives Adams a playground for learned jokes on the Bard.
72672-the-true-history-of-the-ghost:
Professor Pepper wrote The True History of the Ghost, published by Cassell and Company in London in 1890. Pepper was John Henry Pepper of the Royal Polytechnic in Regent Street, famous for the stage illusion called Pepper's Ghost. The book is dated from the Polytechnic at Christmas 1889, and a diagram shows the ghost machinery.

A long dedication letter thanks his lawyer for guiding the sealing of the ghost patent in 1863. Pepper tells how the famous illusion, which projected a spectral figure onto a stage, came to be. The subtitle promises all about metempsychosis, the passing of souls between bodies, as well. The book mixes stage science, patent history, and the Victorian taste for wonders half explained and half believed.
72717-the-illiterate-digest:
Will Rogers gathered his syndicated sayings in this book, printed by Boni in New York in 1924. Most books need an excuse for the author, Rogers says; this one needs an alibi for the title too. He prints the lawyer's letter that threatened it, and his answer, in full.

The Literary Digest's owners had objected in 1920, when Rogers used the name for a film feature. Their magazine, the lawyer wrote, was thirty years old and probably the most influential weekly in the world. Rogers kept the title anyway, and the book sold the joke. Inside, his daily comments on politics, prohibition, and Congress run in his plain spelling and plainer sense. The copyrights run through the McNaught Syndicate. The volume is Rogers in his prime, rope tricks traded for type.
73356-too-close-to-the-forest:
Bryce Walton and Al Reynolds wrote Too Close to the Forest, a tale first printed in Fantastic Universe in July 1954. Marsten, a doctor of the mind, has a great experiment on for the evening, in a hall at Revere University. He sits alone behind a table, a single lamp on his lined face like a statue in a gallery.

The tale's frame gives it away: the gap between failure and success hung from a spider's thread, and built a barrier no ESP could cut. Too much knowledge of a subject, the editor warns, can blot out the one vital point. Fans get a neat, sad tale of mind powers.
7347-the-lincoln-story-book-a-judicious-:
Henry L. Williams compiled the Lincoln Story Book as a judicious collection of the best stories and anecdotes of the great president, many appearing here for the first time in book form. His preface contrasts two Lincolns. One is the Chicago statue's typical Westerner of forum, rostrum, and tribune at his inauguration under the war-cloud in 1861. The other is the Lincoln dear to common people, the speaker of household words.

That second Lincoln appears long and gaunt, divided between two chairs for comfort, head bent forward, smiling broadly at a tale of his own. Williams gathers the jokes, sayings, and human moments that made that figure beloved. The book preserves Lincoln the storyteller beside Lincoln the statesman.
7352-first-and-last:
H. Belloc's First and Last gathers essays whose contents range from weighing anchor and the reveillon through cheeses, the captain of industry, and the inventor. The views of England, the lunatic, the inheritance of humour, and an old gentleman's opinions on historical evidence complete the first sweep. The absence of the past, St Patrick, lost things, the reading of history, victory, and reality follow. Jose Maria de Heredia, Normandy and the Normans, old things, Hastings, and Roman roads in Picardy join them, with the decline of the book among them.

Belloc's table reads like a mind wandering a library and a landscape at once, sure in opinion and rich in phrase. The reward of letters, eye-openers, the public, entries, companions of travel, and sources of rivers close a miscellany with no dull corner. Readers get Belloc at his most various and dogmatic.
73588-the-crow-s-nest:
Sara Jeannette Duncan, writing as Cotes, published The Crow's Nest in New York in 1901. Duncan, a Canadian who lived much in India, had won fame with An American Girl in London and A Social Departure. The crow's nest of the title is a hilltop home in the Himalayas, high above the plains.

The tale opens in a room of carpets, curtains, and an armchair on three casters, as the narrator bids her furniture farewell for a long absence. She jokes that such things made Lot's wife turn her head. In India the sky stands on all four sides without a pattern, and the garden earns her disfavor. The book is a wry, observant account of Anglo-Indian life, told in letters and sketches.
73589-beauty-contest:
Beauty Contest is a science fiction story by Henry Slesar, printed in Fantastic in February 1957. Gorgeous girls answered the announcement from all over the nation, the head note says. A routine that would have exhausted a water buffalo awaited them.

The girl in the yellow bathing suit flings her hairpins down in disgust. A redhead beside her speaks with fellow feeling about her ruined perm. Their dressing room is small and jerry built, meant to be shared by six girls. Thirty such cabins string out like a train at the Omaha space field's edge. The picture caption warns the winner had to be more than beautiful. Readers get a sly tale of a very strange contest.
74015-the-skipper-knows-best:
Murray Leinster set this sea adventure aboard the worn tramp steamer Kingston, under Captain Grover. Grover and his chief engineer McGovern sail the old ship to Ras-el-Kasr, a port on the Persian Gulf. Their job is to hand her over to her buyer, Sheik Abu Nakhl, and be done.

McGovern stays aboard largely for love of the captain's daughter, and he dreads the hot, foul-smelling port. Abu proves false, holding plans against the Gulf pearl boats once he has the ship. Grover answers with a bold trick that gives an old anchor a surprising new use. The tale mixes heat, humor, and danger on a short, tense voyage.
74277-beauty-and-the-beast:
Beauty and the Beast is here retold in a picture book edition, an old tale new told, by a writer who signs only with initials. It was printed at London by Sampson Low. The picture list sets the scenes. A little maid wraps her new scarlet cloak round an old watch dog. A feast waits in a king's garden. A merchant finds a small door into the Beast's garden.

On strange prickly leaves, the list says, someone has carved Beauty's name. Each night after supper the Beast asks Beauty to be his, and the tale runs its known course of fear softening into love. The pictures lead, and the text follows them for young readers. It is the classic tale dressed for the nursery.
74306-life-in-the-eagle-s-nest:
Charlotte Maria Tucker, writing as A L O E, wrote a tale of Afghanistan published at London to earn money for her mission work in India. Her preface says she has often claimed to devote her pen to her adopted country, India. The tale still serves the missionary cause, she argues, in a different way. She wants money for her Mission Plough.

That plough is a school for Mohammedan and heathen boys at Batala. Hours not taken from her city work went to writing the story. A frontispiece shows Assad Khan by torchlight, a striking figure. Tucker spent her later life in India and wrote dozens of such tales.
74454-report-on-the-indian-schools-of-ma:
Bryce, chief medical officer of the Department of Indian Affairs, wrote a Report on the Indian Schools of Manitoba and the Northwest Territories. The Government Printing Bureau printed it at Ottawa in 1907. His letter of June 19, 1907 sends the report to Frank Pedley, deputy head of the department. A short summary maps the whole: a history of the schools first, then their present state, then the health of the pupils.

The history reaches back to the French and English trade on the plains and to the missionaries who moved with the bands or went from post to post. Bryce argues that those teachers, more than trade or force, changed the life of the native peoples. His medical office gives the health section its weight.
74507-the-east:
The East is William Young Martin's narrative of personal impressions of a tour in Egypt, Palestine, and Syria. Tinsley Brothers of London published the book in 1876, with views of Jerusalem's temple court wall and the Dome of the Rock at its head. Martin adds many references to the manners and present condition of the Turks and to current events.

His preface is defensive on one point. The book was written more than a year before it appeared and sat in the publishers' hands before the Bulgarian massacre filled the papers. Any new book on the East, he knew, would be taken for a product of the excitement over the Turkish atrocities. Martin's pages record what one traveller saw and thought just before that storm broke over the Eastern Question.
74581-left-with-a-trust:
Nellie Hellis wrote Left With a Trust, a religious story for the young published in London by Partridge and Company. Hellis had written Three Little Fiddlers, Gipsy Jan, and Little King Davie. A picture shows a dying figure saying, I have something to give each of you before I go. The motto is the Bible line about faithfulness in that which is least. Chapters open at Ninety-Nine, Madeira Street, on the day that followed.

Dora grows methodical, Giles proves himself a manly boy, a race ends oddly, and a cheque arrives for Dora. Hellis wrote improving tales for Sunday schools. This one turns on children keeping a trust left to them.
74670-loved-and-lost:
Loved and Lost is a love story by Bertha Clay, a favourite of millions. The New Bertha Clay Library issued it as number two hundred twenty six. The price was fifteen cents for these love stories with plenty of action. The publisher boasts that countless women have enjoyed Clay works for years.

Her list runs from In Love Crucible and A Sinful Secret onward in order. Between Two Loves, A Golden Heart, and Redeemed by Love fill the shelf. The Broken Trust, For a Woman Honor, and Her Second Love follow them. These tales are clean from start to finish, the notice insists proudly. All titles stay always in print in this authorised edition alone.
7474-the-ancient-east:
D. G. Hogarth, Keeper of the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford, wrote this short history for the Home University Library of Modern Knowledge. He starts by fixing what his title means, since older writers used direction words in their own way. For Herodotus and Greeks of his day, the southern lands were Egypt, Arabia, and India. The northern lands were Thrace and Scythia, while Hither Asia counted as the East.

Beyond that East, those writers pictured only a fabled stream, Ocean, ringing the world. Hogarth then follows his region through time, with chapters on the years 1000, 800, 600, and 400 before Christ, closing with the victory of the West and an epilogue. Maps show the region and its main divisions and the Asiatic empire of the age. It is a compact survey of the ancient Near East before Alexander, written while archaeology was remaking the field.
74901-lucia-s-trust:
Catharine Shaw wrote Lucia's Trust, a story for girls issued in a new edition by John F Shaw of London in 1893. A picture at the front shows coins being poured into Lucia's lap. The tale opens as Lucia enjoys a rare holiday with cousins in the North, away from her London home and the little flock of step-brothers and sisters who keep her busy.

Then a letter comes, and there is no choice: she must go. News of illness at home overturns her happy visit and speaks of changes that may shape her life for years. The chapters that follow promise a cottage, a queen, gifts, and voices in a forest. Shaw wrote many such tales, where a girl's steadiness under sudden duty is the real story.
74953-the-radio-ghost:
The Radio Ghost is a mystery story by Otis Adelbert Kline. Kline had earlier written The Malignant Entity. A magazine headnote praises the tale's sound science. The radio principles throughout are quite accurate, it says. Any good radio man could duplicate the thing.

The tale opens in a doctor's study on a Saturday. Doctor Dorp and the narrator, Evans, debate psychic phenomena. Their talk turns to ectoplasm and spirit matters. The housekeeper interrupts with a visitor. A young lady wishes a professional consultation. She is Greta Van Loan, small and golden-haired. She knows the doctor from newspaper pictures of his investigations. A flying chair in the illustration promises violence ahead.
74958-when-east-met-west:
When East Met West is a complete novelette by Tuttle, a writer of western tales. Its narrator opens by denying the famed line that East and West shall never meet. That poet, he says, was all wrong, and he will tell how he knows it.

The narrator calls himself cautious, burnt once and wary since, like all the Harper tribe. He and Dirty Shirt Jones have been prospecting in the Whispering Creek hills. They return to Piperock to find their partner Magpie Simpkins in Sunday clothes at the shack table. Readers get Tuttle's dry cowboy voice in a tale of East meeting West in a mining town.
75131-from-the-west-to-the-west:
Abigail Scott Duniway wrote From the West to the West, a historical novel of the journey across the plains to Oregon, published by McClurg in Chicago in 1905. Duniway dedicated it to the Historical Society of Oregon and its pioneers. In her preface she explains the book's origin. Readers had asked for years for a reprint of her first little story, out of print for forty years. In its stead she wrote this novel.

Duniway knew the world she describes. Among the relics at the Oregon Historical Society she lists an immigrant wagon, a battered ox-yoke, a home-made loom, and a rusty Dutch oven. She crossed the plains herself as a girl in 1852, and later became the leading voice for women's suffrage in the Pacific Northwest. The novel draws on that crossing: families, wagons, and the long road west, told by a woman who had made the journey.
75327-the-world-of-the-great-forest:
The World of the Great Forest, by Paul Du Chaillu, tells how animals talk, think, work, and live. Scribner published it at New York in 1900 with over fifty illustrations. Knight and Gleeson drew the pictures of forest life for the book. A plate caption coos, here I am dear, waiting for you, at the front.

Du Chaillu wrote Stories of the Gorilla Country and The Country of the Dwarfs before this. He inscribes the book to Charles and Arthur Scribner in a warm letter. Their uniform courtesy over a series of years wins his thanks in that letter. Gorilla, elephant, ant, and bird of the equatorial forest fill his tales for the young. A famed traveller turns storyteller of animal minds for children in these pages.
75349-rambles-in-waltham-forest:
Rambles in Waltham Forest is a stranger's contribution to a triennial sale for the benefit of the Wanstead Lying-in Charity, printed at London in 1827. Its motto is the apostle's word: silver and gold have I none, but such as I have give I thee. The book is mostly verse.

The opening poem praises the forest land of soft showers, far extending vales, and woodlands fanned by summer's gentlest gales. Streams glisten half hid in tangled brake and waving sedge. Rich plenty smiles over golden meadows in the lines. Waltham Forest, the old hunting ground northeast of London around Epping, was then still deep country. The verses sold charity and scenery together. It is a slight, period piece of local patriotism.
75378-needwood-forest:
Needwood Forest is a poem printed at Lichfield in 1776. It praises the forest of Needwood in Staffordshire, a royal hunting forest near the cathedral city. The poem is written in couplets, in the manner of the topographical verse of its century.

The poet opens by calling on the forest he is about to leave. If his early voice taught its echoes to rejoice, if his hounds in full cry filled its banks, then let it take his parting verse. A green-robed nymph steps down the glades and beckons toward the shades. She is no wanton lure to halls of vice. Her mild looks carry the charm of innocence, and a sweet wildness sparkles in her eye. She leads him up the steep lawn and through the leafy mazes where the genius of the place lies listening to a druid's rhymes.
75408-hiram-in-the-middle-west:
Burbank L Todd wrote this farm novel, second of his Back to the Soil series, copyrighted in 1920. Hiram the Young Farmer came first. The subtitle here is a young farmer's upward struggle, and Hiram Strong is the striver.

The contents trace his year: a kernel of wheat, an inventor's luck, and the farm called Sunnyside. Seed testing, a bluebird chapter, and trouble with Turner's bull season the work. A baby tornado and a wheat harvest raise the stakes, and a partnership is formed. Rain streaks the train window as Hiram reaches Pringleton in the first chapter, and the platform glitters with puddles. Todd writes farming as adventure for boys leaving the city in their thoughts.
75441-terror-out-of-the-past:
Terror Out of the Past, by Gallun, appeared in Amazing Stories in March 1940. Perry Wilcox flies over a stretch of hills with the old scientist Roderick Murgatroyd. From the air, Perry spots what ground travellers missed for decades. The hills form a vast triangle, a mile across, with humps along its sides like buried turrets.

The two men read the shape as a fortress. Layers of glacial silt cover it, so it must be very old. No known people could have built it at such a date. Gallun sends his pair down into the earth after the secret. The story mixes aviation, lost races, and deep time in the pulp manner of its day.
75534-the-nile-quest:
Sir Harry Johnston wrote this record of the search for the source of the Nile, printed by Alston Rivers of London in 1906. The book sits in The Story of Exploration, a series edited by J Scott Keltie. Maps come from J G Bartholomew, and the front plate shows Speke, drawn by Johnston himself. Johnston headed the African Society.

The series preface calls the probing of lands and seas one of the most lasting tales of human curiosity. Records left by Egyptians, Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Hebrews, and Chinese start the story more than three thousand years back. Johnston then traces the Nile quest stage by stage, life by life, from the first journeys of record to his own day.
75900-the-adventures-of-a-modern-occulti:
Oliver Bland wrote The Adventures of a Modern Occultist, issued at New York in 1920. Its eleven chapters treat the dead rapper, the automatist, astral light, sex in the next world, the reality of sorcery, incense, possession, and the occultism of the East. A line from Bacon's Essays stands at the front: read not to contradict or to believe, but to weigh and consider.

Bland opens with Harry Carthew, a friend from his Oxford days who had been a keen foe of spiritualism as a young man. Carthew dropped out of sight, worked with oil wells in Mexico, and then wrote from London with psychic problems that puzzled him. Bland holds a rule of not arguing such matters with the ignorant or the scornful. The book weighs the séance-room claims of its day from inside.
76151-the-unbidden-guest:
McVeigh Miller wrote this novel of love and jealousy, first copyrighted in 1900. She was a prolific writer of popular tales, with books such as The Fatal Kiss and Pretty Madcap Lucy to her name. The story's second title, Between Two Passions, points to its core conflict.

Chapter titles trace the plot: a gipsy's curse, Lelia's ingratitude, and jealousy as cruel as the grave. A poor gipsy waif, deadly peril, and a girl who stares death in the face raise the heat. The unbidden guest of the title arrives to stir the household further. Readers get a fast, high-feeling tale of the kind once sold in cheap series to eager crowds.
76354-the-breach-of-trust:
Madeline Leslie wrote The Breach of Trust, a religious tale entered for copyright at Boston in 1869. Its subtitle, The Professor and Possessor of Piety, became the scrap of title in the catalog record. The Lothrop company published the book. Two Bible lines about knowing people by their fruits stand at the front.

The story sets two kinds of church member side by side. One merely professes faith, while the other truly lives it. Chapters follow Helen and her Sabbath school class, her secret, and time in the pastor's study. Later chapters bear names like "The Feigned and the Real" and "The Revelation," pointing to the lesson. Books of this sort were given to Sunday school pupils to teach that outward show is no proof of real faith.
76648-the-infant-moralist:
Lady Helena Carnegie and Mrs Arthur Jacob wrote a book of moral verse for children, printed in Edinburgh in 1903. Each poem takes a fault and follows it to its cost. In one, George frees his cousin Amelia's bird, and Harriet's cat kills it at once. He is told he will be thrashed and sent to bed.

Another poem follows Master Percy, who sets the town hall clock an hour fast for sport. He then climbs the belfry and rings all the bells, throwing the town into uproar. He slips, hangs from the roof, and falls, breaking bones. The verse is plain, firm, and meant to warn young readers.
76737-the-sociable-ghost:
The Sociable Ghost is a comic fantasy written down by Olive Harper and another, and published in New York in 1903. Its long subtitle promises the adventures of a reporter invited by a ghost to a banquet, ball, and convention under the ground of old Trinity churchyard. It calls itself a true tale of things he saw and did not see while he was not there.

The frontispiece shows the first meeting, at the north porch of Trinity Church. Below ground, the reporter meets the leader of the Four Hundred, a gambler doing penance, and a mended ghost. An Egyptian princess appears, the ghosts tell stories and compare notes, and a grand ball closes the convention. Thomas McIlvaine and Schwartz drew the many pictures. The book is a light hearted tour of famous dead New Yorkers.
76788-round-the-horn-before-the-mast:
A Basil Lubbock wrote Round the Horn Before the Mast, first issued in November nineteen two. Dutton brought out the New York edition of nineteen three. The Royalshire, his ship, fronts the book in a picture. He dedicates the tale to his mother.

Frisco opens the contents: choosing a ship and signing on. A seaman's tailor, a sailors' concert, and a cricket match fill his first days. Landlubber crews and hard Yankee ways at sea get plain words. Oakland Creek and Port Costa follow, with sea serpents and mosquitoes. Lubbock went to sea as a gentleman sailor before the mast. His Cape Horn voyage became a classic of sail.
76947-the-land-beyond-the-mist:
Ernest Haycox wrote The Land Beyond the Mist, a western tale of the Oregon emigrant road. Tom Cameron rides at its head, singing against the rain.

It is late fall of 1848, and twenty wagons crawl the Barlow Road over the Cascades. Seven days have brought no sun. Mist seals the train off like a fog bank at sea. Rain soaks canvas, clothes, bedding, and food. Nothing in the whole column is dry. Cameron's pony steams and stumbles under lumps of clay. In the beginning a hundred wagons had crossed the plains together. At Fort Hall most turned south for California gold. These few press on for the Willamette valley.
77031-just-a-bit-too-fast:
Hal Moore wrote this crime tale for Argosy All-Story Weekly, dated March 16, 1929. Its crook is Thought-and-a-half Morgan, a man who reckons he stays exactly that far ahead of slow police. The narrator and Detective Halloran watch a six-cylinder touring car draw up across from the Peninsula Park branch bank.

Neither man thinks much of the car at first, and that is the mistake. Then they notice the young driver, seemingly asleep, has kept his motor running. Halloran had jumped a thousand miles to warn the chief that Morgan meant to try his famous strokes in their city of a million souls.
77163-a-lent-in-earnest:
A Lent in Earnest gives sober thoughts for the solemn days of Lent. Lucy Ellen Guernsey wrote the meditations. Whittaker published them in New York in 1889. A reading is appointed for every day of the season. Ash Wednesday opens the course. Easter Day closes it. Guernsey dedicated the pages to the shut-in.

Her dedication speaks to those kept from church by infirmity. The pages grew out of many days of seclusion. Daily themes follow the church's own rhythm. Repentance, confession, and forgiveness lead the first week. Fasting and abstinence earn several days. Prayer and intercession fill the third week. Enemies, the world, and the flesh succeed. Comfort and the household of God close the middle course. The cross stands at Good Friday.
77254-everest:
Isaac Asimov wrote Everest, a short science fiction story with a teasing premise. A head note asks whether readers have heard the real truth about the great mountain. Everest, it claims, has been climbed twice. The narrator works for an outfit called Planetary Survey, and mountains are not really its line.

The tale begins in 1952, when climbers were near giving up on Everest. Fuzzy photographs kept them going: dark blobs against the snow that men swore were living creatures. The narrator's friend Jimmy Robbons, a climbing enthusiast, can quote every strange footprint report from the ice. He knows the tales of spindly white creatures speeding over the crags. Asimov spins the yeti stories into a cool, wry puzzle about what lives at the top of the world.
77568-the-straight-road-is-shortest-and-:
A Sunday-school tale signed only with its author's initials, published by Frederick Warne at London in 1867. The scene is Cortley Hall, where Marsden, a rich benefactor to every cottage for miles, is preparing for the wedding of his daughter Mina. Her gay cousin Rosa May is making rosettes and favours of white satin ribbon. Mina's young brother Wilfred has been sent three miles to town for orange-blossom on a sultry June day.

The chapter titles promise the moral machinery: a mishap in the woods, then trials headed Fire, Earth, and Water, a chase, conjectures, and a decision. The title states the lesson in advance: the straight road of honesty is shortest and surest. Such tales were the prizes and presents of Victorian childhood, story and sermon in one.
77674-confessions-of-an-anarchist:
W C Hart wrote this attack on the anarchist movement, printed by E Grant Richards in London in 1906. Hart says he spent some ten years among anarchists and in study of their papers. He was secretary to two anarchist groups, a known face in their circles, and a sometime writer for the Torch, Freedom, The Commonweal, Liberty, and The Alarm. The front plate shows the mastheads of those papers.

His chapters charge that anarchy denies morals, that its men are immoral, that police-paid spies work among them, and that bomb-making goes on. A conference and the groups' daily work come under the same harsh eye. The book is a hostile witness report, not a defence, and it must be read as such.
77796-theodosia-ernest:
A. C. Dayton wrote this tale of faith, in two books bound as one. It was put out at Memphis, Tennessee, in 1866. The first book is named The Heroine of Faith. Its frame is a run of nights of study: the first night, the next, and so on to the tenth. A dream stands twixt the nights, and the day past the seventh night breaks the run. A word on Theodosia stands at its front.

The next book takes a new frame: ten days of roam in search of the Church. Day by day the trip is told, first to tenth. The pair of books thus join tale and proof in one work. A maid of faith is led, by study and by search, to the church her heart holds to be the true one.
77804-the-man-who-married-the-moon-and-o:
The Man Who Married the Moon is a book of Pueblo folk stories retold by Charles Lummis. The Century Company published it in New York in 1894. Lummis also wrote Some Strange Corners of Our Country. An introduction salutes the brown story tellers who gave him the tales. The contents list more than twenty stories in the book. The Antelope Boy opens the storytelling. Coyote tales follow in a run of trickster pieces. The Coyote meets crows, blackbirds, a bear, and a woodpecker.

The title story stands eighth in the contents list. The Mother Moon and The Maker of the Thunder-Knives follow it. The Magic Hide-and-Seek and The Race of the Tails give wonder tales. The Moqui Boy and the Eagle brings in a neighbouring people. Lummis dedicates the book to his wife and child.
77861-maud-marian-artist:
Eglanton Thorne wrote this girls' novel, issued by the Religious Tract Society of London. The heroine is Maud Marian, who becomes mistress of her father's house when her loved Aunt Helen marries and leaves. Maud cares for art above all, as the first chapter title says, and a startling proposal soon carries her to Rome.

There she helps open the Studio Mariano and makes new friends among artists. The chapters mix romance with trouble: a passionate act, a serious adventure, a search for the lost, and a bout of fever. Scenes at the Villa Mattei and the ruins of Tusculum give the tale its Italian color. It is a story of talent, duty, and love.
78076-robert-frost:
Gorham Munson wrote this study of the poet Robert Frost, published in New York in 1927. It belongs to a series called the Murray Hill Biographies. A photograph of Frost by Doris Ulmann fronts the book, and Munson gives it to the poet Hart Crane.

Chapters take Frost's books in order: A Boy's Will, the famed Road Not Taken, and New Hampshire. Others treat single poems such as Pan With Us and Into My Own. Munson calls his subject a sensiblist, a poet of felt life, and defends his good sense. Appendices gather British praise and Frost's views on schooling. Readers get an early, keen portrait of a poet still rising.
78327-collected-poems-of-robert-frost:
Collected Poems of Robert Frost gathers the work of the New England poet in one volume, copyrighted in 1930 by Henry Holt and Company of New York. This copy is the fourth printing. The contents open with The Pasture, Frost's invitation poem. Then comes his first book, A Boy's Will, whole. Its poems include Into My Own, Ghost House, Storm Fear, Mowing, Going for Water, and The Tuft of Flowers.

North of Boston follows, with Mending Wall, The Death of the Hired Man, The Mountain, and Home Burial. Frost wrote of farms, stone walls, and hired men in plain speech with deep turns. By 1930 he was America's best-known living poet, and this volume fixed his early canon.
78402-rustlers-roost:
Tuttle wrote Rustlers' Roost, a western novel by the author of Hashknife and the Fantom Riders. It opens behind bars. Like a brown leaf fluttering in the wind, a paper came through the bars of the cell door. It floated past the cot and rested on the concrete floor.

A heavy brogan slid over it, and Tex Rowland, Number 1733, squinted at the bars. A trusty had just passed: a wizened, hump shouldered little old man. Hump Sherrill had been his name before other people's horses came into his possession, and possession gave him a number in a place with little use for the eighth commandment. Hump had known Tex in the cattle country, where they worked for the same outfit. Now the old horse thief is a model prisoner, and a message has come through the bars. Tuttle starts his war in a cell.
78432-the-young-pioneers-of-the-north-we:
The Young Pioneers of the North-West, by Pearson, belongs to the Frontier Series of Lee and Shepard. Boston saw the edition of 1890, though the work was entered for copyright in 1869. Pearson also wrote The Cabin on the Prairie, as the title page notes. Illustrations, one called The Surprise, grace the volume for young readers.

Chapter one brings a fairy of the fort, with pleasure and sorrow mixed. A riderless pony and a buffalo wallow follow in the second chapter. Flight from the wigwam, Indian watch dogs, and tragedy on the river raise the stakes. A little hunchback and an immigrant aunt enter the cast in later heads. Frontier peril and pioneer grit form the stock of such series books for boys.
78644-hashknife-philanthropist:
Hashknife Philanthropist is a western tale by W C Tuttle, author of tales of Piperock. Its hero is Hashknife Hartley, and its narrator is his friend Sleepy. The narrator owns he does not know who Toothpick Thompson was or is. Yet that man earned the hatred of a smiling soul like Hashknife, he says.

Hashknife's one purpose in life, in this telling, is finding Toothpick. With that one exception he loves everybody, the narrator says. He packs his gun handy all the same, for folk who might mistake his devotion. Asking for a toothpick gets a rise out of him at any time. The tale rolls on in cow country talk, with jokes about toothache, bald heads, and corns.
78929-the-pioneer-women-of-the-west:
Pioneer Women of the West, published at Philadelphia in 1873, is Elizabeth Ellet's set of memoirs of wives and mothers on the American frontier. Ellet wrote it as a companion to her Women of the American Revolution. She gathered material from private family records and from people who still remembered frontier life. The sketches run across the whole West, from Tennessee to Michigan.

Most lives here rest on letters and papers sent in by relatives and friends. A few, such as Mrs Boone and Mary Moore, rest on older print. Ellet mixes in accounts of pioneer homes, habits and hardships between the lives. She also notes the public events that shaped each settlement's fate.
78975-the-immoralist:
The Immoralist, by André Gide, in Dorothy Bussy translation, appeared in 1930. Knopf issued the English text at New York and London that year. The French original, L Immoraliste, came from Mercure de France in Paris. A letter frames the tale: three friends have heard Michel story in full.

They write to a fourth, now in high office, to place Michel somewhere. Michel strength and mind seem wasted, even cruel, with no fit use. His friends fear his devotion will soon turn to himself alone. They stay at his house under a clear sky, awaiting word in haste. The letter begs the minister to find work that can hold him.
79039-the-manliness-of-christ:
Thomas Hughes, author of Tom Brown's Schooldays, holds up Christ as the pattern of true manhood in a book issued by Macmillan at London in 1894. First printed in 1879, it reached a second edition here.

Hughes wrote first for the students of the Working Men's College in London. He was its principal then. Those men came from poorer homes than his Rugby and Oxford world. Twelve years after retiring, he found Rugby calling him back. Dr Percival asked him to give layman's Sunday evening addresses to the school. Looking back across a long life, he wished to draw its beginning and end closer together. The book argues that strength, courage, and tenderness meet in one character. Working men and schoolboys alike were his hearers.
79238-with-the-german-armies-in-the-west:
Sven Hedin, the Swedish explorer famed for treks through Asia and Tibet, went to the Western Front as a guest of the German army. Walterstorff turned his book into English, and John Lane published it in London and New York in nineteen fifteen. It holds one hundred nineteen pictures and four maps, and a second edition soon followed.

Hedin rides along the front in the west, where German troops faced France and Britain. He notes guns, trenches, towns, and the men who serve the guns, with a traveler's eye for land and weather. His view favors his hosts, as the title warns. The book stands as a rare look at the first year of the Great War from the German side, in English dress.
79246-when-love-s-labor-s-lost:
Tuttle wrote When Love's Labor's Lost, a comic western tale of the town of Piperock. Tuttle was known for tales such as Sparing the Family Tree. The tale opens in mid-argument, as the town's men back a wild scheme and only Testament Tilton, the preacher, is against it, which the rest say does not count.

The plan is to buy a lion from a circus due at Granite at the end of August. Chances on the beast will be sold at five dollars each to foot the bill and fund the show. Ike, the narrator, doubts any man would pay five dollars for an ordinary lion, and is told this one is African. Tall talk and small-town pride drive the fun.
79554-valiant-dust:
Valiant Dust is a book of short stories by Katharine Fullerton Gerould, published in New York by Scribner in 1922. The stories had first appeared in magazines across the preceding decade, in Harper's, the Century, and the Atlantic among them. Gerould had written Modes and Morals and The Great Tradition.

Twelve stories fill the contents. An Honest Man opens the book: a countess meets Andrew Radin at a hectic function in her cousin's house, an occasion of no known social kind. Habakkuk, Miss Marriott and the Faun, and Martin's Hollow follow. The Knight's Move, Blue Bonnet, East of Eden, and Sea Green stand in the middle. The Penalties of Artemis, a third act, and Belshazzar's Letter close the set. Gerould's tales are cool, exact studies of manners and morals, written with a New England conscience and a traveller's eye.
79577-the-book-of-a-naturalist:
Hudson, author of 'The Naturalist in La Plata,' gathered these essays in a second edition from Hodder and Stoughton. Life in a pine wood opens the contents, and hints to adder-seekers follow. Bats, the beauty of the fox and a sentimentalist on foxes come next in the list.

A discontented squirrel, a neighbour's bird stories and a toad as traveller show Hudson's range. Herons get two chapters, one on the bird as a notable and one as a table bird. Moles, wasps, hawk-moths, rats and dogs fill later pages, all watched at close range by a patient field observer.
8094-certain-noble-plays-of-japan-from-t:
Ezra Pound chose and finished these noble plays of Japan from the manuscripts of Ernest Fenollosa, with an introduction by William Butler Yeats. Yeats explains that he asked Pound for the plays because they might help explain a possibility of the Irish dramatic movement. And he writes with his imagination stirred by masks and head-dresses seen in the studio of Edmund Dulac. The plays are Noh dramas, with their masked actors, choruses, and ghosts.

Pound's versions brought Japanese classical theatre to English readers for the first time in this form, and they influenced modernist poetry and drama deeply. The volume is short but historic, a meeting of Japanese tradition and European experiment. For readers of Pound and Yeats, it is essential, and for theatre lovers, a doorway into Noh.
8122-legends-of-the-northwest:
H. L. Gordon, author of Pauline, gathered these legends of the Northwest after years spent studying the language, history, traditions, customs, and superstitions of the Dakotas. His contents include a prelude on the Mississippi, The Feast of the Virgins, Winona, and The Legend of the Falls. All legends of the Dakotas, plus The Sea-Gull, the Ojibwa legend of the pictured rocks of Lake Superior, and Minnetonka. Gordon notes that Dakota means alliance or confederation, and that Sioux was a name given by French traders.

The legends are retold in verse and prose, preserving stories of love, sacrifice, and landscape. Gordon writes as a respectful student of the peoples he describes, though through nineteenth-century eyes. For readers of Native American legend and Midwestern lore, the volume remains an early and earnest collection.
8143-the-shadow-of-the-east:
E. M. Hull published The Shadow of the East in 1921, opening on an American yacht brilliantly lit off Yokohama harbour. With the full moon glittering on the water to the steps of the landing-stage. Coloured lamps along the sea wall transform the Japanese town into fairyland, though by day the scene is blatant and tawdry. The epigraph, from Ezekiel, warns that the fathers have eaten sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge.

Hull, famous for The Sheik, writes a romance of the East in which past sins shadow the present. Her heroine moves between yacht society and eastern mystery, and the novel's glamour carries its melodrama. For readers of romantic adventure fiction, it is a vivid example of the genre at its height, and a period portrait of Yokohama.
838-jasmin-barber-poet-philanthropist:
Samuel Smiles wrote this life of Jacques Jasmin, the barber-poet of Agen in southern France. Born poor, Jasmin cut hair by day and wrote verse in Gascon by night, winning fame for songs that moved the people. Sainte-Beuve praised him as a poet whose influence might have spared France revolutions.

Smiles follows Jasmin from boyhood in Agen to his triumphs as a singer and giver, for he spent his earnings on the poor. The life is a Smiles lesson in self-help through art and charity. The book gives English readers a vivid portrait of a folk poet, and of the France he sang for.
8389-lectures-of-col-r-g-ingersoll-lates:
Robert G. Ingersoll, the Great Agnostic, filled lecture halls across America, and this volume gathers his later lectures. Contents include Thomas Paine, Liberty of Man, Woman and Child, Orthodoxy, Blasphemy, and essays on heretics, the Bible, Voltaire, and myth and miracle. Ingersoll argues, with courtroom polish, that reason and kindness outrank creed, and that doubt is honest.

His lectures made freethought respectable to middle-class audiences, and his defense of Paine helped restore a founder long smeared as an infidel. Readers get oratory rather than scholarship: jokes, stories, and rolling periods aimed at a live crowd. The volume still reads as a landmark of American secularism, from its most famous voice.
8745-wulf-the-saxon-a-story-of-the-norma:
G. A. Henty tells the Norman Conquest through Wulf the Saxon, arguing in his preface that Hastings. Though its immediate results may seem less than those of other great battles, has in the long run influenced mankind's destiny more than any similar event. The admixture of Saxon, Danish, and British races called English, he says, lagged behind Europe, distracted by internal dissensions. Broad divisions between north and south under weak kings.

Wulf, a young Saxon thane, serves Harold, fights at Hastings, and lives through conquest, resistance, and settlement under Norman rule. Henty mixes real kings and battles with a hero's adventures, teaching the Conquest as personal story. Boys' adventure and history blend in the usual Henty manner, partisan toward Saxon courage. The novel remains a lively introduction to 1066 for young readers, and a period piece for adults.
8873-the-isle-of-unrest:
Henry Seton Merriman sets The Isle of Unrest in Corsica. Opening with Richard Lovelace's lines on going to the wars: tell me not I am unkind to fly from a quiet breast to war and arms. A new mistress, the first foe in the field, and a stronger faith in sword, horse, and shield. Contents promise the moving finger, chez Clement, a by-path, a toss-up, the Rue du Cherche-Midi, neighbours, journey's end, Vasselot, the promised land. Thus far, before surprise, summons, war, and gossip.

Merriman, popular novelist of adventure, uses Corsican vendetta, French politics, and a love story to build a tale of unrest literal and personal. The island's wild beauty and fierce loyalties drive the plot. Readers who enjoy late Victorian romance with a strong sense of place will find a brisk, atmospheric novel.
9300-jennie-baxter-journalist:
Robert Barr wrote this lively novel in 1899 about Jennie Baxter, a young woman journalist in London. Jennie makes her toilette, meets a porter, and confers with two important editors. She interviews a frightened official, learns of a princess's diamonds, and meets a great detective. Soon she solves the diamond mystery herself.

Later chapters mix Jennie with the elite of earth, dodge an offer of marriage, and brush a government secret. Barr writes with humor and pace, letting his heroine outwit men at their own game. The novel still delights as an early tale of a working girl reporter.
9376-the-forest:
Stewart Edward White wrote this book of the north woods, from the calling to the science of going light. Chapters teach making camp, lying awake at night, open-water canoe travel, and walking through woods. Flies, habitants, rivers, hills, and woods Indians all get their turn, with a fish caught and a man who walks by moonlight.

White writes from camp life itself, with practical hints and poetic feeling joined. An outfit list aids the reader who would follow. The book remains a classic of outdoor writing, a guide and a love letter to the forest at once.
9385-the-incomplete-amorist:
E. Nesbit wrote this novel in 1906, in four books: The Girl, The Man, The Other Woman, and The Other Man. Its Balzac epigraph holds that to birth a desire, nurse it, grow it, and satisfy it is a whole poem. Chapters run from the inevitable and irresistible to the prisoner, the criminal, and the escape, then to seeing life and rescue.

On Mount Parnassus, love and Tupper, and interventions lead to truth, and truth with a vengeance. Nesbit, famed for children's books, writes here for grown-ups with wit. The novel remains a clever, modern romance of desire and its discontents.
9390-fifteen-years-with-the-outcast:
Florence Roberts, called Mother Roberts, wrote this memoir in 1912 of fifteen years with the outcast, meaning the poor and despised. Its preface contrasts two speakers at one assembly: a missionary fresh from India, telling of converts and persecution for leaving idolatry, and a noted English hunter just back from Bengal.

Roberts chose the harder field at home, among those society casts out. Her pages tell of rescue, patience, and faith put to work in slums and streets. The memoir remains a vivid record of Christian social work, earnest, plain, and full of human faces.
942-green-mansions-a-romance-of-the-trop:
W. H. Hudson wrote this romance of the tropical forest, about Abel, a Venezuelan traveller who flees into the wild and finds Rima, a mysterious girl of the woods. Rima, who speaks with birds and lives among green mansions of trees, becomes Abel's love and his guide to a world apart from men.

Hudson writes the forest with lush, poetic prose, full of birdsong, mist, and danger. The romance turns tragic, as Abel's world and Rima's cannot both survive. The book, praised by its foreword writer as beyond his power to do justice, remains a beloved classic of nature romance, haunting and beautiful.
945-dust:
Mr. and Mrs. Haldeman-Julius wrote this novel whose chapters trace dust through a life: the dust is stirred, dust in her heart, dust begets dust, dust in his eyes, and Martin battles with dust. Martin's son shakes off the dust, the dust settles, and the dust-bin waits at the end.

The novel uses dust as a figure for the grime of poverty, toil, and small-town life, and for the hope of shaking it off. Its prose is earnest and plain, aimed at readers who know hard work. Dust stands as a period piece of American social fiction, where a family's fate is told through a single, homely image.
9788-ned-myers-or-a-life-before-the-mast:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote Ned Myers, or A Life Before the Mast, in 1843, the true life of an old shipmate. Cooper holds that any man's life, faithfully told, would interest and instruct readers. Myers, a common sailor, tells his voyages, perils, escapes, and opinions from the forecastle. Cooper hopes Myers's experience and moral change may sway young minds for good.

The book follows a foremast Jack through storms, ports, and hard service, with the tang of true sea talk. Cooper, famed for sea tales, here lets a real sailor speak. A reader gets a vivid, honest sailor's life, and a window on the merchant navy of the early republic.
9905-a-deal-in-wheat-and-other-stories-o:
Frank Norris published this story collection in 1903, three years after his great wheat novel The Octopus. The title tale follows a Chicago wheat corner, where a bear broker and a bull fight over prices while farmers and small traders pay the cost.

Other stories cross the old and new West: a wife on the frontier, a bargain with a peg-legged man, and a sudden death remembered in a memorandum. Norris writes with force about money, land, and luck. The book is a strong short introduction to his belief that markets, like weather, crush the little people first.
a-deal-in-wheat-and-other-stories-of-the: Frank Norris gathers stories of the new and old West around a deal in wheat. The title tale follows a bear broker crying to sell a thousand May at one fifty. Other stories treat the wife of Chino, a bargain with Peg Leg, and the passing of Cock Eye Blacklock. Norris writes of speculation, violence, and fate on the western frontier.
a-girl-of-the-limberlost:
Gene Stratton-Porter wrote this novel about Elnora Comstock, a poor Indiana girl who pays for her schooling by collecting moths and butterflies in the Limberlost swamp. The character list at the front describes her plainly: she collects moths to pay for her education and lives the Golden Rule. Her mother, embittered by her husband's death in that swamp, withholds money and love alike.

Across twenty-five chapters Elnora enters high school in hand-me-down shame. With help from the kind Sinton neighbors, she builds her collection into a livelihood. She also sets her heart on a violin and a full education. Philip Ammon, a young visitor, joins the moth hunts and falls in love. The book mixes nature study of the vanishing swamp with a story of endurance at home.
a-lady-of-quality-being-a-most-curious-h:
Frances Hodgson Burnett frames her historical novel as a curious history related by Mr. Isaac Bickerstaff, in the 1896 Frederick Warne edition used here. It begins on November 24, 1690, at Wildairs Hall, where the loud, choleric Sir Jeoffry prepares to hunt. His daughter grows up wild, beautiful, and proud in Queen Anne's England.

Twenty-four chapters follow Mistress Clorinda through horse breaking, suitors, a marriage to an earl, and a deadly war of reputation with a rival beauty. A hidden miniature and a night meeting in a rose garden mark key turns. Burnett mixes costume splendor with a study of a woman too strong for her age's rules.
a-little-boy-lost: William Henry Hudson tells of a little boy lost on the great plain. Martin chases a flying figure, is found by a deaf old man, and meets the people of the mirage. Savages, a great forest, a flower and serpent, and wild horses fill his journey. Hudson writes a fable of childhood wonder and wandering.
a-project-for-flying-in-earnest-at-last: Robert Hardley promotes a claimed secret of aerial navigation in this 1871 pamphlet, priced at twenty-five cents and framed as a letter to the editor of the Tribune. He dismisses the California experiment as the same old useless effort with impossible agents. He insists that a man living within twenty miles of Trinity steeple can navigate the air in calm or storm, with the wind or against it. The pamphlet promises flight at last, in earnest.
a-smaller-history-of-rome-from-the-earli: William Smith writes this compact history of Rome, from its earliest times down to the founding of the Empire, with a continuation to the year 479 by Eugene Lawrence. Published by Harper in New York in 1881 and illustrated by engravings on wood, the volume belongs to the Student's Series in uniform cloth binding. Maps of Italy and a restored Roman Forum accompany a narrative kept brief for school and general readers.
across-india-or-live-boys-in-the-far-eas: Oliver Optic takes live boys across India, the Far East, in this volume of the All-Over-World Library, third series, published at Boston in 1895. The book is dedicated to William Lee, his publisher and friend of forty years. It is the work of an author already credited with more than a hundred volumes. The contents promise a search for longitude and a wreck in the Arabian Sea, with an illustration of a traveller in magnificent Indian robes.
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chapters-:
The final chapters of Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, chapters 36 to the last, give Tom Sawyer full command of Jim's escape, and the work proceeds by his book-learned rules. Digging with case-knives quietly swapped for picks, a rope ladder baked in a pie, and warnings written in blood. Jim, patient and chained in his cabin, endures a glory he never asked for.

The escape ends in a night chase, a bullet in Tom's leg, and Jim risking his freedom to nurse the boy. Then the revelation that Miss Watson had already freed Jim in her will. Aunt Polly arrives to untangle the boys' names, Tom pays Jim for his trouble, and Huck, dreading adoption and sivilizing, plans to light out for the Territory ahead of the rest.
ae-in-the-irish-theosophist:
AE in the Irish Theosophist collects the early writings of George William Russell, who signed himself AE, from the journal of Ireland's theosophical circle. Russell opens with a word on the objects of the Theosophical Society, the movement that joined Eastern religion, occult study, and moral renewal. Twenty four prose pieces follow, and a set of thirty nine verses closes the gathering.

Titles map his young mysticism: The Mask of Apollo, The Secret of Power, The Priestess of the Woods, and A Tragedy in the Temple. Essays take up concentration, the element language, and the states of waking, dream, and deep sleep under their Sanskrit names. Tales and meditations turn toward Ireland in The Legends of Ancient Eire and At the Dawn of the Kali Yuga. Russell later became a poet, painter, and agricultural reformer; here his otherworldly Ireland is still being invented, page by page.
all-s-for-the-best:
T. S. Arthur gathered All's for the Best in Philadelphia in 1869, twelve tales of faith under trial. The opening piece, Faith and Patience, argues with a doubter of fifty. Mr. Fanshaw confesses he has no faith in anything at all. His friend Wilkins answers with talk of internal sight, the mind's eye.

Other chapters ask Is He a Christian and weigh cast down, but not destroyed. Giving that doth not impoverish praises open-handed charity. Was It Murder, or Suicide darkens the collection with a mystery. The Nursery Maid, My Father, and The Christian Gentleman close the set. Arthur's Swedenborgian faith, trust in divine order behind appearances, shapes every tale. The title is his doctrine: rightly seen, all works for the best, even sorrow.
alton-of-somasco-a-romance-of-the-great-: Harold Bindloss sets a romance of the great Northwest around Alton of Somasco, opening with a first encounter in a rugged frontier land. The story follows ranching, mining, and love against the backdrop of western Canada, where hard work and honour are tested. Bindloss writes with first-hand feeling for the country, making landscape part of the adventure.
an-unsocial-socialist:
George Bernard Shaw begins at a girls' school in an old English country house, where a sensible teacher's quiet evening is broken by a strange arrival. Sidney Trefusis, a rich young widower, has walked out of his marriage and his class to preach socialism. He hides near the school under a false name and stirs every mind he meets.

The schoolgirls, their teachers, and the local gentry all collide with Trefusis's talk about property, marriage, and labor. Shaw fills the novel with debates, letters, and comic scenes at the school and on a model farm. It is fiction used as a platform, written with the wit that later made Shaw famous on the stage.
apess-son-of-the-forest:
William Apess, a Pequot Methodist preacher, published A Son of the Forest in 1829. It is the first published autobiography by a Native American. Apess wrote it himself and issued it at his own cost.

He tells of a poor childhood, beatings by white guardians, service in the War of 1812, and his turn to preaching. Throughout, he protests the theft of Native land and the abuse of Native people. His faith and his anger speak side by side. The book opened a path for Native writers and still stings today. Later editions carried his name as Apess, the spelling used here in the title.
at-love-s-cost:
Charles Garvice wrote this romance in his popular, fast-moving manner, opening with a wealthy young narrator cursing his own folly in a rain-soaked carriage. Garvice, among the best-selling English novelists of his day, builds the plot on love tested by money. Stafford, the hero, soon faces his father Sir Stephen's confession of disaster.

Sir Stephen has staked everything, and more than he possessed, on a grand scheme that now threatens complete ruin. Stafford must reckon with debts he cannot fully understand, while the woman he loves stands on the other side of the family's fall. Garvice keeps secrets, sacrifices, and reversals coming in short chapters, true to the formula that made his romances fixtures of railway bookstalls.
august-first:
Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews and Roy Irving Murray wrote this short novel, published by Scribner's in 1915 with illustrations by A. I. Keller. Its opening finds a clergyman alone in a sweltering parsonage, tugging at his clerical collar and crying Whee! at the heat like a boy. The August the first of the title presses on every scene.

Talk turns to faith and the strange timing of rescue: how five minutes can give a man the lift he had to have. One speaker argues that people strain so hard to prevent wonders that they miss them when they come, mistaking a voice for thunder. A young Scot who beat back his own devil figures in the reckoning. Andrews builds a compact tale of a minister's household, doubt, and timely grace.
aunt-jane-s-nieces-out-west:
Edith Van Dyne, L. Frank Baum's series pen name, published this volume in 1914. Beth, Patsy, and Louise are caught by the camera in California, where picture studios turn girls and nonsense into films. A thrilling rescue introduces A. Jones, a quiet, rigidly intent young stranger whose offer the girls must weigh with care.

Jones stays a mystery: an invalid, a damsel in distress, and Isidore Le Drieux complicate his story. Maud, a picture actress, makes memoranda while pearls appear and Uncle John grows puzzled. The yacht Arabella carries the party toward picture number nineteen and a final judgment. Baum, newly a Californian himself, folds the young film industry into the series formula of wealth, secrets, and sunshine after rain.
beauty-and-the-beast:
Marie Le Prince de Beaumont's Beauty and the Beast is the classic fairy tale, written for the entertainment of juvenile readers and ornamented with elegant engravings. A very rich merchant has six children, three sons and three daughters, and spares no cost for their education.

The youngest daughter, admired from childhood as the little Beauty, is as good as she is handsome. Her two elder sisters pride themselves on their wealth and keep company only with persons of quality. When fortune turns, Beauty's kindness is tested by the Beast's enchanted castle. Readers of every age will recognise this telling as the source of the tale's most familiar form.
ben-hur-a-tale-of-the-christ:
Lew Wallace built Ben-Hur around Judah Ben-Hur, a Jewish prince of Jerusalem under Roman rule, and his boyhood friend Messala, now a Roman officer. A falling tile injures the Roman governor, and Ben-Hur is condemned to the galleys while his mother and sister vanish into prison. At sea he saves the Roman commander Quintus Arrius, who adopts him and makes him rich.

Freed, Ben-Hur trains Arab horses and beats Messala in the great chariot race at Antioch. His search for his family leads through leper caves to the crowds following Jesus of Nazareth. Wallace frames the revenge story inside the Gospel story, ending at the Crucifixion. The novel became the best-selling American religious epic of its century.
beth-norvell-a-romance-of-the-west:
Randall Parrish published this romance of the West with McClurg in 1907, fronted by a colour plate from N. C. Wyeth; the Burt reprint lists four editions in four months. Beth Norvell, an actress travelling with a company, lands in a Colorado mining camp where Winston, the frontispiece's weary watcher, keeps his post until dawn. Parrish had written My Lady of the North and Bob Hampton of Placer in the same vein.

Peril arrives at first light in the sampled scene. A stone rattles ahead on the trail; a rifle hammer clicks; a gruff voice warns the riders that one more step will be answered with fire. Beth, mounted and glancing back at the greying east, must climb on with her trailing skirt gathered in one hand. Theatre folk, mine owners, and claim jumpers share a plot built for pace.
big-timber-a-story-of-the-northwest:
Bertrand W. Sinclair published this novel of the British Columbia woods in 1916, with a frontispiece by Douglas Duer. Monohan, the villain, is spotted on a steamer's after deck in that plate, watching the heroine. Stella Fyfe comes west to green fields and pastures new. She marries logging boss Jack Fyfe and learns the toll of big timber. Durance vile, a close call, a resurrection, and a crisis fill the contents.

Marriage and money grind against each other in the sampled talk. Stella notes that their mode of living grows more expensive while she knows nothing of limits. Jack admits he never went into details: operating as he did, the business netted anywhere from twelve to fifteen thousand. Sinclair, who had logged and fished the coast himself, writes the timber trade from inside the camp.
bought-and-paid-for-from-the-play-of-geo:
Arthur Hornblow made the novel Bought and Paid For from the play by George Broadhurst, and Grosset and Dunlap of New York issued it in 1912. Hornblow calls it a story of today, with pictures from scenes in the play. A rich husband's claim on his wife gives the title its sting.

Virginia's sister Fanny pushed the match and bears the guilt when it sours. Jimmie's breakfast-table tale breaks the wife's peace in one blow. A husband who treats a wife as goods bought and paid for loses her respect, and the plot tests whether pride can bend. Drawing rooms and flats of the day fill the scenes. Playgoers could take the hit home in prose, with its moral quarrel kept sharp.
boy-scouts-in-southern-waters-or-spaniar:
G Harvey Ralphson wrote Boy Scouts in Southern Waters, issued in 1915, with Spaniard's treasure as the prize. Ralphson opens with a collision in fog that cripples the boys' motor boat Fortuna. Jack, Harry, and Arnold cruise southern coasts in her.

A hole in the boat, a marooned scout, and a pirate prisoner stack up fast. Pete Lopez of the bayous feeds guests and hides more than he says. Night attacks, a shanghaiing, and treachery at a Spanish fort drive the middle chapters. Greed beats the villains at the fort before the boys can. The treasure chest resolves the long hunt. Ralphson mixes first aid, wigwag warnings, and seamanship into a salt-water chase for boy readers.
britannica-1911-abernethy-john-priest:
John Abernethy the priest receives a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. Abernethy, an Irish Presbyterian divine born at Coleraine in 1680, was licensed before twenty-one and ordained at Antrim in 1703. Synod debate and evangel work made his local name.

A call to Dublin in 1717, refused on conscience, split his church into Subscribers and Non-subscribers. The Non-subscribers were cut off in 1726 despite his pleading against the breach. Wood Street, Dublin, took him in 1730. His 1731 stand fought all laws that bar men of worth from service for mere points of worship, a stand near a century ahead of his age, the entry holds. His Tracts served later fights for free conscience. He died in 1740.
britannica-1911-alost:
Fire in 1879 badly hurt Alost's finest landmark, a fifteenth-century belfry joined to its town hall. The Belgian town, Aalst in Flemish, stands in East Flanders on the left bank of the Dender and was once capital of Imperial Flanders. Feudal Flanders owed fealty to the French king, yet the strip from Alost toward Zeeland answered to the Holy Roman emperor. People numbered 28,771 in 1897 and 31,655 in 1904.

St Martin's church holds a Rubens painting of St Roch, patron saint of lepers, ordered by the Brewers' Gild. Older memories crowd the town: William Clito took a mortal wound outside it in 1128, and Thierry Maartens later set up one of Europe's first printing presses there. Hops and linen bleaching keep it busy now.
britannica-1911-apollonius-the-sophist: Apollonius the Sophist was a grammarian of Alexandria who most likely lived late in the first century after Christ, and his fame rests on one book. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that he wrote a lexicon of Homer, the sole work of its kind that survives. He drew chiefly on Aristarchus and on Apion and his Homeric glossary for his matter. The entry also names the main printed editions and modern studies that readers can use to follow the work further.
britannica-1911-arbogast:
Arbogast, who died in 394, was a barbarian officer in the Roman army of the late fourth century. His race is not sure. Zosimus and Eunapius both call him a Frank. He served with credit against the Goths in Thrace. In 388 the emperor Theodosius sent him west against Maximus. Maximus had seized the western empire and killed Gratian.

Arbogast beat Maximus and his sons and brought Gaul back to peace. Theodosius then made him chief minister to the young emperor Valentinian II. His rule was full of drive. He favoured barbarians in the army and raised them to high posts. Valentinian, jealous of him, leaned on Romans instead. In 392 Valentinian was killed in secret at Vienne. Arbogast raised a teacher named Eugenius in his place and marched into Italy to face Theodosius.
britannica-1911-aristides-the-just:
Aristides, called the Just, lived from about 530 to 468 before Christ and was an Athenian statesman. The 1911 Britannica entry gives him as son of Lysimachus, of a family of moderate means. He followed Cleisthenes and stood with the aristocratic party in city politics. First notice comes as a tribe commander at Marathon in the great battle.

That honour won him the chief archon post for the year after the win. His land power policy clashed head on with the naval plans of Themistocles. The feud ended with his ostracism, dated between 485 and 482 in sources. The famed tale of the voter who asked him to write his own name follows.
britannica-1911-arrest:
Arrest is the subject of a law entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a French term meaning to stop or stay. It names the restraint of a person's body to compel obedience to the law. More exactly, it is the carrying out of an order from a court or officer.

Arrests in England fall into civil and criminal cases, the entry explains. In civil cases the arrest must rest on an order from a court. It must be made by seizing or touching the defendant's body, or as the writ directs. If the defendant escapes, that act is called a rescue. Further process can then be taken against him.
britannica-1911-bakewell-robert-agricult:
Bakewell, Robert (1725-1795), was an English agriculturist. He was born at Dishley in Leicestershire. His father farmed at the same place. The father died in 1760. Robert then took over the estate. Wide farm visits had prepared him well.

Bakewell's chief aim was better stock. Sheep and oxen were his main subjects. His new Leicestershire sheep won world fame. It took little over fifty years. Dishley cattle became almost as famous. His farm-horse type proved particularly useful. He founded ram-letting as a large trade. The Dishley Society guarded breed purity. One ram earned him 1,200 guineas in a year. Grass land improvement matched his breeding. His systematic irrigation had no rival. He died on 1 October 1795.
britannica-1911-bakewell-robert-geologis:
Bakewell, Robert (1768-1843), was an English geologist of the early school. He was born in 1768. Able observation marked all his field work. He ranks among geology's earliest public teachers. His teaching joined general and practical geology. Students gained both principles and field methods from him.

His Introduction to Geology appeared in 1813. It held much sound information for its day. A fifth edition came out in 1838. Germany translated the second edition for its readers.
