America reprinted the third and fourth editions. Professor Silliman of Yale handled those American reprints. Bakewell also wrote an introduction to mineralogy. That companion book appeared in 1819. His Tarentaise travels filled two volumes in 1823. They recorded observations from an Alpine residence. He died at Hampstead on 15 August 1843.
britannica-1911-ball-john-priest:
John Ball (died 1381) was an English priest who took a leading part in the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Little is known of his early years; he likely lived at York and then at Colchester. He won fame as a preacher of Wycliffe's doctrines, pressing hardest on the claim that all men are equal by nature.

Church courts jailed him three times, and in 1366 hearers were banned from his sermons, yet his pull held. Freed from Maidstone prison by the Kentish rebels, he preached at Blackheath on the text: When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then a gentleman? The 1911 Britannica entry ends with his capture at Coventry and his execution before Richard II.
britannica-1911-ballarat-and-ballarat-ea:
Ballarat and Ballarat East were a city and a town in Victoria, Australia, 74 miles by rail west-north-west of Melbourne. Only Yarrowee Creek splits the two, yet each ran its own council. Ballarat held 25,448 people in 1901 and Ballarat East 18,262. Ballarat ranked as the state's second city and its chief gold-mining centre.

The surface gold fields were the richest ever opened, the entry says, but as they gave out, miners worked quartz reefs more than 2,000 feet down. The 1911 Britannica entry notes bishops of two churches, fine public buildings, a 750-acre botanical garden with Lake Wendouree, and the most important school of mines in Australia. Wool, brewing, and iron work also figure.
britannica-1911-barclay-john-scottish-sa:
John Barclay (1582–1621) was a Scottish satirist and Latin poet, born on 28 January 1582 at Pont-à-Mousson in France, where his father William held the chair of civil law. His mother was a Frenchwoman of good family. Schooled by the Jesuits, he wrote a commentary on Statius's Thebaid at the age of nineteen.

Barclay crossed to London with his father in 1603, proud of his Scottish nationality and drawn by James's accession. His Satyricon appeared in parts at Paris and London, and his Sylvae, a book of Latin poems, came out in 1606. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his years in London to 1616 and his editing of his father's anti-papal treatise on the power of the pope.
britannica-1911-barghest:
Barghest, also spelled barguest or bargest, is the name given in the north of England, above all in Yorkshire, to a monstrous goblin-dog with huge teeth and claws. The spectre-hound is a familiar figure in folk-lore, and the entry gathers its local forms from across Britain.

The Demon of Tedworth, the Black Dog of Winchester, and the Padfoot of Wakefield all share the Barghest's traits. In Wales its counterpart was Gwyllgi, the Dog of Darkness, a mastiff with baleful breath and blazing red eyes. Lancashire calls it Trash or Striker, Norfolk Shuck, and the Isle of Man Mauthe Doog. The 1911 Britannica entry stresses its night nature: to see it was a portent of death.
britannica-1911-barkly-east:
Barkly East is a town of Cape province, South Africa, capital of a district of the same name, eighty miles by rail east-south-east of Aliwal North. The town lies north of the Drakensberg range, on the Kraai tributary of the Orange river, at 5,831 feet above the sea.

The district covers 1,564 square miles and held 8,490 people in 1904, half of them whites. Sheep farming is the chief occupation, the pasturage being excellent. Like Barkly West, the town and district are named after Sir Henry Barkly, governor of Cape Colony from 1870 to 1877. The 1911 Britannica entry is short, and it keeps to the district's size, people, altitude, and single main pursuit.
britannica-1911-barkly-west:
Barkly West is a town of Cape province, South Africa, 21 miles north-west of Kimberley, capital of a district and an electoral division in Griqualand West. It stands on the right bank of the Vaal river, crossed there by a bridge, and its population in 1904 was 1,037. Its first name was Klipdrift.

The town was the first founded by diggers after diamonds were found along the Vaal in 1867, and for some years it drew a large floating crowd. When the dry diggings at Kimberley opened, most diggers moved on. Barkly West stayed the centre of the river-diamond trade, its stones noted for purity and lustre. The 1911 Britannica entry adds the wider electoral division, with 48,388 people in 1904.
britannica-1911-bathurst:
Bathurst is a city in New South Wales, Australia, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the south bank of the Macquarie river, 144 miles by rail west-north-west of Sydney, on the far side of the Blue Mountains. It sits 2153 feet up in a rich, rolling plain, and its people numbered 9223 in 1901. Broad streets cross at right angles around a central park. The town hall, government buildings, and two cathedrals are fine public works.

Wheat and metals anchor the town's work. Bathurst is the centre of the chief wheat-growing district of New South Wales. Gold, copper, and silver are mined near it in large amounts. Town works include railway shops, coach factories, tanneries, breweries, and flour mills. The town was founded in 1815 by Governor Macquarie and named for the third Earl Bathurst, then the minister for the colonies. It has been a municipality since 1862.
britannica-1911-bean-feast:
Bean-feast meant first a yearly dinner given by an employer to his workpeople, and then any merry outing, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica hunts for the phrase's origin. The likeliest theory ties it to a Twelfth Night custom in France, Germany, and England. A cake with a bean buried in it was the center of the feast.

Whoever got the slice with the bean became bean-king, master of the revels for the night. The choosing of a king or queen by bean was once a common Christmas game at the English and Scottish courts and at both universities. The entry suggests the bean-king may descend from the mock king of the Roman Saturnalia.
britannica-1911-bell-john-anatomist:
John Bell (1763–1820) was a Scottish anatomist and surgeon born at Edinburgh, elder brother of Sir Charles Bell. From 1790 he ran an anatomy lecture-theatre in Surgeons’ Square, drawing large crowds despite strong opposition to his new-style teaching. His younger brother Charles helped him there for a time.

Bell’s Discourses on the Nature and Cure of Wounds appeared in 1793–1795, and his Principles of Surgery in 1801. A bitter quarrel with Professor James Gregory over hospital posts shut him out of the Royal Infirmary and ended his lecturing. A fall from his horse in 1816 broke his health, and he died at Rome in 1820.
britannica-1911-belmont-august:
August Belmont (1816–1890) was an American banker born at Alzei in Rhenish Prussia. He entered the Rothschilds’ Frankfurt house at fourteen, acted for them at Naples, and in 1837 settled in New York as their man in America. He took American citizenship and married a daughter of Commodore Matthew C. Perry.

Belmont served Austria as consul-general at New York, resigning in 1850 over its treatment of Hungary, then represented the United States at the Hague. Chosen chairman of the National Democratic Committee in 1860, he backed the Union hard through the Civil War and swayed opinion among bankers in England and France. He led his party’s organization until 1872.
britannica-1911-bennigsen-levin-august:
Levin August, Count von Bennigsen (1745–1826), was a Russian general of a Hanoverian family, born at Brunswick. He served as page and foot-guards officer at Hanover, left that army in 1764, and entered Russian service in 1773. Wars against Turks and Poles and in Persia raised him steadily.

Bennigsen took an active, if shadowy, part in the plot that murdered Tsar Paul I. Alexander I made him governor-general of Lithuania and general of cavalry. Against Napoleon he fought Pultusk and bloody Eylau in 1807, claiming the first check Napoleon had met, then suffered the crushing defeat of Friedland. He returned for the campaigns of 1812 onward and retired in 1818 to his Hanover estate.
britannica-1911-bequest: Bequest, from an Old English word meaning to declare or express in words, the same root as “quoth,” is the giving of property by will. In strict legal speech the word covers personal property only, the things a person owns rather than land. Land left by will takes a different name, “devise.” The short entry makes that one distinction and sends readers on to the articles on legacy and on wills for the rules that govern such gifts.
britannica-1911-betty-william-henry-west:
William Henry West Betty, an English child actor who lived from 1791 to 1874, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Shrewsbury and first acted at Belfast before he was twelve. His gifts at once drew huge praise. Folk called him the young Roscius, after the famed player of Rome.

In Dublin he is said to have learned the part of Hamlet in three hours. In 1804 London crowds stormed the doors to see him, and troops kept order. He earned more than seventy-five guineas a night. King George the Third had him shown to the queen, and the Commons once rose early so men could reach his show. The craze cooled, and he left the stage with a large fortune.
britannica-1911-bifrost: Bifrost, in Old Norse mythology, is the rainbow. It was imagined as the bridge by which the gods passed between heaven and earth. The 1911 Britannica entry is a single sentence. It adds one further fact: the bridge was guarded by Heimdal, god of light. No story, source, or place is given in the entry. Nothing more can be drawn from it than that picture. A guarded rainbow road joins the worlds of gods and men.
britannica-1911-brown-john-american-abol:
John Brown, who lived from 1800 to 1859, was an American foe of slavery who led the raid on Harpers Ferry in 1859. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born in Torrington, Connecticut, on the ninth of May 1800. As a boy he moved with his father to Hudson, Ohio. He tried work in tanning, sheep farming, and the wool trade, but met with little luck. In 1842 he went bankrupt at Akron, Ohio.

From youth Brown hated slavery and meant to help end it. In 1855 he joined his sons in Kansas, where free-state and pro-slavery men were at war. He won fame in the Pottawatomie killings of 1856, when five pro-slavery men were slain by his party. The article follows his path from the Kansas fights to the Harpers Ferry raid.
britannica-1911-brown-thomas-english-sat:
Thomas Brown, English satirist born in 1663 at Shifnal in Shropshire, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a farmer there. Entered at Christ Church in Oxford in 1678, he is said to have dodged being sent down by famed witty lines to Dr Fell. He taught school at Kingston on Thames for three years.

London then became his home and his stage. Under a false name he wrote a satire on Dryden in dialogue form, issued in parts from 1688 to 1690. A vast range of poems, letters, dialogues, and lampoons flowed from his pen. They brim with humour and learning, yet run coarse and abusive at times. His work holds worth for its close view of low life in London. He died in 1704 and lies in the cloister of Westminster Abbey.
britannica-1911-bruckmann-franz-ernst:
Franz Ernst Bruckmann (1697–1753) was a German mineralogist born on 27 September 1697 at Marienthal near Helmstadt. He qualified as a medical man in 1721 and practised at Brunswick and afterwards at Wolfenbuttel. Medicine paid his way, but his leisure went to natural history, above all to mineralogy and botany, and it is for that spare-time work that the entry remembers him.

He appears to have been the first to introduce the term oolithus for rocks whose structure resembles the roe of a fish, the root of the modern words oolite and oolitic. His books, all Latin works of the 1720s, cover God's wonders in underground places, a curious natural history of a stone, and an underground treasury of the duchy of Brunswick. He died at Wolfenbuttel on 21 March 1753, leaving a name fixed to a rock term still in use.
britannica-1911-brunnow-franz-friedrich-:
Franz Friedrich Ernst Brunnow (1821–1891) was a German astronomer born in Berlin on 18 November 1821. He attended the Friedrich-Wilhelm gymnasium from eight to eighteen, then entered Berlin university in 1839 to study mathematics, astronomy and physics, with chemistry, philosophy and philology beside them. Taking his doctorate in 1843, he worked actively at the Berlin observatory under Encke.

His papers on the orbits of comets and minor planets filled the Astronomische Nachrichten. Director of the Bilk observatory near Dusseldorf from 1847, he won the Amsterdam Academy's gold medal for a memoir on De Vico's elliptical comet. First assistant at Berlin from 1851, he accepted in 1854 the directorship of the new observatory at Ann Arbor, Michigan. He published a journal, Astronomical Notices, from 1858 to 1862, with tables of the minor planets Flora, Victoria and Iris issued in 1857, 1859 and 1869.
britannica-1911-brush-george-de-forest:
George de Forest Brush (1855–), an American painter born at Shelbyville, Tennessee, on 28 September 1855, is the subject of this 1911 Britannica entry. Brush studied under J. L. Gérôme at Paris and became a member of the National Academy of Design in New York.

From 1883 he won wide notice for paintings of North American Indians, among them “Moose Hunt,” “Aztec King” and “Mourning her Brave,” which show Gérôme's strong influence. He later turned to portraits, above all of mother and child, arranged with care for line and mass and finished in great detail. Several pictures take his own wife and children as subjects, and one hangs in the Boston Museum of Fine Arts.
britannica-1911-budapest:
Budapest is the capital and largest town of Hungary. It is the second town of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy. It lies 163 miles south-east of Vienna by rail. This long 1911 Britannica article surveys the whole city. Budapest stands on both banks of the Danube. It was formed from older towns in 1872. Buda and Ó-Buda lie on the right bank. Pest and Kőbánya lie on the left bank.

The entry contrasts the two halves of the city. Pest spreads flat and regular on a sandy plain. Buda climbs in an older, looser pattern. The Danube there runs 300 to 650 yards wide. The article covers bridges, streets and public buildings. It treats trade, industry and the city's government. It gives the history of Buda and Pest as well. Population figures and district details round out the portrait.
britannica-1911-burger-gottfried-august:
Gottfried August Burger, a German poet who lived from 1748 to 1794, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Molmerswende near Halberstadt, where his father was the Lutheran pastor. He was a backward child, and at twelve his grandfather took him in at Aschersleben. That grandfather sent him to school at Halle.

In 1764 Burger went to university to study theology, but soon switched to law. At Halle he fell under the sway of Klotz, who turned him toward literature. Klotz did little to curb his wild and loose way of life, and in 1767 his grandfather called him home. On a promise to reform he entered Gottingen as a law student in 1768. His first poems appeared in a Gottingen almanac, and by 1771 he was widely known as a poet. In 1772 he became a district magistrate near Gottingen.
britannica-1911-camerarius-joachim-botan:
Joachim Camerarius the younger, a German plant expert and doctor, is the subject of a short life in the 1911 Britannica. He was born at Nuremberg in fifteen thirty four. His father was a well known scholar of the same name. He trained in Germany, then took his degree in drugs and care in Italy. Princes asked him to join their courts, but he chose his home town instead.

At Nuremberg he kept a plant yard and built large sets of plant finds. His chief book was the Hortus Medicus of fifteen eighty eight, with more works on the same lines. He died at Nuremberg in fifteen ninety eight. The note stays brief and gives the bare arc of his life and work.
britannica-1911-cape-coast:
Cape Coast, a port on the Gold Coast in British West Africa, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies about eighty miles west of Accra. Its people numbered 28,948 in 1901, most of them Fantis, with about one hundred Europeans. The town is built on a low bank of rock that runs into the sea and gives the landing place some shelter from the surf.

The article explains the name as an English wearing-down of the Portuguese Cabo Corso. The castle, of good size, faces the sea and held officers' quarters and a prison. Other chief buildings were the district head's house, churches, schools, and the hospital. Many rich natives lived in houses of brick. Hills ring the town on the east and north, and a lagoon lies to the west. The first European settlement on the spot was Portuguese.
britannica-1911-chislehurst:
Chislehurst is an urban district in Kent in England, south east of London by rail. A 1911 Britannica entry gives its people as 7429 in 1901 at the census. It stands three hundred feet above the sea on a furze clad common. Fine country surrounds the settlement on all sides in the survey.

Saint Nicholas church holds a tomb of the Walsingham family of statesmen fame. Sir Francis Walsingham was born here in 1536, and Sir Nicholas Bacon in 1510. A chapel was built to hold the body of Napoleon the Third, who died here. His son body joined it in 1879 before both moved to Farnborough.
britannica-1911-cist: Cist is a word for a box, from Greek and Latin roots for a container. In Greek study it names a wicker holder used in the Eleusinian rites to carry sacred vessels. In early human study it names a coffin of flat stones set on edge with a flat stone lid. The word also covers a burial chamber cut into rock. Cistern, the common word for a water tank, comes from the same root.
britannica-1911-civil-list:
Civil List is the English term for the account holding all expenses for the support of the British sovereign's household and the honour and dignity of the crown. Parliament settles an annual sum on the sovereign at the start of the reign, charged on the consolidated fund. Only from William IV has that sum been restricted solely to the personal expenses of the crown. Before his accession many ordinary government charges sat on the civil list.

History here dates from William and Mary, since before the Revolution no line divided the sovereign's personal support from peace-time government costs. Hereditary revenues and life taxes were meant to cover both, and savings swelled the privy purse. Charles II and James II showed the evils of that system, since control of large revenues made them independent of parliament. The entry traces how reform slowly separated crown expenses from state expenses.
britannica-1911-cloud-burst:
Cloud-burst is a sudden and violent storm of rain, the name probably arising from an old picture of clouds as solid masses full of water. Those masses were imagined to burst at times, with disastrous results on the ground below. One mechanism offered here turns on a whirlwind passing over the sea. Such a whirlwind sometimes carries water upward in a whirling vortex as it moves across the surface.

Passing over land, the whirlwind's motion is checked, and a deluge of water falls from it at once. Inland cases on high lands far from the sea also occur in the account given. Violent storms there send rain down in sheets, sweeping away bridges and culverts and tearing up roads and streets. Those inland bursts are put down to great and rapid condensation and vortical whirling of the resulting heavy clouds.
britannica-1911-cock-lane-ghost:
The Cock Lane ghost was a supposed haunting that drew huge crowds in London during 1762. The house stood in Cock Lane, Smithfield, and was held by a man named Parsons. Night knockings and odd noises were reported there. A glowing figure was said to appear. People linked it to a Mrs Kent, who had died in the house two years before.

Close inquiry found a plain cause. Parsons's daughter, a child of eleven, made the sounds herself. The family hoped to charge the dead woman's husband with murder and gain money by threat. Parsons was put on trial and sent to the pillory. Dr Johnson was among the crowds who came to see. The poet Charles Churchill mocked him for it in a poem called The Ghost.
britannica-1911-constans-jean-antoine-er:
Jean Antoine Ernest Constans is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a French statesman. He was born at Beziers in 1833. He began his career as a professor of law. In 1876 he was elected deputy for Toulouse. He was one of the 363 of the crisis of May 1877. He was re-elected in October of that year.

In May 1880 he joined Freycinet as minister of the interior. He held that portfolio until November 1881. In February 1889 he took the same office again. He became prominent as a staunch opponent of Boulangism. He helped make the senate a high court of justice. He also took police measures against the Ligue des patriotes. He resigned in March 1890, and the cabinet fell with him. He resumed his portfolio a few weeks later. He had been elected senator at the end of 1889.
britannica-1911-coromandel-coast:
Coromandel Coast is a 1911 Britannica article on the eastern seaboard of India. The name was once applied in official use to that shore. It ran from Cape Calimere to the mouths of the Kistna river. The shore is low along its length.

It has not a single good natural harbour. At all times a heavy sea beats on it. Talk with ships can be had only by catamarans and flat-bottomed surf-boats. The north-east monsoon lasts from October till April. For three months after its start it is exceedingly violent. From April till October, hot southerly winds blow by day. At night, sea-breezes temper the heat. The chief places used by shipping are named in a list. Pulicat, Madras, Pondicherry, and Tranquebar are among them. Coast readers get beauty and danger in one long, harbourless shore.
britannica-1911-crest:
Crest is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica from a Latin word for a plume or tuft. In its first sense it is the comb on the head of a bird or beast. From there it means any soft tuft of the kind. It then moves to the cone of a helm, and by shift to the helm itself.

In the lore of arms a crest has a strict sense. It is a sign first worn as a mark on the helm of a knight. In full arms it sits on a wreath above helm and shield. It can stand on its own on a seal or on goods. A kin term in building names a trim that caps a wall or a roof ridge. One church roof in Exeter bears a row of small lead flowers as its crest work.
britannica-1911-crusius-christian-august:
Crusius, Christian August is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a German philosopher and theologian. Born near Merseburg in Saxony on the tenth of January 1715, he became professor of theology at Leipzig in 1750. He died on the eighteenth of October 1775. He first came to notice as an opponent of the philosophy of Leibnitz and Wolff, attacking it from the ground of religious orthodoxy.

The article weighs his influence and his later work. He attacked determinism for the moral evils that flow from it. His books were diffuse and neither brilliant nor deep, yet they were widely read for a time. His criticism of Wolff, based on sound sense, influenced Kant while the Kantian system was forming.
britannica-1911-cumberland-richard-drama:
Richard Cumberland (1732–1811) was an English dramatist born in the master's lodge of Trinity College, Cambridge, on 19 February 1732. His father became a bishop in Ireland, and his mother was the youngest daughter of Richard Bentley, the great scholar. The boy rose to head his school at Bury St Edmunds, then moved to Westminster. Schoolfellows there included Warren Hastings, Colman, Churchill, and Cowper.

At Trinity from his fourteenth year, Cumberland took his degree as tenth wrangler in 1750 and won a fellowship. Early projects mixed classical study with trials at Spenserian verse and unprinted drama. The long entry follows his double life in office work and playwriting. It closes with lives and memoirs drawn from his own autobiography. His portrait by Romney, whose talent he was early to back, hangs in the National Portrait Gallery. A German history of English literature fixes his place in the drama of his century.
britannica-1911-cunningham-william-econo:
William Cunningham, an English economist born in Edinburgh in December 1849, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was taught at Edinburgh Academy and University and at Trinity College, Cambridge. He took a first-class degree in moral science in 1873 and took holy orders the same year. He lectured on history at the university from 1884 to 1891. He then held the economics chair at King's College, London, until 1897.

Cunningham also lectured at Harvard and served as vicar of Great St Mary's, Cambridge, from 1887. In 1906 he became archdeacon of Ely. The article names his two histories of English industry and commerce as the standard works on the subject. It lists his other books on money, immigration, free trade, and the West. It also notes his weight as a critic of free-trade policy from 1903 on.
britannica-1911-ernesti-johann-august:
Ernesti, Johann August (1707–1781), was a German theologian and philologist born on 4 August 1707 at Tennstädt in Thuringia, where his father was pastor. At sixteen he was sent to the famed Saxon cloister school of Pforta. In 1731 he became conrector of the Thomas school at Leipzig, and rector in 1734.

Ernesti was made professor of ancient literature at Leipzig in 1742, professor of rhetoric in 1756, and professor of theology in 1759. With Baumgarten of Halle he helped free the dogmatic theology of the day from its scholastic and mystical growths. The entry credits him as much for the impulse he gave to sacred and secular criticism as for his own works. His lasting claim as a theologian lies in hermeneutics, above all the Institutio Interpretis Novi Testamenti of 1761. He died on 11 September 1781.
britannica-1911-erskine-john-jurist:
Erskine, John, of Carnock (1695–1768), was a Scottish jurist, the son of Lieutenant-Colonel John Erskine, born in 1695. He was admitted to the faculty of advocates in 1719. In 1737 he was appointed professor of Scots law in the university of Edinburgh.

In 1754 Erskine published his Principles of the Law of Scotland. He retired from his chair in 1765 and spent his last years preparing his great work, the Institutes of the Law of Scotland, which he did not live to publish. He died at Cardross in Perthshire on 1 March 1768. The Institutes appeared in 1773 and have been reprinted many times. The entry judges the work so full of learning, accuracy, and good sense that it has always held the highest authority on Scots law. It falls short only of Lord Stair's grasp of principle.
britannica-1911-essay-essayist:
Essay, as a form of writing, is examined in a literature entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. An essay is a prose piece of modest length on a set topic. It treats its topic in an easy, light way, through the mind of the writer. Doctor Johnson called an essay an irregular, undigested piece.

The entry grants the first word but fights the second. Fine essays, it argues, are the brief fruit of long thought and deep study. Montaigne coined the word for his own tries at a new kind of writing. He meant them as attempts that felt their way toward fuller truth. In England that first sense faded in the eighteenth century. Later bids to coin a word for a still smaller piece all failed to stick. The entry sets the essay apart from both the long monograph and the plain journal article.
britannica-1911-eucharist:
Eucharist, from the Greek word for thanksgiving, is an ancient name for the sacrament of the Lord's Supper. The term first marked the act of thanksgiving within the rite. By the 2nd century it covered the bread and wine themselves, and then the whole celebration. Other names stress other sides: Mass, Communion, Lord's Supper, Sacrament, the Mystery, the Sacrifice. The article first traces the rite's history to A.D. 200 in dated documents.

Paul's account in First Corinthians anchors the early picture. The faithful met to eat the Lord's Supper together. Some ate their own provisions first, leaving the poor hungry while the rich drank deep. Paul orders them to wait for one another, and the hungry to eat at home. What made the meal the Lord's, the entry argues, was shared brotherhood, not the food. Later parts compare early and later usage and weigh the original rite's meaning.
britannica-1911-exorcist:
An exorcist, in the Roman Catholic church, holds the third grade of the minor orders, between acolyte and reader. The office carries the right to exorcise devils ceremonially. In practice it is now only a step on the road to priesthood. The first record of a special ordination for exorcists is canon 7 of the council of Carthage, A.D. 256. At ordination the bishop hands the man a little book of the exorcisms.

With the book he receives power to lay hands on the energumeni, baptized or catechumen. The office was no sinecure in earlier ages. Paulinus called the exorcist a terror to demons. Firmilianus wrote to Cyprian that through exorcists the devil may be whipped, burnt and tortured. The figure even survived the Reformation among Protestants. The entry is a short companion piece to the article on exorcism.
britannica-1911-faust:
Faust, or Faustus, was a magician and charlatan of the sixteenth century who became famous in legend and literature. A real man did exist, the entry argues, but he forms only the small core around which a great mass of legendary and invented material gathered. Early witnesses already treat him as a worker of marvels. Melanchthon reports that the devil killed him by wringing his neck, and that his dog was really a devil.

Other early accounts fill out the picture. Luther is linked with a saying about warding off Faust's sorceries. Bullinger names him among the magi of scripture. Johann Wier, a pupil of Agrippa who opposed witch persecution, calls him a drunken vagabond who studied magic at Cracow and practised deceit across Germany before 1540. The long entry traces the Faust-books, the legend's growth, and its place in occult tradition, ending with a full bibliography.
britannica-1911-francis-of-sales-st:
Francis of Sales (1567-1622), bishop of Geneva and a doctor of the Church, was born at the castle of Sales near Annecy in Savoy. His father had served in state affairs before settling on the family estates. The boy was schooled at La Roche and Annecy, then at the Jesuit College of Clermont in Paris, and took a law degree at Padua while studying theology with still greater zeal.

Sent to win back the Chablais district, which had turned Calvinist, Francis found hearers barred to him and spread his message on written sheets passed from hand to hand. Those sheets, later printed as Les Controverses, began his work as an author. By October 1598 nearly the whole district was Catholic again. The entry traces his gentle but firm character, his later writings, and the many lives and studies his career produced.
britannica-1911-gansbacher-johann-baptis:
Johann Baptist Gansbacher (1778-1844) was an Austrian composer, born at Sterzing in Tirol. The 1911 Britannica entry says his father, a schoolmaster and music teacher, began his training, and that from 1802 he studied under the celebrated Abbe Vogler. That link, the entry admits, does much to explain his lasting place in music history.

At Darmstadt in 1810, again under Vogler, Gansbacher formed a close lifelong friendship with Weber and Meyerbeer. His own merit was real, though: he directed the music at St Stephen's cathedral in Vienna from 1823 until his death on 13 July 1844. His works are mostly church music, including 17 masses, litanies, motets and offertories. He also wrote sonatas, a symphony and a few small dramatic pieces.
britannica-1911-ghost:
Ghost now most often means the spirit of a dead person. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tracks the word older wider sense. It is common to the western Teutonic tongues in old forms. At first it named spirit in general, or the life breath itself.

That broad sense is now nearly dead in daily speech. Bible language keeps it in the phrase to give up the ghost. The third person of the Trinity is still the Holy Ghost. Ghostly can still mean spiritual set against bodily things. A ghostly adviser sounds stiff and old fashioned today, though. Want of substance gave the word a fresh field of use. Men speak of not the ghost of a chance or idea. Paid hacks who write for others also bear the name.
britannica-1911-goldfuss-georg-august:
Georg August Goldfuss, a German student of fossils who lived from 1782 to 1848, is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Thurnau near Bayreuth, he was educated at Erlangen. He took his doctor's degree there in 1804 and became professor of zoology in 1818. Later he held posts in zoology and mineral study at Bonn.

With the aid of Count Munster he issued a major work on the fossils of Germany, from 1826 to 1844. It was meant to picture all the backboneless fossils of that land. The work was left unfinished, though. It covered sponges, corals, crinoids, sea urchins, and part of the molluscs before it stopped. Goldfuss died at Bonn in October 1848.
britannica-1911-grabe-john-ernest:
John Ernest Grabe, an Anglican divine who lived from 1666 to 1711, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Königsberg, where his father was a professor of theology and history, he came in his studies to see the Reformation as a schism. He set that case in a memorial to the church court of Samland in Prussia.

Grabe had resolved to join the Church of Rome. A commission of Lutheran divines then pointed out flaws in his argument, and drew his eye to the English Church. That church seemed to hold the apostolic succession and the fidelity to ancient ways that he desired. He came to England, settled at Oxford, was ordained in 1700, and became chaplain of Christ Church. His leanings lay with the nonjurors. His labours won him an Oxford degree and a royal pension.
britannica-1911-gregory-st:
Saint Gregory is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a bishop called Thaumaturgus. That surname means the miracle worker in later tradition. He lived from about 213 to about 270. He was born of noble and wealthy pagan parents. His birthplace was Neocaesarea in Pontus. His original name was Theodorus at his birth. He took up the study of civil law as a youth.

With his brother Athenodorus, he set out for Berytus to train. At Caesarea on that journey he met Origen. He became Origen's pupil and then his convert in 233. Returning to Cappadocia five years later, he meant to live retired. He planned an ascetic life away from the world. But Origen urged him toward service in the church. Phaedimus of Amasia at last almost compelled him onward. After many attempts to evade the dignity, he yielded. He was consecrated bishop of his native town about 240.
britannica-1911-griqualand-east-and-griq:
Griqualand East and Griqualand West are divisions of the Cape Province. Both lie in the Union of South Africa. Both take their names from their Griqua inhabitants. Griquas under Adam Kok settled the eastern division in 1862. It forms part of the Transkeian Territories. The western division covers 15,197 square miles. It is high tableland between the Orange river and Bechuanaland.

Griqualand West is mostly dry and barren. Irrigated soil, though, proves very fertile. Sheep-farming, horse-breeding and asbestos working all figure in its economy. Its real wealth is diamonds. They are found along the Vaal and the Riet rivers. From 1867 to the end of 1905 the yield was put at £95,000,000. Kimberley stands as the centre of the mining industry.
britannica-1911-guest: Guest is a very short word-entry. The word is common to the Teutonic languages. German has Gast and Swedish has gäst. It is cognate with the Latin hostis. That Latin word first meant a stranger. It later came to mean an enemy. A guest is one who receives hospitality in another's house. That other person is his host. The word is also applied to a parasite.
britannica-1911-hahn-august:
August Hahn, a German Protestant church scholar who lived from 1792 to 1863, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Grossosterhausen near Eisleben, he studied at the university of Leipzig. In 1819 he won a chair at Konigsberg and a post as pastor in that city. He rose to a full chair there in 1822, then moved to Leipzig in 1826.

At Leipzig Hahn won fame with a tract of 1827 on the true nature of rational thought in faith. In a second open tract that year he urged rationalists to leave the state church of their own free will. He stood with the school of Hengstenberg in that fight. A later tract drew the eye of King Friedrich Wilhelm the Third. Hahn was called to Breslau in 1833 and rose to head of the church in Silesia in 1843, a post he held until his death.
britannica-1911-hammerfest:
Hammerfest is the most northern town in Europe. Its population in 1900 was 2,300. It stands on Kvalö island off Norway's north-west coast. Its latitude is 70 degrees 40 minutes north. That matches the extreme north of Alaska. Yet its mean annual temperature is 36 degrees Fahrenheit. The warm Atlantic drift explains that mildness. The North Cape lies 78 miles to the north-east.

The sun never sets there from 13 May to 29 July. Fishing fleets then sail as far as Spitsbergen. Trade is brisk with Russian, British and German vessels. Cod-liver oil and salted fish are the chief exports. From mid-November to late January the sun never rises. Fire destroyed much of the timber town in 1890. A column on Fuglenaes marks a meridian-arc survey station. Sabine chose the town for pendulum experiments in 1823.
britannica-1911-haverfordwest:
Haverfordwest is the chief town of Pembrokeshire, South Wales. Its Welsh name is Hwlfordd. Its population in 1901 was 6,007. It is a borough and a county of itself. Slopes above the West Cleddau river hold the town. Two stone bridges cross the river there. The Great Western Railway serves it from the east bank. From that side the castle-keep dominates the view.

The tidal river takes vessels of only 150 tons. Coal, cattle, butter and grain are exported. Ruined warehouses testify to declined trade. St Mary's church has a fine carved-oak ceiling. Its monuments remember the Philipps family of Picton. The castle-keep now serves as the police-station. Fenton called it Wales' largest town in 1810. Milford's rise drained its shipping away. It is now a quiet country town.
britannica-1911-havet-eugene-auguste-ern:
Eugène Auguste Ernest Havet (1813–1889) was a French scholar. He was born in Paris on 11 April 1813. The Lycée Saint-Louis and the École Normale educated him. For many years he taught Latin eloquence at the Collège de France. He held that chair until his death in 1889. Two capital works carry his reputation. His Pascal edition appeared in 1852, with the authentic text.

Le Christianisme et ses origines filled four volumes (1871–1884). Its thesis gave Greek philosophy the larger credit for Christianity. The Hebrew prophets, it argued, contributed less. That argument made the work controversial and famous. Havet had two scholarly sons. Louis became professor of Latin philology at the Collège de France. Julien, the younger son, is noticed separately. The entry is brief, resting on the two big books.
britannica-1911-hawkhurst:
Hawkhurst is a town in the southern division of Kent, England. London lies 47 miles to the north-west. A branch of the South-Eastern & Chatham railway serves it. Its population in 1901 was 3,136. The town lies mainly on a ridge. Below runs the Kent Ditch, a tributary of the Rother. The neighbouring country is hilly, rich and well wooded. That pleasant, healthy situation has spread the old village. It is now a considerable residential locality.

The Kent Sanatorium is established at Hawkhurst. One of the Barnardo homes stands there too. St Lawrence church is Decorated and Perpendicular in style. Battle Abbey in Sussex founded that church. Its east window, of the earlier period, is specially beautiful. The entry is a short gazetteer notice. It gives position, population and the church as the main facts.
britannica-1911-hilda-st:
St Hilda, strictly Hild (614–680), was the daughter of Hereric, a nephew of Edwin, king of Northumbria. She was converted before 633 by the preaching of Paulinus. After a year in East Anglia, Aidan recalled her to Northumbria in 648 or 649. She lived a year in a small community north of the Wear, then succeeded Heiu as abbess of Hartlepool.

From Hartlepool Hilda moved to Whitby, where in 657 she founded the famous double monastery. It housed five future bishops and the poet Cædmon. Churchmen from all over Christian England, and from Strathclyde and Dalriada, visited her house. Oswio placed his daughter Ælfled in her care after the battle of Winwæd in 655. At the synod of Whitby in 664 she sided with Colman and Cedd against Wilfrid. She died in 680, after a painful illness of seven years.
britannica-1911-hildegard-st:
St Hildegard (1098–1179) was a German abbess and mystic, born of noble parents at Böckelheim. From her eighth year she was schooled at the cloister of Disibodenberg, and she succeeded its abbess Jutta in 1136. She saw visions from earliest childhood but kept them near secret until 1141, her forty-third year.

Written down by the monk Godefridus, the visions form her Scivias, finished in 1151. St Bernard backed her as a prophetess, and Pope Eugenius III recognized her at Trèves in 1148. That year she moved with eighteen nuns to the Rupertsberg near Bingen, ruling there for life. By letters and journeys she held wide influence, and popes and emperors wrote to her.
britannica-1911-hochst:
Hochst, a work town on the Main River in Germany, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica place note. It lies west of Frankfurt in the Prussian lands of Hesse Nassau. Its folk count for nineteen oh five was fourteen thousand one hundred twenty one. Large dye works lead its trades. Shops make tools, snuff, cloth, gelatine, and food goods as well. Boats bring a fair river trade to its banks.

The church of Saint Justinus stands out for its age and form. First built in the ninth century, it gained a Gothic choir in the fifteenth. A palace of the electors of Mainz stood here till war wrecked it in sixteen thirty four. One fine tower still stands. Two old battles at the town close the note.
britannica-1911-honey-locust:
The honey locust is a tree, Gleditsia triacanthos, of the legume order, native to the more eastern United States. It grows from 75 to 140 ft. high, with a trunk 2 or 3 ft. thick, sometimes 5 or 6, and slender spreading branches forming a broad, flat crown. Its branchlets carry many sharp, stiff spines, simple or three-forked, above the leaf-axils. Those forks give the species its name.

The long-stalked leaves run 7 to 8 in., with eight to fourteen pairs of narrow leaflets. Its flowers, of two kinds, hang in racemes in the leaf-axils. The brown pods, often 12 to 18 in. long, hold a sweet pulp between the seeds and twist as they dry. Bishop Compton first grew the tree in Europe, at Fulham near London, late in the 17th century. It is now widely planted as an ornamental tree. The genus name honours Johann Gottlieb Gleditsch, an early writer on scientific forestry.
britannica-1911-horst:
Horst is a term article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a word used in physical geography and geology for a block of the earth's crust. A horst is a block that has stayed in place while the land on either side of it has sunk away. The word is also used for a block against which the rocks of a mountain range have been crushed. The Vosges and the Black Forest stand as examples of the first kind.

The Table, the Jura, and the Dole serve the article as examples of the second kind, where the range was pressed against the standing block. In a wider use the term covers great stable tracts of the continents, such as the Russian plain, Arabia, India, and Central South Africa.
britannica-1911-host:
Host is a word with three separate roots and three families of meaning. First, through Old French from the Latin hospes, a guest or host, it means one who takes another into his house and gives lodging and entertainment, often for payment. Biology borrows this sense for the animal or plant on which a parasite lives.

The second host comes from the Latin hostis, stranger or enemy, in medieval Latin a military expedition: a large body of men armed for war, and then any multitude. In Bible use it names the angels of heaven, the sun, moon and stars as the hosts of heaven, and renders Jehovah Sabaoth, the Lord of hosts. The third host, from hostia, a victim, is the sacrifice of Christ's body and blood in the Eucharist. The short entry sets the three apart by their roots.
britannica-1911-hubert-st:
St Hubert (d. 727) was bishop of Liége, and his festival falls on the 3rd of November. The Bollandists have printed seven lives of him, of which the first, by a contemporary, is the only one of value, and it is sparing of detail. It shows Hubert succeeding Lambert in the see of Maestricht in 708, and raising a basilica to his memory.

In 825 Hubert's remains were carried to a Benedictine cloister in the Ardennes. That house took his name, St Hubert in the Belgian province of Luxemburg, and grew into a great resort of pilgrims. The later legends carry no authority. One of them, copying the tale of St Eustace, tells the famous miracle of his conversion: the stag met in the hunt, bearing a cross between its antlers. That story, not the sparse early life, made Hubert the patron saint of hunters across Europe.
britannica-1911-hugh-st:
St Hugh of Avalon (about 1140 to 1200) was bishop of Lincoln, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells of his monastic start. He was born of a noble family at Avalon in Burgundy. He must be kept apart from Hugh of Wells, and from a later saint of Lincoln. At the age of eight he entered a priory of canons with his widowed father.

At nineteen Hugh was ordained deacon in that priory at Villard Benoît. He was soon made prior of a dependent cell of the house. The holy fame of the monks of the Grande Chartreuse drew him away. He entered that house at last, against an oath he had given his superior. He stayed there about ten years. He rose to the key office of procurator, which brought him wide contacts.
britannica-1911-hughes-thomas-dramatist:
Thomas Hughes was an English dramatist of the Elizabethan age, and this 1911 Britannica entry centres on his one known play. A native of Cheshire, he entered Queens' College, Cambridge, in 1571 and became a fellow in 1576. He later joined Gray's Inn in London. In February 1588 his play The Misfortunes of Arthur was performed at Greenwich before the Queen.

Other men of Gray's Inn helped with parts of the show. The plot, drawn from old British myth, turns on incest and crime and follows the model of Seneca closely. A ghost opens the play, a messenger reports the dark events, and a chorus comments as the action unfolds. The entry cites a modern study showing the play is largely a patchwork of Seneca turned into English, with some lines of Hughes's own.
britannica-1911-hypocaust:
Under the floors of Roman baths ran a heating system called a hypocaust. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains the Greek roots of the word as beneath and to burn. Hot air from a furnace passed through the hollow space below. In hot rooms the air also rose through flues in the walls.

The floor rested on short piers of tile set on concrete. Layers of crushed brick and marble cement lay above them. In colder lands such as Germany and England, living rooms used the same plan. Fine mosaic floors found above these systems in England form a key part of the entry.
britannica-1911-impost:
Impost comes through Old French from the Latin impositum, a thing laid upon another, and the modern French form is impôt. Its first sense is a tax or tribute, above all a duty charged on goods brought into or sent out of a country.

In building, the word has a narrower use. In Italian it can mean a doorpost, but in English it is the top part of that post, the block from which an arch springs. An impost may sit level with the arch moulding, or stand out as a plain band or a richly cut moulding. In some work the whole entablature of a smaller order serves as the impost, as in the Venetian window. In Romanesque and Gothic work, capitals and their abaci take the place of impost mouldings.
britannica-1911-januarius-st:
Saint Januarius, or San Gennaro, is the patron saint of Naples in Italy. The 1911 Britannica entry tells his legend in full, rich detail. By that tale he was bishop of Benevento in the late 200s. When Diocletian and Maximian launched their purge of Christians, he was seized. He was brought at Nola before Timotheus, who ruled Campania then.

The saint was cast into a fiery furnace and came out unharmed. Next day wild beasts were loosed on him and his fellow martyrs. The beasts lay down tame at his feet, the legend claims. Timotheus then was struck blind, and the saint's prayer healed him. Five thousand men turned to the faith at that wonder, it says.
britannica-1911-john-gospel-of-st:
The Gospel of St John is the fourth and latest of the Gospels in the Bible, and, next to Mark, the shortest. First come the book's structure and contents, then a comparison with the Synoptic Gospels, then its chief traits and final aim. Then come the stories found only in this Gospel, its problems, and the questions of authorship.

The study of contents turns on a break at the start of chapter thirteen, at the washing of the feet. Before that point come signs and debates addressed to the outer world. The work opens with the prologue on the Logos, the Word who was with God and was God. The Cana wedding, the cleansing of the Temple, and the talk with Nicodemus fall in the first part. The closing part weighs the proof for who wrote the book and when.
britannica-1911-joist:
Joist is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a beam used in building work. A joist is one of a row of beams set on edge. The row runs from one wall or wall part to the next. Floor boards rest on its top edge as their base.

The laths of the ceiling hang from its lower edge in turn. In double flooring there are three sets of such beams in use. They are binding, bridging, and ceiling joists in the trade names. The binding joists bear the true weight of the floor. The word's old form was giste, from a French word for a beam. By root it meant that on which a thing lies or rests.
britannica-1911-kahnis-karl-friedrich-au:
Karl Friedrich August Kahnis (1814–1888) was a German Lutheran theologian, born at Greiz on the 22nd of December 1814. His segment sits in a hosted file shared with the Kagera, Kahlur, and Kahn entries. He studied at Halle and in 1850 became a full professor at Leipzig. Ten years later he was made canon of Meissen, and he died at Leipzig in June 1888.

He began as a neo Lutheran, blessed by Hengstenberg and his pietist friends, then joined the Old Lutheran party in a broad and liberal spirit. His chief work, the Lutherische Dogmatik of 1861 to 1868, made grants to modern criticism. It softened the old dogmas, attacked the idea of an infallible canon, and stressed the human side of Scripture and the growth of revelation. Old friends turned on him in print as a heretic, and he answered Hengstenberg in a strong pamphlet of 1862.
britannica-1911-lobeck-christian-august:
Christian August Lobeck was a German classical scholar of the nineteenth century. He lived from seventeen eighty one to eighteen sixty. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Naumburg, he studied at Jena and at Leipzig in youth.

Lobeck settled at Wittenberg in eighteen o two as a private teacher. In eighteen ten he gained a professor post at the university there. Four years later he took the chair of rhetoric at Konigsberg. His work centred on Greek religion, tongue, and letters of old Greece. His greatest work Aglaophamus, from eighteen twenty nine, still serves students well.
britannica-1911-lucia-st:
Saint Lucia, or Lucy, a virgin martyr of Syracuse, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Her name stands in the canon of the mass. Her festival falls on the thirteenth of December. By the legend she lived under the emperor Diocletian.

Her mother was cured of an illness at the tomb of Saint Agatha. Lucia then persuaded her to give all her wealth to the poor. Her betrothed denounced her to the prefect Pascasius in revenge. No force, it is said, could drag her from where she stood. Boiling oil and burning pitch failed to harm her, until she was slain with the sword. The article notes her chief records, an old martyrology and an inscription found at Syracuse. Her pictures often show her bearing her eyes in her hand.
britannica-1911-lucian-satirist:
Lucian, a Greek satirist who lived from about the year 120 to 180, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Samosata on the river Euphrates in north Syria. His means were small, so he was first put to learn the trade of a sculptor. He broke a slab of marble, was beaten for it, and ran home.

A dream then set him on the path of learning, the entry says. He made money for a time as a speaker in the courts. He knew the rival schools of Greek thought well, and he lashed them all in his work. The Cynics felt his scorn most of all. The piece presents him as a scoffer who held that men's deeds always fall short of their claims.
britannica-1911-luke-gospel-of-st:
The Gospel of St Luke is the third of the four canonical Gospels of the Christian Church. The article opens with the question of who wrote it and when. The first sign of the belief that Luke, the companion of Paul, was the author stands in Justin Martyr. In his Dialogue with Trypho he cites a saying found only in this Gospel. He ascribes it to memoirs made by the apostles and those who followed them.

The first clear naming of Luke as the author comes in Irenaeus, in his famed passage on the Four Gospels, written about the year 180. The article holds that tradition to be weighty. It notes that the tradition first stands clear in a writer of the late second century. The piece then goes on to weigh what that late date means for the trust placed in the ascription.
britannica-1911-malachy-st:
Saint Malachy is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Malachy was archbishop of Armagh and papal legate in Ireland. He lived from about 1094 to 1148 and was born at Armagh. Once ordained, Malachy served as vicar to the archbishop. He carried out many reforms that brought Irish practice closer to Roman usage.

The article tells how he spent four years with a bishop in Munster to learn the Roman rite. He later governed a decayed monastery and was chosen bishop of Connor. War drove him out, and a friendly king helped him build a new monastery. He was named to succeed at Armagh, though he took the post with reluctance. In 1139 he set out for Rome to seek the pallium for his see. On the way he began a lifelong friendship with Saint Bernard.
britannica-1911-malling-east-and-west:
East Malling and West Malling are two villages in Kent in England, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They lie five and six miles west of Maidstone, with a station on the South Eastern and Chatham railway. Their counts in 1901 were 2,391 and 2,312 in turn. They stand in a rich farming district on the west slope of the Medway valley.

East Malling has large paper mills as its chief work in the text. At West Malling stand the remains of Malling Abbey, a Benedictine nunnery founded in 1090 by Gundulf, bishop of Rochester. Those remains take in the Norman west front of the church, the cloisters, the chapter house, and the gate house. Near West Malling, at Addington, are old remains of mounds, standing stones, stone circles, and pits in the chalk.
britannica-1911-mansfeld-ernst:
Ernst, Graf von Mansfeld, a German soldier, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born about fifteen eighty, he was a son of Peter Ernst, Prince von Mansfeld. He passed his early years in his father's palace at Luxemburg. His first military service came in Hungary under his half brother.

Later he served under the Archduke Leopold, the entry tells. That prince's ingratitude, real or fancied, drove him to the foes of the Habsburgs. Though he remained a Roman Catholic, he allied himself with the Protestant princes. In the early part of the Thirty Years' War he became a famed commander for hire.
britannica-1911-margaret-st:
Saint Margaret, a virgin and martyr in church legend, is the subject of this short 1911 Britannica entry. The Roman church kept her feast on the twentieth of July, while the Greeks knew her as Marina and kept hers on the seventeenth. In the tale she was born at Antioch, the daughter of a pagan priest named Aedesius, who scorned her for her Christian faith. She lived in the country with a foster mother and kept sheep.

A Roman official named Olybrius offered to marry her if she would give up her faith. She refused, was put through cruel torments, and was at last put to death. The entry is candid that no firm records set her apart from Saint Pelagia, so who she was stays a question of stories. Her cult still spread widely in England, where more than 250 churches bear her name.
britannica-1911-mark-st:
St Mark is held by tradition to be the author of the second Gospel. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that his name occurs in several books of the New Testament, and most likely points to one man in each case. In the Acts he is John, whose surname was Mark, and his mothers house in Jerusalem was a hub of early church life.

The entry ties him by kin to Barnabas of Cyprus, which marks him as a Greek speaking Jew. When Barnabas and Paul came back from a relief trip, Mark went with them. He joined their first great mission trip as a helper, in charge of small tasks of travel and work. The head breaks off as their plans grew and strain began to show.
britannica-1911-mast:
Mast, in sea speech, is the tall spar on a ship from which yards and sails are hung. The 1911 Britannica article starts with the word and a quaint guess at its birth. One fancy holds that man himself was the first mast. Standing in his dugout canoe, he let the wind push the craft along. Its true start is lost before all records.

The first masts were single spars of tough, springy wood, and pine woods gave the best sticks. Such masts still serve on small craft. The tale then splits in two: how masts grew in number, and how each mast was built up. Old ships had one mast with one sail. In time ships came to bear four or five. The front mast tipped forward by degrees and became the bowsprit, while the rest took the names used at sea today.
britannica-1911-matthew-gospel-of-st:
The Gospel of Saint Matthew is the subject of an entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the first of the four canonical Gospels of the Christian Church. Signs of its use in the generations after the Apostolic Age are plentiful. They are more plentiful than for any of the other Gospels.

Through church history it held a place second to none of the Gospels. It was central both in public teaching and in private reading. The entry seeks the reasons for that deep hold in the traits of the book itself. An old belief that it was the work of an apostle is also noted from the start.
britannica-1911-matthew-st:
Matthew, Saint is a Bible article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about one of the twelve apostles. Tradition credits him with the First Gospel. In that Gospel he is shown as a tax gatherer, or customs officer, in the service of the tetrarch Herod. His call to follow Jesus came as he sat in the customs house of a town by the Sea of Galilee.

The town seems to have been Capernaum, and the call is told in a few words in the ninth chapter. The like accounts in Mark and Luke name the man Levi, son of Alphaeus. If they are the same man, then James, son of Alphaeus, may have been his brother. Matthew, meaning Yahweh's gift, may have been a Christian surname taken later. The article notes a snag: Jews did not bear two native names in that way.
britannica-1911-maximus-st:
Saint Maximus, known as the Confessor, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born of noble stock at Constantinople about the year 580, he was schooled with great care. He rose to be private secretary to the emperor Heraclius.

The article centres on his stand in a great church dispute. In 630 he left court life for a monastery across the strait. He fought the view that Christ had one will only, at councils and in open debate. He swayed church meetings in Africa to his side in 646. Pope Martin's council at Rome in 649 backed his stand. Seized by the emperor's men, he was tried and exiled twice. In 662 his tongue and right hand were cut off, and he died in exile that year.
britannica-1911-meineke-johann-albrecht-:
Meineke, Johann Albrecht Friedrich August is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a German classical scholar. Born at Soest in Westphalia on the eighth of December 1790, Meineke held teaching posts at Jenkau and Danzig. His fame rested on conjectural criticism, the art of repairing corrupt Greek texts by informed guesswork. The comic writers and the Alexandrine poets were his favourite authors.

The article lists his editions and studies. His largest work gathers the fragments of the Greek comic poets. He also edited Aristophanes, Callimachus, Theocritus, Alciphron and Strabo, and the fragments of Rhianus, Euphorion and other Alexandrine poets.
britannica-1911-menander-dramatist:
Menander (342-291 B.C.) was a Greek playwright and the chief name of the New Comedy, and his life is told in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Athens to well-off parents, he was a friend of Theophrastus and close to Demetrius of Phalerum. The king Ptolemy Soter asked him to court, but he chose to stay free in Athens.

The entry says he wrote more than a hundred comedies yet won the prize just eight times. His rival Philemon was more liked by crowds, though Menander thought his own work better. It also notes his death by drowning while bathing, and the tomb and statue raised in his honor.
britannica-1911-mica-schist:
Mica-Schist is a rock article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a common layered stone. The rock is made essentially of mica and quartz, built in thin parallel bands. Layers rich in mica alternate with layers mostly of quartz. The stone splits easily along the mica films, and its surfaces shine with plates of muscovite or biotite. Some bands lie flat and yield smooth slabs, while others are crumpled.

The article then lists what else the rock can hold. Garnet is the most frequent extra mineral, with staurolite and kyanite in some kinds. The white mica-schist of the St Gothard carries both kyanite and staurolite. On origin, the article states that mica-schists are almost always old sedimentary rocks, clays and shales changed by recrystallization. In some districts every step can be traced from slate through phyllite to full schist.
britannica-1911-midhurst:
Midhurst is a market town in Sussex, England. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes its site, old houses, and past rule. It stands on rising ground near the river Rother. Rail lines linked it to Chichester, and its 1901 count was about seventeen hundred.

The church is a large late Gothic building with two saint names. Old houses line the town, and ruined Cowdray mansion stands by the river. A grammar school founded in 1672 was reopened in 1880 after long closure. A large hospital for chest sickness opened near the town in 1906. Lords held the town from Norman times through great families. Midhurst sent members to Parliament for centuries before losing the right in 1885.
britannica-1911-miguel-maria-evarist:
Dom Miguel, who lived from 1802 to 1866, was a Portuguese prince known for his claim to the throne of Portugal. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born at Lisbon on the twenty-sixth of October 1802. He was the third son of King John the Sixth. In 1807 he fled with his parents to Brazil. There he grew up, by the article's harsh account, with little schooling and wild habits.

His mother, an extreme foe of reform, schemed to put him on the throne in his father's place. Plots led to his exile in 1824. When John died in 1826, Pedro of Brazil gave the crown to his young daughter Maria, with Miguel as regent. Miguel swore to keep the new charter, then broke his word in 1828. He cast out the Cortes and had himself named sole true king.
britannica-1911-miller-william-second-ad:
William Miller, leader of the Second Adventists in America, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Miller lived from 1782 to 1849 and was born at Pittsfield in Massachusetts. He served as an army officer in the War of 1812 and left the army in 1815. He then settled at Low Hampton in New York state.

After two years of close Bible study, Miller came to expect the return of Christ in the year 1843. He read a span in the book of Daniel as a count of years from an old date. When 1843 passed, he named a day in October 1844 instead. Many followers left work and waited in white robes on hills and roofs. The hope failed, but many still held that the time was near. Groups that grew from his work are listed with their counts.
britannica-1911-musaus-johann-karl-augus:
Johann Karl August Musaus, a German author who lived from 1735 to 1787, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Jena in March 1735 and read theology at the university there. He would have become a parish pastor, but the peasants held out against him. Their charge was that he had been known to dance.

From 1760 to 1762 he brought out his first work, a tale meant to mock the hero of Richardson, who had soft fans in Germany. In 1763 he took charge of the court pages at Weimar, and in 1769 he became a teacher at its school. His best work is his folk tales of the Germans, printed from 1782 to 1786. He had gleaned the tales from the folk, yet his bent for satire kept them from the plain tone of true lore.
britannica-1911-owen-john-welsh-epigramm:
John Owen, a Welsh epigrammatist who lived from about 1560 to 1622, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Plas Dhu in Carnarvonshire, he was educated at Winchester School and at New College, Oxford. He was a fellow of his college from 1584 to 1591, when he became a schoolmaster, first near Monmouth and then at Warwick.

Owen won fame for a perfect mastery of Latin and for the humour, felicity and point of his epigrams. The scholars and wits of the continent called him the British Martial. He was a staunch Protestant and could not resist turning his wit against the Roman Catholic Church. That habit put his book on the Index of forbidden books in 1654, and it cost him his place in the will of a rich Catholic uncle. His Epigrammata run to twelve books, the first four published in 1606.
britannica-1911-palimpsest:
Palimpsest is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a reused writing surface. The custom is to remove writing from a surface. That prepares the surface to receive another text. The practice has been followed from earliest times. The term comes from Greek words for again and I scrape. Catullus uses the term, apparently of papyrus, the text notes. Cicero uses it of waxen tablets in one passage.

Plutarch tells that Plato compared Dionysius to a palimpsest book. His tyrant nature, hard to wash out, showed through. It showed like the imperfectly erased writing of such a book. In that passage the reference is to washing papyrus clean. The word in its first use can only fit one thing. It fits texts that were actually scraped or rubbed. Such texts must be of a material strong enough to bear that treatment. The entry opens a history of reused books.
britannica-1911-pelagia-st:
Pelagia is the name of saints of Antioch and of Tarsus. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sorts legend from firm record. One Pelagia was a virgin of fifteen at Antioch. She leapt from a roof to death rather than face dishonor.

Ambrose names that girl, and Chrysostom preached on her twice. Her feast day fell on the eighth of October. The same day honors two more saints of the name. One was a famed dancer and courtesan of Antioch. A bishop preaching moved her to tears and baptism. She then dressed as a male penitent in hiding. Three years of strict penance on the Mount of Olives followed. A scholar tried to read the saint as Aphrodite in disguise. The entry holds the first Pelagia to be a real person.
britannica-1911-penshurst:
Penshurst is a village in Kent in England, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands where the Eden and the Medway meet, south-west of Tonbridge. Its people numbered 1,678 in 1901. The village is noted for old houses, one a timbered house of the fifteenth century, and for a famed works that makes gear for cricket.

The church holds many monuments of the Sidney family. Penshurst Place is famed as the home of that house. It came to Sir William Sidney, a chamberlain of Henry the Eighth. His grandson, Sir Philip Sidney, was born there in 1554. The house is built round a court, with a hall of about 1341 that has an open timber roof and a gallery for minstrels. Its rooms hold portraits, armour, and family relics. The park and house were sung by Sidney in his Arcadia and by Ben Jonson and others.
britannica-1911-pentecost:
Pentecost began as a Jewish harvest feast, a feast of first fruits from the work of the fields. It ran through the seven weeks that match the grain harvest in Canaan. It was thus the closing feast of the harvest joy. The entry traces this farm root back to Canaanite practice. It also notes that the feast did not rank with the other two great farm feasts of early Israel.

Those other feasts marked the start and the close of the year's crops. One marked the start of the corn harvest, the other the gathering in of all crops. The entry shows that a scheme in Ezekiel leaves Pentecost out. Later hands added a note on the feast of weeks to the Hebrew text. Early law codes name the feast in brief terms.
britannica-1911-philip-the-evangelist:
Philip the Evangelist is a Bible figure described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He is first named in Acts as one of the seven men chosen to handle daily affairs of the church in Jerusalem. That choice followed complaints by Greek speaking believers against the Hebrew speakers. After the killing of Stephen, Philip went to a city in Samaria.

There he preached with much success, and Simon Magus was one of his converts. He next taught and baptised an Ethiopian official on the road from Jerusalem to Gaza. The entry follows him to Azotus and then through many cities, preaching as he went, until he reached Caesarea. Years later he hosted Paul there on the way to Jerusalem. At that time he had four daughters who prophesied, the article notes.
britannica-1911-picard-louis-joseph-erne:
Louis Joseph Ernest Picard lived from 1821 to 1877 and was a French politician. The 1911 Britannica life opens in Paris, where he was born in December 1821. He took his doctorate in law in 1846 and joined the Paris bar. Voters sent him to the law making body in the year 1858. There he joined the small group round Emile Ollivier at first.

As Ollivier drew near the throne, Picard veered to the left. He was one of the famed Five who stood in dissent. In 1868 he founded a weekly journal called L'Electeur libre. Voters chose him for two seats in 1869, and he sat for Herault. In 1870 he held the purse strings for the defence regime.
britannica-1911-pigeon-post:
Pigeon Post is the use of home bred pigeons to carry notes, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica traces it far back. The art is as old as Solomon, the entry says. The Greeks, who most like learned it from the Persians, sent the names of Olympic winners home by this means.

Before the wire that speaks by spark, the bird post had wide use. Stock men and money men prized it most. The Dutch state set up a civil and army bird post in Java and Sumatra in the early last age. Birds for it came from Baghdad. Full facts on bird use in the siege of Paris are sent to a linked entry. That siege sparked new zeal for war birds. Groups sprang up in all the great lands of Europe to keep such birds in train. The piece is a neat brief on fast wings before wires.
britannica-1911-poltergeist:
Poltergeist is a German word for a racketing spirit, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica uses it for strange events that no cause can be found for. Such events include objects that move with no traceable cause, and noises with no traced source. At times they seem to show a mind, as when raps answer a question by a code.

In the word itself, the events are laid to a spirit, the old folk account of all left over puzzles. As schooling spread, that account gave way to one that named electricity. Sceptics in all ages, the entry notes, have laid all such things to imposture. Fraud has often been caught, it grants, but it is not sure that fraud explains all the cases. What most drew the writer is how such tales appear in the earliest cultures, spread so wide, and stay so much the same.
britannica-1911-provost:
Provost is a title borne by officers in church and in state. The 1911 Britannica entry traces it through French to a Latin root. That root, praepositus, means one set over others in charge. Church fathers first used it for any church ruler of rank. In time the word took a far more narrow and fixed sense.

In a monastery the provost stood next below the abbot in rank. The rule of Saint Benedict set that order for the house. The dean ranked with him as a paired officer in the rule. Cathedral chapters took the same plan from the monks in time. There the archdeacon most often held the provostship as his right.
britannica-1911-rammelsberg-karl-friedri:
Karl Friedrich August Rammelsberg (1813-1890) was a German mineralogist, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives his posts and his books. He was born at Berlin and trained for medicine, graduating at Berlin University in 1837. In 1841 he became a lecturer there, and in 1845 a professor of chemistry. In 1851 he left to take the chair of chemistry and mineralogy at the Royal Industrial Institute.

In 1874 he became professor of inorganic chemistry and head of the second chemical laboratory at Berlin. He won his name by research in mineralogy, the study of crystals, and chemical analysis, and he worked on metallurgy too. Through it all he found time for a run of weighty textbooks. The entry lists his handbooks on mineral chemistry, on the chemistry of crystals, and on metallurgy, praising the mix of learning, sound judgment, and clear statement in them.
britannica-1911-remigius-st: Saint Remigius is the subject of a short life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Remigius was bishop of Reims who lived from about 437 to 533. He was the friend of Clovis, king of the Franks, whom he brought to Christianity. By one account, three thousand Franks were baptized with Clovis by Remigius on Christmas Day in 496. As papal power grew, tales grew up around his name. One tale says he anointed Clovis with oil from a sacred vessel.
britannica-1911-renan-ernest:
Ernest Renan, who lived from 1823 to 1892, was a French thinker and scholar of the east. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Tréguier in Brittany. His father, a cutter captain, held views for the republic. His mother came from royalist trade folk. Renan felt pulled between those two strains all his life. His father died when the boy was five.

His sister Henriette, twelve years older, then led the house. She went to Paris to teach in a girls' school. Ernest was schooled in the church school of his home town. His reports praise him as mild, patient, and thorough. In the summer of 1838 he swept all the prizes at his college. Word of that feat reached Paris through his sister. It won him a place at a church college for gifted boys.
britannica-1911-reyer-ernest:
Reyer, Ernest is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French composer. Born at Marseilles on the first of December 1823, he went to Algeria at sixteen. His time there produced a symphonic ode, Le Sélam, whose musical orientalism had already been anticipated by Felicien David in Le Désert. A one-act opera followed at the Opéra comique in 1854, and a ballet, Sacuntala, at the Opéra in 1858. La Statue in 1861 first brought his name before the public.

His opera Erostrate failed, first at Baden-Baden and again at the Paris Opéra. He worked meanwhile on Sigurd, produced at Brussels in 1884 and then at the Paris Opéra. The article calls Sigurd a work of great value, showing its maker's high ideas of lyrical drama. The article adds that Reyer also wrote musical criticism and became librarian of the Opéra.
britannica-1911-richard-st:
Richard, St is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English saint and bishop. Richard was educated at Oxford, where he taught and became chancellor. About 1235 he became chancellor of the diocese of Canterbury under Archbishop Edmund Rich, and shared the archbishop's exile in France. After Edmund's death he returned to England and became vicar of Deal.

The article follows his contested rise to a bishopric. In 1244 he was elected bishop of Chichester and consecrated at Lyons, though the king refused him the see's revenues. He received them in 1246. As bishop he reformed his clergy, favoured the Dominicans and preached a crusade. He died at Dover in April 1253. Miracles were reported at his tomb in Chichester cathedral, and he was canonized in 1262.
britannica-1911-richards-william-trost:
William Trost Richards was an American marine painter of the nineteenth century. He lived from eighteen thirty three to nineteen o five. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Philadelphia in Pennsylvania, he was a pupil of Paul Weber.

Richards lived much in France, Italy, and London during his career years. He held membership in the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts. He also belonged to the American Water Colour Society in his time. His works hang at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. They also hang at the Corcoran Gallery and at Hamburg in Germany. He died at Newport, Rhode Island, in November nineteen o five.
britannica-1911-riehm-eduard-karl-august:
Riehm, Eduard Karl August is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a German Protestant theologian. He studied at Heidelberg and at Halle under Hupfeld, who led him to add Arabic and Syriac. He entered the ministry in 1853, served as a vicar and garrison preacher, and began lecturing at Heidelberg. In 1866 he became a full professor at Halle, where he stayed.
