Later sections defend the Lucan account, verses 34 and 35, as the keystone of the narrative, without which the text resembles an unfinished arch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-willem-hessel:
Willem Hessels van Est, known as Estius, was a Dutch theologian famed for his notes on the letters of Saint Paul. Born at Gorcum in 1542, he died at Douai in 1613. He studied classics at Utrecht, then spent about twenty years at Louvain on philosophy, theology, and Scripture, teaching philosophy there for a decade. He took his doctorate in theology in 1580 and held the Douai theology chair for thirty-one years from 1582.

Estius lived amid fierce religious strife: Calvinists seized his home town in 1572, and his uncle Nicolas Pieck with eighteen other churchmen was put to death at Brielle. Estius wrote the standard history of those Martyrs of Gorcum, later canonized in 1867. His Paul commentaries shaped Catholic reading of the epistles, though his debt to his old teacher Baius on grace and free will means those passages need care. Benedict XIV called him the most solid of doctors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-forre:
William Forrest was a Tudor priest and poet whose verse lights up the politics and faith of Henry VIII and Mary. His birth and death dates are uncertain. Thought kin to John Forest, the Franciscan martyr, he was tied to Christ Church, Oxford, likely a student, and was present in 1530 when the university debated Henry's divorce. He drew a pension from the college in 1555 and became a royal chaplain soon after Mary's accession.

Nothing is known of him after Mary's death, though a 1592 state paper may catch him as a fugitive priest receiving a grey nag at a Northampton alehouse. A skilled musician, he gathered manuscripts of leading English composers, now kept at Oxford. Most of his poems stay in manuscript and lack high poetic merit, yet they brim with reform ideas and sharp period detail. Among them is his long poem on Catherine of Aragon, Grisild the Second.
certain-noble-plays-of-japan-from-the-ma:
Ernest Fenollosa studied Japan's Noh drama and left translations in manuscript; Ezra Pound chose and finished them for this volume, and William Butler Yeats wrote the introduction. Yeats explains frankly that he wanted the plays as a model for Ireland: a distinguished, indirect, symbolic drama that three musicians and a few players could perform in a room.

The plays themselves are slow, masked, and sung, with a chorus carrying much of the feeling. In one, a priest will not return the feather robe of a Tennin, a heavenly being, whose fading and distress the chorus describes. Dance, not action, brings each climax. Pound's versions helped reshape what English-language poets thought a play could be.
cheerful-by-request:
Edna Ferber published twelve short stories in 1918, and the title story explains the whole book's commission. An editor, lunching a writer, begs for something less drab than the year's realistic tales. Not pink, he says, and not all grey either. Mauve will do. Josie Fifer, an unknown of the theatrical firm Hahn and Lohman, becomes his example.

The Gay Old Dog, The Tough Guy, and The Eldest follow in the same spirit. That's Marriage and The Woman Who Tried to Be Good test cheer against harder material. The Girl Who Went Right and The Hooker-Up-The-Back keep Ferber's working women centre stage. Sophy-As-She-Might-Have-Been dreams an alternate life. Shore Leave closes the set.
children-of-the-frost:
Jack London published ten northern tales in 1902, most of them told from inside Native life in Alaska and the Canadian Arctic. The first story sends Professor Avery Van Brunt beyond the Barrens. He finds unrecorded forests and an unrecorded village where no white man has entered. His pride in arriving first drives the tale.

The Law of Life lets an old man accept the tribe's hard custom. Nam-Bok returns home a liar in his people's eyes, because his true story sounds impossible. Keesh, son of Keesh, hunts by headcraft and rises to chief. Lone Chief's sickness, Ligoun's death, and Li Wan the Fair fill the middle. A league of old men closes the book in planned revenge.
children-of-the-mist:
Eden Phillpotts published his Dartmoor novel in 1898, in four books with granite in their titles and weather in their hearts. Phoebe Lyddon opens the story above a river valley. She is nineteen, fresh as a ripe apple, with eyes as grey as Dartmoor mists. Will, her sweetheart, soon exits under a cloud in Book I.

Book II, The Enterprise, centres on Newtake Farm, a brothers' quarrel, and a difference with the Duchy. A will and a hundred pounds complicate the love story. Book III raises a granite cross over loss. Book IV keeps a secret through flight, a battle, and a pair of handcuffs. It ends on New Year's Eve at a night of jubilee. Dialect and moorland weather fill the pages.
conjuror-s-house-a-romance-of-the-free-f:
Conjuror's House: A Romance of the Free Forest, by Stewart Edward White, was copyrighted in 1903 and published in New York by Grosset & Dunlap. A frontispiece shows Paul Gilmore in The Call of the North, the play made from the tale. The story stands at a Hudson's Bay post. A girl stands on a bank above a river flowing north. A dozen whitewashed buildings crouch at her back. Before her stretches the stern Northern wilderness.

Once a summer the ship from England feels through the Hudson Straits to the River of the Moose; once a year voyageurs force their sledge dogs over the ice. Virginia, the girl, hears how a loyal Company servant was ruined. Enemies in high places worked against him unseen. He was given hard posts, inadequate supplies, and scant help. Then he was held to account for what he could not do.
criminal-psychology-a-manual-for-judges-:
Hans Gross, the Austrian judge who founded criminalistics, wrote Criminal Psychology as a manual for judges, practitioners, and students, here in the Modern Criminal Science series translation. The contents divide the work between the subjective conditions of evidence, the mental activities of the judge, and the psychology of witnesses. Part one begins with method, urging the natural-science habit on legal men.

Gross teaches how memory fixes time by associated events and places, how witnesses err honestly, and how suggestion corrupts testimony. Sections treat women, children, the aged, and the senses as evidence sources. His book effectively created forensic psychology, and its case-based teaching still informs how investigators are trained to doubt politely and systematically.
dearest:
A tale of an unseen child fills H. Beam Piper's short story, made here from Weird Tales for March 1951. A caption in the magazine urges a man to ask about an invisible playmate. Colonel Ashley Hampton sits in the library of Greyrock, among bookcases and old weapons, with five people he counts as enemies.

His nephew Stephen leans at the fireplace with a whiskey and soda, too sure of his coming rights. Myra, Stephen's wife, sits by in smart dress. Talk turns on a child's unseen friend, and the house's peace breaks down. A man with a sword cane and a leather box, a call to a hospital, and two men shot with a .45 close the sampled scene. Piper turns a ghost tale on family greed.
derrick-vaughan-novelist:
Edna Lyall's Derrick Vaughan, Novelist quotes Lewes's Life of Goethe on its title page: only through deep sympathy can a man become a great artist. The narrator, Vaughan's friend since boyhood pony days in a large old mansion, attempts not a formal biography but a life in scenes. Derrick's ambition to write collides with a father who despises fiction and a sweetheart who misunderstands him.

A long-suffering son, a major napping on the sofa, and a postman's double knock without letters fill the domestic middle. Vaughan's slow road to honest work, neither sentimental success nor cheap failure, made the novel a favorite manual for young writers. Lyall writes the artistic conscience as her real subject.
doe-osti-1251392-high-spectral-resolutio:
Operating guidance for a high-spectral-resolution lidar fills this instrument handbook, numbered DOE/SC-ARM-TR-157 and dated September 2025. R Bambha of the University of Colorado-Boulder leads the author list. J Garcia, I Razenkov, and E Eloranta, all of the University of Wisconsin-Madison, join him. The handbook serves the Department of Energy's Atmospheric Radiation Measurement user facility.

Raw lidar measurements are photon counts, and the handbook shows how their uncertainties can be derived. Counts can be summed across laser shots for one range bin, or across neighbouring bins, to cut uncertainty to a level that can be accepted. That gain costs time or space resolution, and the text states the trade plainly. The handbook is a working manual for users of the instrument's data.
doe-osti-1406255-stereo-cameras-for-clou:
Guidance for a pair of stereo cameras that watch clouds fills this instrument handbook, numbered DOE/SC-ARM-TR-204 and dated May 2026. D M Romps and R Öktem wrote it, both at the University of California, Berkeley. The handbook serves the Department of Energy's Atmospheric Radiation Measurement user facility at Richland, Washington.

Many views round a cloud let the whole cloud surface be drawn out, the text explains. At the ARM Southern Great Plains site, a ring of stereo cameras feeds the PCCP data streams. From them the COGS product is built, a four-dimensional map of cloudiness, on work by Romps and Öktem from 2018. The handbook tells users what the cameras see and how the data products are made.
doe-osti-17169490-task-i-model-intercomp:
William Hamilton of the National Laboratory of the Rockies and an international team compare software tools for designing hybrid solar plants, in an October 2026 case studies report. Hybrid plants pair concentrating solar power and its thermal storage with photovoltaic panels and batteries. Interest is strong: of 28 concentrating projects being built in China, 27 add photovoltaics.

Four tools were run on shared cases: MoSES, HOPP, AESOPT, and YACOP. They differ in how they size the plant and schedule its output. AESOPT alone solves design and dispatch together in one mixed integer program. The others pair black box sizing, by genetic algorithm or Bayesian search, with mixed integer or heuristic dispatch. A common plant configuration had to be fixed before any fair comparison could run.
doe-osti-2575626-solar-tool-capacity-bui:
Abbreviated final technical report NLR/TP-5400-95295, by Laura Beshilas of the National Laboratory of the Rockies and dated January 2026, closes award 41068, which ran September 2023 to March 2025. The project built solar planning capacity inside Midwestern Tribal governments. Tribes weighing solar projects often lack staff trained on the modeling tools that size systems and test their economics.

The remedy was hands-on, tailored training rather than generic webinars. Tribal environmental staff learned photovoltaic and storage modeling on their own projects and data, with instruction shaped to each nation's questions. The report is the short form of the final record: project summary, the barriers the training targeted, and what was delivered. It was funded by the Solar Energy Technologies Office under a 2023 Just In Time award, and written when the laboratory was still the National Renewable Energy Laboratory.
doe-osti-2583393-characterization-of-roo:
Texas A&M International University's closing report, led by Kenneth J. Tobin and covering September 2022 to May 2025, sharpens a soil moisture map farmers can actually use. SMERGE, a NASA product, estimates root-zone moisture across the country from 1979 to 2019, but at an eighth of a degree per pixel, too coarse for a single field. Root-zone moisture drives plant growth more directly than rainfall, so the team built a prototype downscaled below one kilometer.

The test ground straddled Kansas and Oklahoma, where the original product performs best. Three machine learning methods, random forest and two gradient boosting variants, did the downscaling. Checks ran four ways: sparse ground sensors, airborne retrievals at the Marena testbed, vegetation greenness benchmarks, and streamflow after storms. At the testbed, correlation with measured moisture rose by 0.4 over the default product. The finer maps are meant to feed species models for the region's reptiles and amphibians.
doe-osti-2583506-scribe-and-interface-mo:
Report NREL/TP-5F00-94922, dated March 4, 2025, pairs Joseph Luther's NREL team with Tandem PV on perovskite module stability. The goal was explicit: at least double module lifetime without giving up starting efficiency. Laser scribes split a module into cells. Those scribe lines, and the joins between layers, are where moisture creeps in and decay starts. Work proceeded on 3-by-3-inch minimodules.

Barrier materials came first. Candidates were picked from the literature, made into coatable inks, and screened for fit with perovskite materials. Microscopy, X-ray diffraction, profilometry, and light transmission tests judged the coatings. Testing followed IEC standards, with outdoor exposure beside lab aging. Scribe and interface changes were then applied to the minimodules to test whether the stability target could be met in practice. For Tandem PV, a two-times stability gain is the difference between a lab record and a product.
doe-osti-2583517-corrosion-and-mechanica:
Element 16 Technologies stored heat in molten sulfur while NREL tested what the sulfur did to its container metals, work reported in NREL/TP-5700-94263 dated November 15, 2024. Youyang Zhao was NREL's contact. Sulfur is a tempting heat battery for industrial process heat: abundant, cheap at sixty to one hundred dollars a ton, and with a heat capacity in the same conversation as solar salt. The catch is storing it at 400 to 420 degrees Celsius without eating the tank.

Coupons of candidate materials went into long-term molten sulfur exposure. The team then measured corrosion rates, worked out the corrosion mechanisms, and tested how much mechanical strength the coupons kept. Those three numbers decide whether a sulfur thermal storage system lasts decades or fails young, and what it costs to build safely. The results feed the engineering design of sulfur storage for industry, where process heat is a vast, hard-to-decarbonize load.
doe-osti-2586884-airport-ground-support-:
Ranjan Bose, Praveen Kumar, Ingrid Busch, Wan Li, and Michael Rodgers of Oak Ridge National Laboratory wrote this final report, ORNL/TM-2025/3999, dated July 9, 2025. It documents the 2025 data development, modeling, and analysis behind an assessment tool for electrifying airport ground support equipment. Dallas Fort Worth International Airport is the case study.

Ground support equipment covers the working vehicles of an airport: cargo loaders, forklifts, pushback tractors, and tug tractors among them. The tool weighs what it would take, in vehicles, chargers, and logistics, to switch that fleet to electric drive. A generic DFW layout map illustrates how freight moves between aircraft and the cargo terminal, and which equipment types do each leg of that work. The report gives airport planners a data-backed way to scope an electrification program before committing money.
doe-osti-2588470-evaluation-of-pozzolan-:
Katie Hill and Christine Langton of Savannah River National Laboratory wrote this evaluation, SRNL-STI-2025-00222, dated September 2025. Hanford Tank Waste Operations and Closure requested the work. Cast stone, a cement-like grout, is the planned waste form for Hanford's pretreated low-activity tank waste. Its recipe uses Class F fly ash. That supply is in doubt as coal plants retire or convert to gas.

Three natural pozzolans stood in for fly ash: Hess pumice, tephra pumice, and clinoptilolite zeolite. At the standard water-to-dry-mix ratio of 0.4, solidifying one liter of waste grew the volume about 75 percent with fly ash. The substitutes grew it slightly more, by about 78, 82, and 91 percent. The picture flips at higher water ratios. Hess and tephra mixes calculated at ratios up to 1.4 shrank the waste form volume by as much as about 29 percent against the baseline. That is a path to higher waste loading.
doe-osti-2589166-colorado-technology-pri:
Barbara O'Neill, Michael Coddington, and Doug Arent of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory are the technical contacts for this CRADA final report, NREL/TP-7A40-96545, dated September 2025. The partner was the Colorado School of Mines. The project ran a technology primer: summer schools teaching economists and social scientists how the electric grid actually works.

Energy economists model a system many have never seen up close, and policy analysis suffers for it. The primer gave them a week of grounding in the technical parts of the electrical distribution system. In phase one, Mines and NREL hosted 28 PhD students and recent graduates across two one-week sessions in July and August 2017. Participant feedback rated the classes successful, the program came in under budget, and attendance beat the proposal. The leads logged improvements for the 2018 sessions. One softer metric mattered to them: participants kept working together outside class, a seed of future collaboration.
doe-osti-2997306-identifying-and-classif:
Alexander Cerjan, Raktim Sarma, Taisuke Ohta, and Terry Loring wrote Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-11920R, dated September 2025. The report builds math tools for finding states that stay put inside materials with no energy gap. Gapless systems, which conduct freely, defeat the usual tests for protected localized states. Those tests lean on momentum, which messy or finite samples do not have.

The project extends a tool called the spectral localizer, which probes a sample at a chosen place and energy. Chapters adapt it to non-Hermitian systems, to light-guiding structures bathed in open surroundings, and to crystal slabs that leak radiation. Local markers for crystal-based topology work in disordered, finite samples where momentum methods fail. Designers of photonic metamaterials and electronic materials gain tests that run on real, imperfect hardware.
doe-osti-2997906-critical-knowledge-gaps:
Department of Energy workshop report DOE/SC-2026 gathers research priorities for the coasts of the southeastern United States. Co-chairs Elizabeth Herndon, Kenneth Krauss, Xingyuan Chen, and Havalend Steinmuller led a March 2024 workshop in Gaithersburg, Maryland, for the Biological and Environmental Research program. South Atlantic and Gulf coasts face sea level rise, storms, and land loss acting together.

Sessions named the most vulnerable systems and the gaps that block prediction. Missing pieces include maps of how coastal systems connect, the microbial and soil processes under ecosystem function, and how systems answer several stressors at once. One flagged need is understanding peat collapse, the sudden failure of organic soils that hold marsh platforms up. Data on photosynthesis, canopy structure, and microbial traits are called out as too thin for the models in use. Funders get a ranked agenda for the region's coastal science.
doe-osti-2998584-basic-physical-processe:
Sergei Krasheninnikov's final report for Energy Department award DE-FG02-06ER54852, from the University of California, San Diego, covers dust in fusion plasmas. Dust means tiny solid grains that form or enter the hot plasma inside machines such as tokamaks and stellarators. The work focused on the cooler edge region, where dust can change how the plasma behaves.

Computer modeling followed burst injections of carbon and tungsten dust into divertor plasmas like the one in the DIII-D tokamak. The team also studied forces on grains that are not round, in both magnetized and plain plasmas. Planned DIII-D injection tests were meant to check grain paths against the DUSTT code. Side work covered neon-deuterium ice pellets at JET and boron granules at Japan's LHD device. Six papers came out of the project.
doe-osti-3001069-transformational-sorben:
Gökhan Alptekin of TDA Research, in Golden, Colorado, files the final report for award DE-FE0031734. It covers June 2019 to May 2025, on a sorbent system for capturing carbon dioxide from coal plant exhaust. Instead of liquid amines, the process uses a metal-organic framework, a crystalline sponge with vast internal surface, in a vacuum and concentration swing cycle. Efficient vacuum pumps keep the energy penalty low. Stated performance: over 95 percent of emissions captured, at 95 percent purity, for roughly 30 dollars per tonne.

Work moved the system from proof of concept to components validated in a relevant environment, technology readiness level 5. The sorbent was optimised and demonstrated at increasing scale. Techno-economic analysis projects a low cost of electricity for a pulverised coal plant fitted with the system. Remaining steps toward a full prototype are laid out. The report is long and detailed, documenting sorbent chemistry, cycle design and costing.
doe-osti-3001199-fast-ion-diagnostics-an: William Heidbrink of UC Irvine files a final report, a single short page, on his group's role in Britain's MAST-Upgrade tokamak programme. The hosted record is a summary only: it names contributions rather than presenting data. UC Irvine installed a solid state neutral particle analyser, written up by doctoral student Garrett Prechel in a 2022 journal paper. Heidbrink also supplied an analysis tool for the 3 MeV proton diagnostic, advised on the FIDA camera, and contributed to a 2024 fast ion study. Talks by Prechel and postdoc J. Lestz complete the output.
doe-osti-3006516-developing-the-science-:
Sandia report SAND2025-14653, printed November 24, 2025, is the DuraMAT 2.0 final project report on how polymer encapsulants in solar modules break down. Seven authors are listed, led by Mark A. Wilson, Hannah Dedmon, and Samantha Kruse. The 18-month effort ran across fiscal 2024 and 2025. Its goal was to quantify the molecular-scale processes that drive aging of encapsulant films such as EVA, the clear polymer that seals photovoltaic cells.

Degradation is driven by water and oxygen diffusing in, by reaction by-products such as acetic acid, and by heat and ultraviolet light. The team combined accelerated aging experiments on films with atomistic modeling, aiming at a predictive model rather than a purely observed lifetime. Later chapters compute activation energies for reaction models grouped by contaminant environment: water alone, acetic acid alone, and a water, oxygen, and acetic acid mix.
doe-osti-3007478-finish-development-test:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-28152, by Christopher Matthews, Conor Galvin, Anton Schneider, and Michael Cooper, finishes a baseline modeling capability for uranium nitride fuel swelling. The chain runs from atom-scale data through the Centipede code up to the BISON fuel performance code. New lower-length-scale data and fracture strength calculations for uranium nitride feed the chain.

Under steady running, high temperatures let gas pressure escape through grain boundaries, so later power ramps cause little extra release. Fuel first irradiated at low temperatures, 1000 to 1100 kelvin, keeps high-pressure bubbles that can crack the fuel in a transient. Chemistry effects, a log transform, and time dependence were added to the Centipede cluster model. Transient gas release also grows sharply with burnup: none at 1.1 percent burnup, but heavy release at 3.1 and 5.7 percent.
doe-osti-3007479-trust-contact-thermal-c:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-31754, by Thomas Allard, James Valdez, and Samantha Ceballes, reports fiscal 2025 work on contact thermal conductance, how well heat crosses the joint where two solids touch. The TRUST testbed measured metal-to-metal joints and joints padded with foam. Grading criteria in the report set how each measurement was judged.

A measurement matrix varied surface roughness, and a literature review gathered published foam conductivity values for comparison. The report opens with the TRUST program background and that foam review before the new data. Analysis sections treat bare metal contact and foam-filled interfaces separately, and the year's data were uploaded to a shared store. The results help engineers predict temperatures at bolted or pressed joints instead of guessing the joint's resistance.
doe-osti-3010996-characterization-result:
An August 2025 sample of overhead condensate from the Tank Farm 2H evaporator was checked by Cintina Craig at the Savannah River lab in report SRNL-STI-2025-00683. The sample arrived clear and colourless, with no visible solids in it. Each test ran in duplicate so the two readings could be checked against each other for agreement.

Caesium 137 averaged 302 dpm per millilitre, well under the Effluent Treatment Project waste acceptance limit of 1,300 in the same units. Strontium 90 averaged 3.33 dpm per millilitre. All three radionuclides that were measured, caesium 137, strontium 90, and iodine 129, fell within their waste acceptance limits. The overhead stream thus met the criteria set for it.
doe-osti-3011861-preliminary-assessment-:
Solar and storage options for the Energy Coordinating Agency in Philadelphia are assessed in a July 2025 presentation by Xiangkun Li, Grant Ellwood, Kumaraguru Prabakar, and Ben Bruxvoort. The REopt platform optimised system sizing against lifecycle cost. The site holds access to 600 photovoltaic panels rated at 305 watts each and weighed pairing them with batteries for savings and a microgrid.

Cost optimal photovoltaic capacity came out at 28.7 kilowatts, cutting lifecycle costs by 1.6 percent over the analysis period. Battery storage was not cost effective for grid connected operation. First year energy cost fell from 24,102 dollars to 20,849 dollars in the optimal case.
doe-osti-3012739-energy-efficient-direct:
University of Cincinnati's final report, submitted January 12, 2026, for award DE-FE0032128, covers a direct air capture project led by Joo-Youp Lee from October 2021 to September 2025. The team developed a modified amine sorbent, a chemical coating that grabs carbon dioxide from open air, coated onto honeycomb monolith blocks. The blocks sit in a passive air contactor that lets wind do the air moving.

The modified sorbent released its carbon dioxide with far less heat than the standard version: desorption heat fell from 73.74 to as low as 31.82 kilojoules per mole in lab sorbent tests, a saving near 57 percent. Monolith blocks held up over a 100-cycle test and released gas above 90 percent purity. Computer modeling then guided designs for larger contactors under real wind speeds.
doe-osti-3017355-development-fiber-optic:
Brandon Demory, Sarah Sahota-Dhillon, T Bond, and Jorge Arteaga of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this abbreviated final report, LLNL-TR-2015636, in February 2026. Project 23-ERD-001 developed a fiber optic system to detect subsurface gas leaks directly. Underground storage of carbon dioxide, natural gas, and hydrogen is growing. A storage well is nearly leak-proof when built right, but proving that over decades is the hard part.

The approach runs light through hollow-core fiber and reads gas by its Raman signal, a fingerprint in scattered light. One objective measured how the fiber takes up carbon dioxide, linking fiber length, diffusion time, detectable concentration, and signal strength. A second developed a drilling recipe to open extra diffusion ports along the fiber core. More ports mean faster, more sensitive leak checks along a well. Storage operators get a possible early-warning line buried with the well itself.
doe-osti-3020128-mitigating-data-center-:
NLR technical report NLR/TP-2C00-98424, by Saurav Talukdar and co-authors from Verrus LLC and the lab, addresses a new grid risk. Large data centers can drop off the power system all at once. A lightning fault in Northern Virginia on July 10, 2024, showed how fast a big load loss can spread. The report presents Verrus's StabiliGrid architecture, designed to keep a data center connected and helpful during short grid faults.

The strategy works in four steps. It detects the fault with fast power-quality monitoring and uses protection settings that allow ride-through. It then dispatches on-site batteries and backup power systems, supporting the grid for the seconds the fault lasts. The team replayed the Virginia event on controller hardware-in-the-loop equipment at the lab. The battery-backed data center rode through repeated undervoltage and overvoltage events instead of disconnecting.
doe-osti-3023143-development-of-advanced:
Final technical report SC0017810 covers work on optical detector technology that can survive heavy radiation inside future particle physics experiments. The goal was ultra-compact, precision electromagnetic calorimetry, the measurement of particle energy, for colliders such as FCC-hh and FCC-ee and for muon collider and fixed target setups. Target performance included timing near 50 picoseconds and tight energy resolution.

The team built and studied a modular sampling design called a RADiCAL module. Beam measurements gave a high-energy timing limit of 17.5 picoseconds under the stated conditions, and tests also used LuAG:Ce ceramic filaments valued for radiation hardness. The authors judge that the technique can meet, and possibly beat, FCC-hh timing needs, with more work needed for FCC-ee.
doe-osti-3024024-balancing-interface-pre:
Hannah Cohoon, Drew Paine, Dan Gunter, and Lavanya Ramakrishnan reflect on building a custom GPT for the STRUDEL project, in report LBNL-2001754, dated March 31, 2026. STRUDEL is an open source effort that helps science teams plan and build user-centered software, funded here by Sloan Foundation gifts to Berkeley Lab. Their planning framework had earlier been delivered as quizzes; a chat bot promised a friendlier interface.

The bot was stocked with the project's own websites, repositories, tutorials on user research methods, the earlier quiz advice, and the STRUDEL typology of science software projects. Its instructions listed assumptions it may make, such as users having little experience with user research, and rules for when to offer certain recommendations. The paper weighs the appeal of that flexible interface against how certain users can be of the information's quality.
doe-osti-3024791-review-of-shock-vibrati:
Marina Miletic, Melissa S Louie, and Brian D Ehrhart of Sandia National Laboratories review the test regimes for Type IV hydrogen composite pressure vessels meant for rail use. Their review is SAND2026-18622, printed March 2026. Type IV tanks are fully composite, light and strong, and trains will subject them to shock and vibration unlike a parked car's duty. The review gathers what standards already demand and where rail service pushes past them.

Sections move through types of loads and failure modes, then the test catalogue. Hydrostatic methods get close treatment: the water jacket method common in the United States and Canada surrounds a liquid-filled, pressurized cylinder with a water jacket. It measures expansion by displaced water. The checks run both under pressure and after release. Proof pressure testing with gas is set alongside it for contrast.
doe-osti-3347395-prairie-state-generatin:
Roland Okwen of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign lays out the build plan for a carbon storage field in report DOE-UIUC-31892-19, issued May 4, 2026. The Prairie State Energy Campus project, near Marissa in Washington County, Illinois, would inject carbon dioxide into the St. Peter and Everton sandstones. Maquoketa Shale caps the complex, the Knox Group floors it, and the deepest drinking water sits in the Pennsylvanian section.

The plan calls for two injection wells, six injection-zone monitoring wells in three phases, and two wells above the cap rock. Capture and compression gear and pipelines complete the build. Class VI permit applications, the federal well class for carbon burial, were prepared from the Lively Grove number 1 well data and handed to the company. Ninety-three old wells pierce the sealing layers nearby.
doe-osti-3362958-final-technical-report-:
Kevin Solomon of the University of Delaware, with Mark Blenner and Aaron Wright, reports final results under award DE-SC0022018, covering September 2021 to August 2025. Yellow mealworms can chew plastic, but past claims about which plastics they truly break down were messy and hard to repeat. The project asked a sharp question: is it the worm, or the microbes in its gut, that deconstruct low-density polyethylene, one of the most made and most tossed plastics on Earth?

Careful materials checks settled that the gut microbiota did the work, not chewing alone or the host gut by itself. One planned aim, rebuilding the microbial team from parts, was dropped after a co-investigator move. In its place the team wrote best practices for enzyme discovery and validation, aimed at cutting false positives across the field.
doe-osti-3365975-data-driven-modeling-an:
Texas A&M University-Kingsville's final report for grant DE-SC0023546, led by Xuewei Zhang, covers data-driven modeling and control of systems where plasma meets surfaces. Glow, barrier, and arc discharges striking a surface form patterns that theory still struggles to predict. The project combined modeling and experiments inside a framework that keeps correcting models with measurements.

Two target systems carried the work. One was plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition, modeled with ordinary differential equations. The other was a direct-current discharge over a thin insulating oil layer, where charge penetration and interface stability are the open questions. The team built multiphysics capacity in OpenFOAM alongside Python, MATLAB, and COMSOL. A four-tier outreach pyramid, from regional webinars to a plasma certificate, anchored the work at a minority-serving South Texas campus.
doe-osti-3375374-in-search-of-strategic-:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2005867, dated June 2026, is an edited volume from the lab's Center for Global Security Research. Kimberly Peh and Mike Albertson edited the book. Its theme is the global race for new technology and what counts as a real lead. Chapters weigh fields where the United States and China both pour in funds. The editors frame the book as a check on alarm as much as a warning.

One chapter maps patent citation networks in quantum technology. The Chinese web is larger, the authors find. Yet both nations carry heavy deadweight in patents that no one picks up. Each side has produced a like count of patents that others build on. That pattern reads as parity, not a runaway lead. The chapter also notes a stark split: neither side cites the other, a don't-cite-the-rival habit.
doe-osti-3375600-gan-core-shell-nanofin-:
A final scientific report for award DE-AR0001789, by Patrick Fay of the University of Notre Dame and dated May 13, 2026, closes the CoNVerT power transistor project. The award ran from June 2024 to January 2026. CoNVerT is a gallium nitride transistor built as a core-shell nanofin standing upright. The shape aims at the best traits of GaN: high voltage hold-off with low on-state loss. Power switches for cars and grid gear are the target market.

The report is frank about a missed goal. Task one asked for a superjunction drift region that holds more than 1.5 kilovolts. Its on-resistance had to stay under 0.2 milliohm square centimeters. The built parts leaked too much current to hold that voltage. Design studies with TCAD software did flag hopeful shapes, and drift region growth work moved ahead. The gap sits in the made hardware, not the plans.
doe-osti-3391256-overview-of-impact-data:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-26-91438, dated March 2026, gives an overview of the IMPACT data acquisition system and its data reduction process. Austin Fleming, Geran Call, and Calvin Downey are the authors. IMPACT, the Irradiated Material Property Accelerated Characterization Test at the Advanced Test Reactor, measures thermal conductivity inside running fuel, specifically U-10Zr metallic fuel, with an instrumented probe.

The acquisition system handles both passive temperature watching and active interrogation of the probe with controlled alternating and direct current. A reduced-order thermal model built on the thermal quadrupoles method supports interpretation, letting the team solve the inverse problem of extracting conductivity from the signals. Machine learning enters the reduction too: convolutional neural networks flag gas gaps and other shifting features that change the thermal response during irradiation, feeding a wider digital twin effort.
doe-osti-3413701-mcstas-simulations-of-t:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4731,, by E. B. Iverson and dated July 2026, documents McStas simulations of the Moderator Test Station neutron beamline. McStas traces neutron paths through instrument parts in software. A test station lets staff try moderator designs before building them.

Model files in the pages set part positions, rotations, and saved neutron states. One code block restores a neutron's state after sampling on a second flight path. Careful bookkeeping keeps simulated neutrons from being counted twice. Instrument designers can test beam layouts on screen and save costly hardware trials for the best designs.
doe-osti-3422012-colorado-technology-pri:
Report NLR/TP-7A40-100328 from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, dated August 2026, covers a technology primer course for economists and social scientists in Colorado. Barbara O'Neill and Michael Coddington were the lab contacts. The work ran under CRADA number CRD-19-00790.

Course material explains how electricity markets work, both regulated and deregulated. Students learn how revenue flows to firms and who bears which costs. The class builds on graduate courses in industrial organization and environmental economics. Policy students gain the market grounding they need before judging energy rules with real price effects.
doe-osti-3625671-h2-scale-validating-an-:
The final report for CRADA CRD-18-00741 with Honda R&D Americas is National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5700-99290, dated August 2026. Sam Sprik and Genevieve Saur were the lab's technical contacts, and the report date is February 12, 2026. Honda builds electrolysis systems that squeeze hydrogen inside the cell itself, rather than relying only on outside compressors. That built-in step can reach high output pressure.

Compressing hydrogen for storage and dispensing adds cost and lowers reliability, so the built-in route matters. The lab readied its Energy Systems Integration site and its hydrogen test facility for outside checks. Work covered benchmark tests of Honda's stack and full system. Runs also mimicked supply from renewables and grid service duty. The aim was data across many operating settings, drawn from over a decade of lab work with low-temperature electrolysis. Such proof is meant to speed the product toward market.
dotty-dimple-out-west:
Sophie May sends the Parlin children west by train in Dotty Dimple Out West, entered for copyright in 1869 by Lee and Shepard of Boston. The book is one of six Dotty Dimple volumes, sold at seventy-five cents each. Dotty and her small cousin Katie, the Flyaway, ride with family toward new faces and wide country.

Chapter heads list the captain's son, a baby in a blue cloak, a pigeon pie postponed, and the major's joke. On the train, Katie holds court, sure she is a big girl who can walk and knows better than babies. Woods, camps, and kind strangers fill the later pages. May wrote the trip as a string of small wonders seen through small eyes. For child readers of the day, the West came close: not gold or war, but seats, meals, jokes, and the thrill of going far from home.
draculas-guest:
Bram Stoker died in 1912, and this set of his weird tales came out in 1914, after his death. His widow put the set in print, from the tales he had left at his death. The first tale in it holds a place of its own in the Stoker world.

'Dracula's Guest' is the cut first part of Dracula, left out of the 1897 book. A man lost in snow near Munich meets wolves and a strange tomb on Walpurgis night. The rest of the set holds short tales of ghosts, rats, and dread from Stoker's full range.
dust:
Emanuel Haldeman-Julius and his wife Marcet set their novel Dust on the open Kansas prairie. Dust coats the weeds, horses, and covered wagon of the Wade family in the first paragraph. Martin Wade takes up a big farm and battles the dust for a lifetime. Chapter titles chart the war: dust stirred, dust in her heart, dust begets dust.

Martin's drive enriches him and starves his wife Rose of every joy; his son Bill rises at five to milk cows in the dark and cold. The Haldeman-Juliuses, socialist publishers from Girard, Kansas, wrote a parable of accumulation: a man who gains a farm and loses a family. Its plain anger made it a Little Blue Book favorite.
effie-maurice-or-what-do-i-love-best:
Fanny Forester teaches a small girl the first commandment in Effie Maurice, a tale from Gall and Inglis of London. On a winter Sabbath evening, little Effie asks her mother whether Christians at home can break the rule against other gods. She had thought it was for the Burmans and Chinese, where the missionaries go.

Her mother answers that idolaters live in Christian lands too. Nine chapters work the lesson out through New Year plans, a miser, a poor widow, and a funeral. A frontispiece shows Effie whispering to give her gift to the poor woman with the sick baby. A later scene has a widow cling to her child as her all, unable to say thy will be done. The book is Sunday-school fiction at its plainest: one doctrine, learned through small acts of giving.
eothen-or-traces-of-travel-brought-home-:
Alexander William Kinglake wrote Eothen, published in 1844, the record of a journey he made in 1834 and 1835 through the Ottoman East. He rides from Belgrade through Constantinople, crosses to Asia, and travels by Damascus and Jerusalem down to Cairo. Along the way he visits Lady Hester Stanhope in her Lebanon retreat, faces plague and strict quarantine, and crosses deserts with a small party and much dry humor.

Kinglake refuses the guidebook manner. He gives few dates and fewer ruins, and instead renders what travel felt like: fear, boredom, wonder, and the talk of dragomans and sheikhs. Eothen became a classic of English travel writing, praised for a voice so personal that the East serves mainly as its mirror.
fenton-s-quest:
Braddon spins a tale of love and loss in Fenton's Quest, a sensation novel of 1871. M. E. Braddon wrote it, and this text follows the cheap uniform edition of her works. The book opens with a chapter called The Common Fever, then turns to Marian's Story. A long run of chapters follows, as the title's quest takes shape.

The sampled pages find a man on a lonely lane, on his way to the Grange. His thoughts are full of the woman he loves and of an unknown rival. He asks himself what right he has to weigh that rival's temptation or strength. If the man loves her truly, he resolves, he will step back and be her friend. Love, doubt, and self-denial set the key for the tale that follows.
fifteen-years-with-the-outcast:
Roberts gives her life's work in Fifteen Years with the Outcast, printed in 1912. Florence Roberts, known as Mother Roberts, spent those years among women the world had cast off. Her preface opens with a tale of a missionary and a hunter, and turns it to her own field: the lost at home, not only abroad.

The sampled pages hold a talk with a woman called Miss Loraine. Roberts asks why she could not have kept a decent lodging house. The woman says she met the wrong people, and that she sends money home for her father's rent. When word of his death comes, she vows, she will leave the life for good and vanish to a far corner of the world. Roberts writes with pity, not scorn, of the women she served.
first-and-last:
Hilaire Belloc's First and Last gathers essays on subjects from weighing anchor to the end of the world. Belloc opens by confessing that he would call weighing anchor getting it up, but that print calls it weighing anchor, and in print one must bow.

Contents include On Cheeses, The Captain of Industry, The Inventor, The Views of England, The Lunatic, St. Patrick, The Battle of Hastings, The Roman Roads in Picardy, and On the Decline of the Book. Belloc writes with gusto, paradox and historical imagination, whether on Normandy, on entries, or on companions of travel. Readers who enjoy the familiar essay at its most combative will find First and Last a delight.
florence-and-northern-tuscany-with-genoa:
Hutton guides the traveler in Florence and Northern Tuscany with Genoa, in a second edition of 1907 and 1908. Edward Hutton wrote the book, William Parkinson painted sixteen of its pictures in colour, and sixteen more plates stand beside them. The route starts at Genoa and works south along the coast.

Porto Venere, Sarzana and Luna, Carrara, Pisa, and Livorno lead the way toward Florence. The sampled pages pause at a church front of the fifteenth century. Hutton praises how the builder held back from a mere copy of the antique. The façade, he says, caught the beauty of Roman things as the age itself felt them, and adds to the rosy spire of the campanile behind it. Inside, a sort of twilight fills the chapels. The book is a learned companion for slow travel.
four-weeks-in-the-trenches-the-war-story:
Kreisler, the celebrated violinist, served as an officer in the Austrian Army in the war's first weeks. His recollections, he warns, are uneven: some events stand out with absolute clearness, others blur and merge. He dedicates the little book to his wife Harriet, his stanchest comrade.

The sampled pages prepare for a Russian frontal attack. Trenches were strengthened overnight, artillery masked with transplanted bushes, and ranges marked by bundles of hay. At nine in the morning everything stood ready to meet the onslaught. Fritz Kreisler's four weeks ended in wounds, and this memoir made his service famous on another stage.
frank-the-young-naturalist:
Castlemon introduces Frank Nelson as a boy naturalist with his own museum, a hundred miles north of Augusta. The first Gun-Boat Series volume stays home: fishing excursions, a coon hunt, trout, and wild geese. The Regulators and Bill Lawson's revenge darken the country peace.

The boys' pleasures run to the water. Sixteen sail-boats in company cannot resist trying their speed, though not a word about a race is said. Every skipper silently makes up his mind to touch the opposite shore first. Harry Castlemon published Frank, the Young Naturalist in 1892, the foundation stone of his many series.
from-jest-to-earnest:
From Jest to Earnest, by Edward Payson Roe, begins with a practical joke and spends thirty two chapters paying for it. Roe titles his opening movements plainly: A Practical Joke, The Victim, Puzzled and Interested, and A Little Pagan. A sleigh ride and something more follows, then plain talk, as the joke's target and its makers are drawn into each other's worlds.

Hemstead is the story's young man of the world. He sees what the contents call our set. He survives a lover quenched and midnight vigils. He fires a heavy gun that recoils. Miss Marsden asks sombre questions, a rationalist of the old school argues back, and a meeting on a crumbling ice floe supplies the crisis. Roe was a minister whose novels outsold nearly everyone in America, and his recipe shows here: society comedy first, then earnest religion earned through danger at a Christmas close.
game-and-playe-of-the-chesse-a-verbatim-:
Caxton's Game and Playe of the Chesse is given here in a verbatim reprint of the first edition of 1474. William E. A. Axon supplies an introduction to this 1883 reprint. The book is among the first printed in English. It uses the chess board as a mirror of society. Each piece stands for a rank or trade, and each chapter draws the duties of that estate. The text keeps the old spelling, with long s and thorn, explained in a transcriber's note.

The moralizing runs sharp: officers grown rich in their posts, one passage says, do less harm than poor new men would. Illustrations are copied from Caxton's original. The reprint serves students of early print and of manners alike.
girls-of-the-forest:
Eight sisters in a wild forest home are the heart of L. T. Meade's Girls of the Forest, published in 1902. Their father, whom they call Paddy or the Padre, rules the brood with love. Verena, the tall, golden-haired eldest, holds the respect of them all. Word comes that Aunt Sophia, fashionable and conventional, is to visit, and the girls press their father to describe her.

The sisters live free of town rules, and the coming visit threatens their easy ways. Meade builds the tale on the clash between wild, warm family life and prim outside manners. Each sister has her own temper and gifts, and the talk among them is lively. It is a family story in Meade's sunniest manner, set far from the schools she so often used.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NitrateTest_Nit:
General Atomic of San Diego wrote this letter on August 12, 1968, to Howard L. Roffman. The company notes that its work on the Oswald case is reported in General Atomic Report GA-6152. Appended to the letter are neutron-activation analysis results, run on hand blanks from shooting cases.

Neutron-activation analysis was the era's high-technology test for bullet lead and gunshot residue. Laboratories measured trace elements to link samples, or to rule links out. The hand blanks were control samples, the baseline against which a shooter's hands were compared. The letter and its tables show a defense contractor's laboratory doing forensic work for the Oswald debate, and reporting it in the flat form of test results.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-QuigleyJohnLest: nsia-QuigleyJohnLester Quigley John Lester: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-StudentsforaDem: Under the headline Spies Eye SDS, the Guardian reported on the House Committee on Internal Security's 1969 hearings. The hearings looked at Students for a Democratic Society, the best-known student protest group of the Vietnam era. Government interest in SDS was intense, and the article covers officials watching a movement they saw as a threat. It is a period piece on surveillance of student activism.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ThreatsAgainstJ: An Associated Press dispatch from Athens reported a plot aimed at President Kennedy's son. Greek security forces announced the arrest of eight people in the case. The short wire report carried the news to American papers, where threats against the Kennedy family still drew wide attention years after the president's death. The dispatch survives as a brief, tense sample of that coverage.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
During Jimmy Carter's presidency, United States officials drew up a highly sensitive blacklist of Colombian officials they believed were corrupt. Michael Evans edited this briefing book, posted in April 2024, which brought that list to light. The names had stayed secret for decades.

A blacklist is a working tool, not a speech. It shows which Colombians Washington quietly distrusted while dealing with their government in public. Because the list was so sensitive, its release lets readers compare private American judgments with the public diplomacy of the Carter years in Colombia. The list's survival in the files made this release possible at all.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba-cub:
Saturday, October 27, 1962 was the most dangerous single day of the Cuban Missile Crisis. This briefing book was posted exactly sixty years later, on October 27, 2022. It gathers declassified records on those twenty-four hours.

By that Saturday the standoff over Soviet missiles in Cuba had reached its peak strain. American forces were on high alert and both leaders faced choices that could start a nuclear war. A day-by-day documentary record lets readers slow the crisis down and see how close the decisions came, hour by hour, to disaster. It remains the standard example of a crisis survived by hours.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
On September 9, 1949, Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter handed President Harry Truman a carefully worded report. It described abnormal radioactive contamination in the Northern Pacific, far above normal atmospheric levels. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted seventy years later in September 2019.

The contamination was the fingerprint of the first Soviet nuclear test, which had ended the American atomic monopoly years earlier than expected. Detection by air sampling, not by spies, was the breakthrough. The documents trace how scientists confirmed the finding and how it was phrased for a president. Every later nuclear monitoring system descends from this first success.

In early August 1977, Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev wrote directly to President Jimmy Carter with an alarming report. Soviet surveillance had detected a nuclear weapons test site in South Africa. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in October 2023, on that discovery and what followed.

Brezhnev asked the United States to act on the finding. A Soviet warning to Washington about an ally of the West is one of the Cold War's stranger cooperative moments. Joint pressure did follow, and South Africa's test was called off. The documents show rivals sharing intelligence when a new bomb program threatened them both.

US Nuclear Weapons in the Netherlands: A First Appraisal - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records.
green-mansions-a-romance-of-the-tropical:
W H Hudson subtitled Green Mansions a romance of the tropical forest, and set it in the Guayana wilderness of Venezuela, a land of rivers and forests without end. Abel, a young Venezuelan fleeing revolution, penetrates a forbidden forest and hears a voice like a bird's. It belongs to Rima, a girl raised among the trees.

The foreword, by a devoted admirer, calls Hudson the rarest spirit among living writers for conveying nature from inside. Abel and Rima's idyll darkens as hostile Indians and Abel's own people close in. Hudson, who spent his youth on the Argentine pampas, wrote the forest as both paradise and warning. The novel remains his best-loved work.
harvest:
Mrs. Humphry Ward, author of Robert Elsmere, published Harvest in 1920, a novel of England farming through the Great War. It opens at Great End Farm, where two old laborers come out of the lane with bags slung on sticks over their shoulders. The taller, Peter Halsey, is a handsome fellow with a delicately humorous mouth, his stoop and gray locks showing him near his old-age pension. Yet he carries still a look of youth, for he had been a splendid creature in his time.

The war has taken the young men, and the land must still be fed and worked. Ward sets her tale among farmers, land girls, and the strain of wartime prices and loss. Her interest is in character under pressure, in her grave, careful manner. Harvest is a home-front novel, written while the fields it describes were still under the plough of war.
heart-and-soul-by-maveric-post:
Victor Mapes, writing as Maveric Post, published Heart and Soul with the Century Company in 1921. His apology at the front owns that the book was not written with any idea of being published, but simply because he could not help it. He got thinking about various things, in the lives of people about him and in his own life, and his thoughts would not let him alone. They kept coming back, to trouble and haunt him, until he set them down on paper for peace.

Friends who heard parts read aloud urged him to publish, thinking the thoughts might help others who felt the same way. The book is thus a set of meditations on conduct, faith, and the inner life, in a plain, earnest voice. Mapes was a playwright; here he drops the stage and speaks in his own person. It is a period piece of American devotional thought.
heart-of-the-west:
O Henry's Heart of the West gathers nineteen Texas stories, opening with Hearts and Crosses, where Baldy Woods reaches for a bottle he usually gets. The contents promise the ransom of Mack, Telemachus the friend, the handbook of Hymen, and the Pimienta pancakes. Ranch hands, rangers, and small-town schemers fill the range.

The princess and the puma, a call loan, Christmas by injunction, and the reformation of Calliope close the table. In the middle, Collins bids Ranse Truesdell shake the hand of a cowpuncher who is plumb white and none better in any camp. O Henry's twist endings and cowboy dialect made these tales magazine gold; the best of them also carry genuine tenderness.
historic-girls-stories-of-girls-who-have:
Elbridge S Brooks wrote Historic Girls to remind his progressive age that girls of the distant past equaled men in valor, shrewdness, and ability. His contents span Zenobia of Palmyra, Helena of Britain, Pulcheria of Constantinople, Clotilda of Burgundy, Woo of the Yellow River, Edith of Scotland, and Jacqueline of Holland. Saint Theresa, Elizabeth Tudor, and Christina of Sweden close the march.

Jacqueline, the little Lady of Holland whom her father called Dame Jacob for her boyish ways, shows Brooks's method: documented youth retold as adventure. The preface argues history to the girls and boys of today directly. The book, a companion to his Historic Boys, preserves a nineteenth-century idea of heroines, royal, martial, and devout.
how-to-become-like-christ:
Marcus Dods gathered these sermons under the title How to Become Like Christ. The lead sermon takes its text from Paul's second letter to Corinth. We are changed into the same image, from glory to glory, it reads. Dods grants that all admit likeness to Christ is the greatest attainment.

Yet most men apologize for not being like him, Dods charges. Companion sermons treat the Transfiguration and indiscreet importunity. Naaman's cure and the lame man at the temple gate follow. Peter's honest delight at the Transfiguration is praised as unforced. Church readers get plain, searching counsel on character, the one thing carried out of life.
how-to-sing-meine-gesangskunst:
Lilli Lehmann, the great German singer, wrote this manual on the art of song. Richard Aldrich translated it from the German for Macmillan in 1902. Lehmann states her purpose and her title to write at the start. Sections then take up practice, breath, and the singer's body in order.

Breath is her ruling theme, handled with a physiologist's care. The tremolo, she argues, comes when breath strikes the cords too directly. Driven first against the chest by the belly's pressure, it should reach the cords in small, governed streams. Equalizing the voice follows from that control. Singers got a master's hard-won method, set down without mystery.
in-luck-at-last:
Walter Besant opened In Luck at Last with praise for second-hand bookselling as a way of life. The narrator weighs a modest shop against great collectors' stores and street carts. That trade frames a London tale of love and fortune. Iris and her grandfather talk of marriage in the middle chapters.

The old man compares a good marriage to binding two scarce volumes into one. Iris objects that they should not be second-hand volumes. Mr. Arbuthnot learns why the family is glad at her choice. Besant mixes book trade lore with a courtship plot.
indian-unrest:
Valentine Chirol wrote Indian Unrest as a reprint, revised and enlarged, from The Times, issued in London in 1910. Sir Alfred Lyall wrote the introduction, and Chirol dedicated the book to Viscount Morley. A general survey opens the account. Swaraj on the platform and in the press follows.

Hindu revival, Bengal's partition storm, and the Punjab fill the middle. Native state rulers answer the Viceroy with plans against disaffection, Chirol reports. Congress, depressed castes, and western education close the survey. The book is a Times man's warning about rising Indian nationalism in his time.
italy-at-war-and-the-allies-in-the-west:
E. Alexander Powell, a New York World correspondent, reported Italy at War and the Allies in the West in 1919. The book is volume four of The War on All Fronts. A caption tells how Italy's king refused the Prince of Wales a shelled trench. I want no historic incidents here, the king said dryly.

British armies land at Rouen and march through the square where Joan of Arc was burned, Powell notes. Napoleon waited at Pont des Briques to invade England, where Britain's great base camp now stands. Powell links such ironies across the fronts. His reportage covers Italy and the West together.
james-otis-the-pre-revolutionist:
John Clark Ridpath wrote this short biography of James Otis, the Boston lawyer he calls the pre-revolutionist, meaning a man who fired the Revolution before it began. Otis rose fast at the Massachusetts bar after moving to Boston in 1750. Ridpath tells of a young advocate who refused doubtful cases and once exposed his own client's fraud in open court, winning the judge's praise.

Otis became famous opposing writs of assistance, the general search warrants British officers used in the colonies. Ridpath presents his speeches as the first clear argument that Parliament's acts could bind no free people unjustly. The life is admiring and brief, written to give young Americans a hero of words rather than battles.
jasmin-barber-poet-philanthropist:
Samuel Smiles chose an unlikely hero for Jasmin: a barber of Agen in southern France who shaved customers by day and wrote Occitan poetry behind his shop. Sainte-Beuve's praise opens the book: ten poets of Jasmin's influence, he said, would spare France its revolutions. Smiles traces Jasmin's poor childhood, his detested schooling, and grandfather Boe's death.

Jasmin taught himself, recited in his little back shop, and won honors in Toulouse and Paris while keeping his barber's trade and giving much to the poor. Smiles uses him to prove self-culture possible at any station. The biography also preserves a vanished provincial France of fairs, vintages, and spinning women.
jennie-baxter-journalist:
Robert Barr wrote Jennie Baxter, Journalist, entered in Canada in 1899. Contents follow Jennie from her toilette to conferences with two editors. She interviews a frightened official and learns of a princess's diamonds. A great detective helps her solve the diamond mystery in chapter six.

A princess lends Jennie her own maid Gretlich in Vienna in a warm scene. It is not every friend I would lend her to, she says. Jennie insists she cannot rob her of rooms and maid both. Government secrets, a terrible night journey, and eluded proposals fill Barr's brisk tale of a woman reporter.
kindred-of-the-dust:
Kindred of the Dust is a novel by Peter B. Kyne, published in 1920 and illustrated by Dean Cornwell. Kyne dedicates it to Irene, his foster-sister from childhood. The story opens at The Dreamerie, on Tyee Head. Hector McKaye, the Laird, owns the Tyee Lumber Company and most of the coast town's life.

Hector plans greatness for his son Donald, recently out of the navy. A caption quotes Donald's cry to his father: 'I can't give her up.' The woman in question is Nan Brent. The Laird holds her beneath his house's idea of a match, as the title hints. Kyne sets a father's pride against a son's love in a lumber town. It is a romance of class, money, and the Northwest woods.
lady-mary-and-her-nurse-or-a-peep-into-t:
Catharine Parr Traill wrote Lady Mary and Her Nurse as a peep into the Canadian forest. A nurse tells young Lady Mary about the woods around her. Each chapter mixes story with natural history.

The first chapter treats flying squirrels, wolves, and wild rice. Later ones cover sleighing, fur caps, otters, and snowstorms. Indian names and animal habits get careful attention. Traill knew Canadian settler life from her own experience. Her book teaches children about a new land through warm, direct talk. Questions from a child drive each lesson forward naturally. Traill answers with facts drawn from woods she knew well.
lady-merton-colonist:
Mrs. Humphry Ward published Lady Merton, Colonist in 1910. Albert Sterner drew its frontispiece. A foreword explains a lake that appears late in the story.

Ward calls that place Lake Elizabeth, a lake of dream. A real lake in the northern Rockies inspired it. Her friend Mrs. Schäffer had found that lake two years earlier. The novel sends its English heroine into Canada's mountain west. Landscape, travel, and new colonial life shape her change across the story. The Rockies dominate the frontispiece scene described in the foreword. Ward treats the landscape as a force that remakes her travelers.
lanier-of-the-cavalry-or-a-week-s-arrest:
Charles King wrote Lanier of the Cavalry, a military novel of a week's arrest. King was known for stories of army life in the American West. This edition was prepared from page images held by the Internet Archive.

The title promises both romance and discipline trouble. A cavalry officer under arrest faces disgrace and must clear his name. King builds the plot from garrison life, duty, and honor. Suspense comes from the narrow time frame of one week. Readers of his many army tales will find his usual brisk, loyal tone. King's own army service on the frontier informs such tales. Honor under arrest is a theme he returned to often.
lavengro-the-scholar-the-gypsy-the-pries:
George Borrow called his book Lavengro: The Scholar, the Gypsy, the Priest. Macmillan issued this illustrated edition in 1900, with an introduction by Augustine Birrell. The work first appeared in Macmillan's Standard Novels in 1896.

Lavengro mixes Borrow's own life with fiction and travel. He meets gypsies, scholars, and priests across England and Wales. Languages fascinate him, and Romany speech fills many scenes. Birrell's introduction praises Borrow's strange, forceful character. The book remains a singular blend of memoir, road tale, and linguistic adventure. Gypsy lore and word origins interrupt the road story often. Borrow treats language itself as a form of adventure.
lays-from-the-west:
M. A. Nicholl, writing as Stella, published her poems as Lays from the West. She dedicated the book with gratitude to Mrs. T. Spottiswood Ash of Bellaghy, Ireland. An opening poem gives her songs to a guiding spirit.

The spirit calls the poems tiny germs and seeds of flowers. They should root among the coming hours, it says. Many poems look back to Ireland from the northwest of Canada. One line vows not to forget old Ireland, however fair the new land. Emigrant longing shapes the whole collection. Irish places are named with homesick precision throughout. The west of the title is a new home, never a replacement.
lectures-of-col-r-g-ingersoll-latest:
Robert Green Ingersoll's latest lectures fill this collection of his speeches. Titles include Thomas Paine, Orthodoxy, Blasphemy, and Intellectual Development. A lecture on liberty of man, woman, and child stands near the front.

Ingersoll was America's most famous freethought orator of his century. He attacked religious dogma with humor, logic, and warm feeling. Letters on suicide, Chinese religion, and the Bible also appear. Reviews of his reviewers close the volume in fighting style. The book shows Ingersoll's platform range at full stretch. Ingersoll filled halls that few lecturers could match. Print spread his voice far beyond the platform circuit.
legends-of-the-northwest:
Hanford Lennox Gordon wrote Legends of the Northwest in verse. A prelude on the Mississippi opens the book. The Feast of the Virgins, a Dakota legend, follows.

Winona and the Legend of the Falls also come from Dakota tradition. The Sea-Gull retells an Ojibwa legend of Lake Superior's Pictured Rocks. Gordon studied Native languages, customs, and traditions for years, he says. He shaped that study into long narrative poems. His book preserves settler-era versions of Indigenous tales from the upper Mississippi country. Minnetonka closes the contents on a lyrical note. Gordon hoped his verse would preserve tales already fading then.
lost-in-the-backwoods-a-tale-of-the-cana:
Lost in the Backwoods is a tale of the Canadian forest by Catharine Parr Traill. It first won young readers under the title The Canadian Crusoes. This edition, issued at Edinburgh in 1882, gave it the new name. The story opens in a deep, fertile valley between Rice Lake and Lake Ontario.

Young settlers are lost in the woods and must live by their wits. The tale teaches woodcraft, courage, and trust through their trials. Traill knew pioneer life from her own years as a settler in Canada. Her book mixes real forest knowledge with a gripping survival story. It became a classic of Canadian writing for the young.
love-s-labour-s-lost:
Love's Labour's Lost is a comedy by William Shakespeare, kept here in old spelling. The editor's notes explain the odd letters, like u and v exchanged. Printers of Shakespeare's day packed type into blocks and made do with shortages. So this text shows the play much as early readers saw it.

The King of Navarre and three lords swear off women for three years of study. At once the Princess of France arrives with three witty ladies. Oaths break, love poems fly, and mockery fills the park. A clown, a bragging Spaniard, and a schoolmaster add broad fun. Then sudden news of death ends the laughter on a sober note.
maurice-guest:
Henry Handel Richardson set Maurice Guest among music students in Leipzig. Part one opens at noon outside the new Gewandhaus hall. A crowd pours out from a public rehearsal into the sun.

Young Maurice Guest stands back and watches a scene new to him. Players thread through the crowd with violin cases in hand. Some fans wait at the back door for a famed Belgian violinist. Talk, heat, and keen youth fill the square as the tale begins. Talk in many tongues shows how wide the music world had grown. Guest must earn his place in that bright, stern crowd.
moby-hyphenation-list:
Grady Ward released this hyphenation resource into the public domain in January 2001. It documents the Moby Hyphenator II, a program for MSDOS systems. The package needs about three megabytes of free disk space. After unpacking, its vocabulary files sit in ordinary ASCII text.

The heart of the product is a hyphenation list, naming where each English word may break. A special character, ASCII 165, marks the break points and guides alphabetization. Words that should never be hyphenated are included anyway, for completeness. Typesetters and software builders used such lists to set justified text without breaking words wrongly.
moby-part-of-speech-list:
Grady Ward's Moby Part-of-Speech list tags English words with their grammatical roles. Ward released the database to the public domain in January 2001. This second edition added fifteen thousand new entries to the first. Thousands more were scrutinized for correctness and modernity, making it, he claims, the largest such list in the world.

Each entry joins a word or phrase to a code after a backslash delimiter. Symbols mark nouns, plurals, noun phrases, and verbs, with case significant throughout. Including phrases lets parsing programs tokenize in units larger than single words. Ward argues that this raises both the speed and accuracy of language software.
moby-pronunciation-list:
Grady Ward's Moby Pronunciator II tells computers how English words sound. He granted the documentation and database to the public domain in January 2001. The package needs about nine megabytes of disk space, the largest of his Moby sets. It bundles three files: a CMU dictionary list, a pronunciation list, and a phone set list.

Each entry pairs a word or phrase with an IPA-equivalent code written in ASCII symbols. The legend explains every sound by example: one mark sounds like the a in dab, another like the a in far. Spaces inside phrases become underbars. Speech researchers used such lists to build early talking software.
moby-thesaurus-list:
Grady Ward's Moby Thesaurus II is a machine-readable store of English synonyms. Ward placed it in the public domain in January 2001. This second edition added more than five thousand root words, passing thirty thousand. The synonyms and related terms grew past two and a half million.

Ward calls it the largest thesaurus data source available for commercial use. Each flat ASCII record starts with its root word, then lists related terms alphabetically. Accents are stripped, so etude loses its mark. A supplementary file reprints Roget's 1911 thesaurus as a model of category organization. Writers' software and word processors drew on this free data for years.
mr-standfast:
John Buchan published this Richard Hannay novel in 1919. Hannay is a British agent in the mold of the bold amateur hero. The book is dedicated to South African troops on the Western Front. Its parts use names drawn from Pilgrim's Progress, like the Wicket-Gate.

Hannay's chase spans the last months of peace and the war that followed. Hannay moves fast, chased by foes he also hunts. Contents promise air raids, a Picardy chateau, and an underground railway. Old friends from The Thirty-Nine Steps return. Buchan mixes spy craft, war, and faith into a tense chase across Britain and France.
myths-and-legends-of-california-and-the-:
Katharine Berry Judson compiled these Native tales of California and the Southwest. Judson had edited myth books on Alaska and the Northwest. A second, illustrated edition is used here. Her preface opens with a Zuni tale of the world's making.

The first fathers lived in four caves, each darker or lighter. They rose at last into the World of Knowing and Seeing. Judson praises the fine speech of the Pacific and desert tribes. Tales of creation, stars, and tricksters fill the book. She gathered them to save lore then fading fast, told with respect for the peoples who made them.
narrative-of-a-survey-of-the-intertropic:
Captain Phillip P. King surveyed Australia's north and west coasts from 1818 to 1822. His two volumes pair with an Admiralty atlas of charts. King was a fellow of the Royal Society and the Linnean Society. An appendix treats water science and natural history.

King's preface notes the swift growth of the Australian colonies. Every fact about that vast continent drew interest, he says. One fruit of the voyage was a post at Port Cockburn. It stood between Melville and Bathurst Islands on the north coast. The survey gave traders and sailors their first true charts of wild, little-known shores.
nasa-tm-19670001541-optical-astronomy-pa:
E. H. Wells, of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, wrote this executive summary, dated August 5, 1966. Numbered TM X-53496, it reports a feasibility study for the Apollo Applications Program. The question was whether an optical astronomy package could be adapted for Apollo missions, including work on the surface of the Moon.

The study looked at adapting the Goddard Experiment Package, built for the Orbiting Astronomical Observatory, to lunar surface missions. Wells considered a complete mission using typical astronomy experiments, not just the telescope hardware alone. The summary offers data to help NASA plan lunar surface astronomy missions and equipment. Growth options were weighed too, and the study judged five to six years realistic from project start to flight.
nasa-tm-19680012441-apollo-saturn-5-flig: Apollo and Saturn 5 flight readiness testing is the subject of this Kennedy Space Center era document. The catalog record describes procedures and equipment for the Apollo/Saturn 5 flight readiness test, the full rehearsal before launch. The hosted sample is an illegible scan of a chart-like page, with no readable text at all. Only the title and catalog facts can be stated, and the document's contents cannot be described.
nasa-tm-19680012870-instrumentation-and-:
C. D. Tackett, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this report in February 1968. It covers the instrumentation and flight of Astrobee 1500 flight 16.02 GT, a two-stage sounding rocket mission. A companion Goddard report presents the same flight's vibration data in detail.

The contents open with the rocket's general design and performance characteristics, then review the history of Astrobee flights. Flight 16.01 gets its own instrumentation and flight analysis. The heart of the report documents flight 16.02's instrument suite sensor by sensor. Temperature transducers and strain gauges watch the vehicle's structure. Solar aspect sensors and magnetic aspect sensors record its orientation, while a clamshell position indicator tracks the heat shield. An ogive transducer and a stable platform round out the package, together capturing how the rocket and its payload behaved in flight.
nasa-tm-19700008067-development-of-reali:
R. L. Kinsley of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this report in September 1969. It asks how sounding rocket parts should be shaken in ground tests before flight. Test levels that are too weak or too strong both cause trouble.

Staff in the Structural Dynamics Branch felt the test methods then in use could be improved. Kinsley reports an investigation into more realistic vibration levels for rocket subsystems. The study confirmed the branch's view that the methods needed change. Its aim was tests that match what parts really face in flight, without needless damage on the ground.
nasa-tm-19700015519-an-experimental-stud:
M. W. Pharo, L. R. Scott, H. G. Mayr, L. H. Brace, and H. A. Taylor Jr. of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in December 1969. It reports a hands-on study of ion chemistry and heat balance in the E and F regions above Wallops Island. Those regions are charged layers of the upper air over the Virginia coast.

Earlier studies, the authors note, often mixed ion readings from one flight with heat readings from another time or place. Their rocket flights on August 26, 1966, gathered the matching profiles nearly all at once. The set covers positive ion makeup plus electron concentration and temperature in the F region. Supporting flights the same day added nitrogen and sunlight measurements for comparison.
nasa-tm-19700020679-optimization-of-self:
Bernard J. Hamrock of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 lubrication conference in Cincinnati. It works out the best design for self-acting step thrust bearings. These bearings ride on a thin film of gas or oil and need no outside pressure supply.

Hamrock analyzes a step bearing of fixed width and rectangle shape. He gives its load capacity and stiffness in a standard series form. Load capacity is the weight the bearing can carry. Stiffness is how firmly it resists being pushed off center. His results let designers pick step sizes that carry the most load with the most stiffness.
nasa-tm-19700026342-mobile-quarantine-fa:
NASA issued this Apollo working paper, number 1146, on an altitude test of the mobile quarantine facility. The test ran in the Space Environment Simulation Laboratory. Crews returning from the Moon would stay in the facility while doctors checked them for Moon germs, so it had to work at altitude conditions.
